LAURENCE EDWARD DAYTON
Grand Master October 14, 1966 ~ October 13, 1967
In the forefront of these Proceedings, it is fitting and prop er that we
reflect upon that w hich has been accomplished by a soft-spoken, efficient and effective leader, the One Hundred-and-First Grand Master
of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons of
the State of California, and of the Lodges in our 50th State of Hawaii.
The measure of the man and the Mason which follows is necessarily
in the form of an affirmation, for he has already attained a permanent
place in our hearts and minds, carved, as it were, in the time-honored
tradition and with the same skill displayed for all ages by our ancient
operative brethren - his mark finely etched upon the trestleboard of the
Craft in this Grand Jurisdiction.
Laurence Edward Dayton was born on November 28, 1900, in College View, Nebraska; he was brought to California as an infant and
grew up in Sonoma County, where he attended public schools in
Sebastopol before entering the University of California at Berke ley; he
then worked ten years as a newspaper reporter and editor; and then he
gravitated toward his chosen profession by serving as a law clerk to
Earl Warren, then District Attorney of Alameda County. In 1932 he
was admitted to the California Bar and commenced what was to be a
quarter century of distinguished legal service as Trial Deputy and Assistant District Attorney in the District Attorney's office of Alameda County.
After retirement he resumed his legal career as Chief Assistant and then
as United States Attorney for Northern California. Following his second
"retirement" he became project director for the City of Oakland's project
to encourage sel(help community improvement programs at the neighborhood level.
His Masonic career is equally impressive. He was raised in Live Oak
Lodge No. 61 in Oakland on February 28, 1941. and was soon selected
to serve as an officer, advancing to Master in 1951. The following year
he was elected President of the East Bay Masters and Wardens Associaiton. And four years later he again advanced to the east, this time as the
Fourth Master of Northern California Research Lodge. From 1950 to
1962 he served this Grand Lodge as either a member or chairman of half
a dozen committees. And in October of 1963 he was elected to the office
of Junior Grand W arden , from which station he regula rly advanced to
that of Grand Master.
Brother Dayton and his wife, the former Marion Ahern, have two
married daughters, Laryon and Teryl. and seven grandchildren. four
boys and three girls. The brightest light from the Dayton hearth appears
dim when compared to the radiant glow of love and affection which encompasses this home and family.
LAURENCE E. DAYTON
Grand Master
October 14, 1966 - October 13. 1967

In addition, and concurrently, he actively participated in community

affairs, especially in those areas of civic responsibility which concern the
welfare of our youth. His personal involvement and commitment in this
area is reflected by membership and offices held in Dads' Clubs, on the
Governor's Advisory Committee on Children and Youth, and a fifteen
year tenure on the Alameda County Committee for Prevention of Juve nile
Delinquency.
As we conclude the details of this most impelling and manifold career.
it is all too apparent that for this man and Mason each task well done was
rewarded with the addition of still another more demanding and challenging assignment. And thus it was so twelve months ago when we
elected him to the highest office in Masoruy. On that occasion he bid
us join him in making the light of our M asonic teachings more clearly
visible - he asked that we strive to "increase our candlepower." With
great care and equal skill during this past year he symbolically filled
the bowl. trimmed and adjusted the wick, polished the chimney and
ignited the lamp - the constructive details of which are visible throughout this volume, specifically under the title "Grand Master's Message."

Devotional
Most Worshipful Grand Master and members of the Grand Lodge:
It is not always easy to give a subject for any address, much less this
one. Possibly this is so because the last time I tried a subject we had a
disastrous experience. My young assistant decided that we needed a
punch line on our outdoor bulletin board. rather than the usual names,
numbers and positions of the ecclesiastical team. So he put these words
in capital letters: "If you're tired of sin, come in!" This was fine, except
that following our first evening service, we found written in lipstick
across the bottom of the sign, "If you're not, dial 565.7585." This can
be catastrophic. The other time I had such an experience was in Santa
Maria, where I had the good fortune to be raised by Hesperian Lodge
No. 264. I gave my sermon theme to the caretaker to put on the bulletin
board. He put the subject out - "What Is Hell Like?" Then, seeing
there was a lot of empty space left. he very thoughtfully put the following - "Have you heard our new Minister yet?"
I want to indicate to our beloved Grand Master, Most Worshipful
Laurence E. Dayton, what a particulMly gracious privilege it has been

for me to serve him, and you. in Grand Lodge as Grand Chaplain. As
always. much more is gained by the individual in Mason.ry t.ha n he can
possibly give, and this year w ill go down as one of the highlights of my
life. The opportunity of working with Larry and the other members of
the Grand Lodge team has served to make lasting friendships . and t.o
point up the really outstanding work Masonry is accomplis~ing ~n .ca~1fornia and H awa ii. To those Lodges who have been so gracious m mv1ting me to their various funct ions and activi ties, I express my since~e

experience, I a m eternally grateful. My appreciation , also, to the tremendous Grand Lodge office staff - with Brother Ed Siems and the

Washington Irving, in that delightful short story. tells how Rip Van
Winkle spent a night out with the boys on the mountain, which lengthened into many nights. He started to sleep it off under the reign of Kin~
George the Third, and woke up when George Washington was President. In other words. Brethren, he slept through a revolution! Now. except in the case of fiction, it might be delightful to sleep thro~gh a revo.lution. But we simply cannot afford to do that. For we are m revolution
today-it is all around us. Are we sleeping throug h it. or do these tensionfilled hours ca use us to be all the more aware? You and I are ca lled upon
to live in one of the most disruptive periods in human history. This is
nothing new, for it happens in every age and throughout his tory. It is
even said that as Ada m a nd Eve were leaving the Garden of Eden. Ada m
said tenderly to her, " My dear. don't worry, we are simply going through
a period of transition ." We live in a time of cataclysmic change, ~nd
the dangers are not all in the realm of maps and politics. There 1s .a
change in thoughts, in ideas, in philosophies of life. Y et some people m
our times, some in positions of real leadership, seem oblivious to what
is happening around them. We exist in a world be~et by .revolut~?n· bemoaned by philosopher s and bewildered by the God 1s dea d .theologians. All about us we find the cynic - a ma n who knows the price of
everything . and the value of nothing. It is important for us to remember
this. If you think this day is not destructive, let me cite a few facts. (No
address. you know, is worth its salt w ithout sta tistics to sleep by.)
One out of every three marriages in America today ends in divorce.
One million illegitimate children are sired annually, and a hundred thousand girls enter the faithless army of prostitute.~. Th.ere ~re more ~a~­
keeps than there are barristers. (I u~; the w~rd ba.r nster .beca~se 1t 1s
good alliteration. I could have said lawyer . and 1f you lived m England it would be "solicitor" , but I know better than to call a lawyer a
soli~itor in this country.) There are more cocktail waitresses in our

country than co-eds. The crime ra te increased 90 percent last year while
the population increased 19%. There's a crime every 22 seconds; a rape
every 52 minutes. There's a murder every forty minutes. and 80 % of
crime is connected with alcohol. Five percent of the people you live and
work with will become alcoholics. Brethren. we spend more on toys than
textbooks; more on cat food than in religious education in your Church or
Synagogue. We spent more on bubble gum than missions. and the bartenders in California are making more money per capita than a re the
professors in California's State Colleges. These are but a few things
that prove we are in a revolutionar y day. And what happens to the
person, the man, the individual?
Well, he lives the "Elegy Of The Organizatio n Man" -And wow
he lived. as wow he died : going whop to the office, and blooie, home to
sleep; and zip got married, and bang had children, and oof, got fired .
Zowie did he live and zowie did he die. You and I rub elbows every day
with people like this, and it would seem as we convene this Grand Lodge
that we, who ha ve the privilege of all that is within a Master Mason, need
to understand the reason for our existence and why we have these rich
blessings of home and heritage. It would be well if we did a little more
about inculcating those basic tenets, those strengthenin g things. those
basic fundamenta l truths of honesty, integrity and patriotism, into our
lives and into lives of those with whom we come in contact. Because we
are living on too small a scale, we are inadequatel y designing our lives
in a day when so many have so little faith. We live in a world of locks
and burglar alarms, of pistols and detectives, of cedar-lined closets and
lead-lined hearts·. Caught up in the frantic pace we breathe faster . run
harder, buy more, crack up oftener and bury quicker than any nation
on earth. We take barbituates to sleep on, caffeine to wa ke up on, and
tranquilizers through the day to calm our shot nerves. It isn't a nice
picture, but it's true. We're in an age of mistakes. If you would list some
mistakes of mankind, you would include these:
(I) The delusion that individual advancemen t is made by crushing
others. That's America, isn't it? ( 2) The tendency to worry about things
that cannot be changed. We do that, too. ( 3) Insisting that a thing is
impossible because we cannot accomplish it. ( 4) Refusing to set aside
trivial preferences. ( 5) Neglecting developmen t and refinement of mind
by not reading and studying. ( 6) Attempting to compel others to live
as we do. Well. you may say, these are true, this is our life. But let me
remind you that the one who wrote this list was Cicero, 2.000 years ago.
These mistakes are as contempora ry as this very breathing moment.
That was something old. Here is something new - the characterization of America today : ( 1 ) The so-called beatnik, who makes out of
his pad a piece where nonconform ists of every order can hold forth. and
where angry young men and women can engage in the dangerous pastime of flirting with freedom without any responsibili ty. ( 2) The neon

sign. symbol of our haste to get nowhere. Here is the mad dash in every
direction, up and down, in and out. more colors than Carter's got pills.
the flashing ever-changing colors representative of our flashing. everchanging moods. ( 3) The can opener. symbol of our inordinate worship
of gadgets and our open-mouthed wonder as we bow at the altar of
materialism in a machine-conscious age. ( 4) You've guessed it, the
Aspirin bottle. the symbol of America's monumental headache. We are
so fettered with all the panaceas of prosperity that it is the man who has
the most medicine bottles on his bathroom shelf that has achieved the
dubious distinction of "having arrived." Somewhere along the line we
have learned to care about the wrong things, about self and custom,
about prestige and power and the proven. As we care about the wrong
things. we tend to give first-rate loyalties to second-rate causes and we
emphasize the wrong things. When you came down the hall of your
motel this morning on your way to Grand Lodge, you saw on many a
door a little sign that characterizes much of America's attitude todaya little sign with three words, "Do not disturb." We don' t want to be
disturbed. We like being chaplains of the status-quo. We like it just
the way it is, so don't bother us. for we get ulcers by mountain climbing
over molehills.
Brethren, I submit to you that as M asons we ought to be realizing
what we are, and by God's grace what we can become. If we know what
we are, we realize how much is lacking, and how tremendous life can be
through His help. Tear up the sign that asks not to be disturbed, and
instead pray, "God, let me be aware."
There is a poem called, "God, Give Us Men." I quote only the first
line - "God, give us men, a time like this demands strong minds, great
hearts, true faith and ready hands." I want to bring these demands to
your attention as we remember our brethren who now comprise that
Celestial Grand Lodge above, where the Supreme Grand Master forever presides.
( 1 ) A time like this demands strong minds, minds that know what
duty is, minds that understand the meaning of responsibility. Infantilism
is the inability to free ourselves from emotional impulses. One said, "Men
are four - He who knows not, and knows not that he knows not, is a
fool - shun him; He who knows not, but knows that he knows not, is
simple - teach him; He who knows . and knows not that he knows is
asleep - wake him; He who knows, and knows that he knows, is wise follow him." A strong mind is not a closed mind. It is a mind able to
comprehend, to sort out the chaff, to take that which is right, to keep
that which is important, and give strength, courage and conviction to do
the task we have as Masons in the days ahead. Keep a strong mind, my
brother.
( 2) A time like this demands great heart. You will remember that
little ditty that swept the land some time ago - "You gotta have heart!"

I think you do. Here is an example of greatness of heart. Henry Hudson.
that intrepid explorer, was cast adrift on June 24, 1611, on the great bay
that was afterward to bear his name. He had sailed into what his crew
thought was another ocean. They desired him to tum back. but he would
not. The crew mutinied, and put Hudson and his small son, and two of
his officers. John King and Philip Staffe. into a small dinghy and thrust
them from the side of the galleon. Then they sailed away. and all the
little group could see was sun and sky and water. After the first emotional reaction subsided, Hudson's biographer has him say. "Well, I seek
it still, my great adventure and my guiding star. For look you. friends.
our voyage is not done. We hold by hope as long as life endures. So
point her up. John King, nor'west by north. We'll keep the honor of a
certain aim, amid the perils of uncertain days, and sail ahead and leave
the rest to God." Isn't that tremendous? That is great heart! How's your
heart?
( 3) A time like this demands true faith. Perhaps you can call it
dedication. The word is overused, and doesn't mean what it once did.
Here is a man who goes to the office on time, takes advantage of every
coffee break and retirement and pension program, goes home on time
and takes nothing of his job with him. Simply because he is doing what
he is paid for, we call him " dedicated." He is not! Dedication is reserved
for those who come early and stay late; take the time to do the job, not
counting the minutes and time- docks; and whose life is in the work.
Dedication is what you find in the Lodges of Masons who come early
and stay late, who do the task whether their names are up in lights or
not, who live outside the Lodge those precepts inculcated therein. This
is what we need in this day. Maybe you would call it faith. Have you
been in New York City? Even Los Angeles would look good after New
York. When I come up out of a subway there. the subway breathes a
sigh of relief. One particular cold, drizzly Friday afternoon the people
were pouring out of office buildings to the subways. intent on getting
home. They didn't care about anybody else and were bumping, shoving.
pushing their way through the streets as they do through life. In the
midst of this maelstrom, at a little table near the subway entrance. two
young Communist youths were selling copies of the "Daily Worker."
They had a little sign, it was almost obliterated because the rain had
gotten to it, but you could still make out the words. "We are tired, we
are cold. we are hungry. but we are winning the world." Are they.
Brethren? Perhaps no one will ask you to sell copies of the California
Freemason out in the cold and wet of your town , but you get the picture.
Are they right? Have you ever been cold, or tired or hungry because you
were behind a cause you thought would win the world? Perhaps another
picture will illustrate. Two young men walk up the street. One of them
faints, and is carried into a drugstore. The druggist says to one, "This
lad has nothing wrong with him, except that he has not eaten for several

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

11

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

days. H e is hungry. You are dressed neatly. Don't you have enough
money for food?" The young man says, "Sir, we belong to the Young
Communist League. We have to get a paper out, a nd we pay for the
ink, the paper and rental of the press out o f our pockets, a nd we are
broke. You see . sir, we have to get the message out!'' He had to get his
message out. How long has it been since you tried to get the message
of Masonry, of America, out to your community? Better get with it,
where the action is, because we do have a message to get out.
( 4) A time like this demands read y hands. Hands that mean something. Hands are important. Masonry knows what it is to build. F irst
you dream it and have visions of it. Then you put those dreams on paper.
After that comes the strong foundation and the cornerstone, and finally
the rising of the structure. You build it strong and sturdy and with the
beauty of King Solomon's Temple.
In Leicestershire, England. there is an inscription on an ancient
chapel: "In ye year 1653. when all things were throughout the whole
nation demolished or profaned. Sir Robert Shirley, Baronet, builded
this Church; whose singular praise it was to have done the best things
in the worst times. and to have hoped them in the most calamitous."
Brethren. this is for us - to do the best things in the worst time, and to
hope them in the most calamitous. When everyone else was knocking
it down, this man was building. When everything around you is being
knocked or torn down. are you building? Are we accentuating the positive and eliminating the negative? Masonry. a t least in part, exists to
build firm and strong when all else falls and wavers.
Don't say again. "I don't care." You do care! Never utter, "It doesn't
concern me." It does concern you! Aren't you tired of hearing. "I don' t
wan t to get involved. I'll stand aside while somebody gets knifed. or gets
his reputation ruined, because I don't want to get involved."? But we
are involved, aren't we? And it does concern us. Don't ever again say,
"It doesn't make any difference - the little, small part I play in the
Lodge; it doesn't make any difference whether I am there or not." It d oes
make a difference, because you are the difference.
A time like this - a time of revolution, of cataclysmic living. of tension-filled days - demands strong minds, great heart, true faith and
ready hands.
" The things that haven't been done before, are the tasks worthwhile today.
Are you one of the flock that follows , or one who will lead the
way?
Are you one of the timid souls that quails at the jeers of the mocking crew?
Or dare you, whether you win or fail. strike out for the goal that's
new?"

Vocal Sol<>--Necrology
Since its inception, our Grand Lodge of Masons in California has
paused during each Annual Communication to pay a deserved tribute
to those who have gone ahead of us. This Committee on Necrology is
honored to be the instrument of recognition to these Brethren-indeed
we could ask no greater honor! Unfortunately, I possess neither that
eloquence of diction, nor the necessary ability, to adequately express
the great loss to this Grand Lodge in the passing of those members who
were most dear to us. To say that their presence, their service, and their
inspiration to us, is an irreplaceable loss is to completely understate the
fact. Members of the Committee on Necrology voice the respects of this
Grand Lodge to certain of these beloved Brethren.
William Bryan M cKe sson. We pause for a moment in memory of
our departed Brother who was called from labor on March twenty-first
of this year at the age of seventy-one.
Brother McKesson was raised to the sublime degree of a Master
Mason on August 23. 1934, in Southland Lodge No. 618. He dimitted
in 1944 to join a new Lodge, San Marino No. 685, and in I 946 he became Worshipful Master of that Lodge, a nd in that year he began a
long period of useful service to the Grand Lodge of Masons in California, to wit: Jurisprudence Committee 1946. Grand Orator 1947,
Special Committee on Grand Lodge Ritual 1949. Co-Chairman, Constitution Month Observance Committee 1954-1955, Special Committee
on Juvenile Welfare 1957, and Commercialism Committee 1958. In addition to his excellent Masonic work, exemplified by the outstanding perfor mance of his. Masonic duties, he was active and successful in his
business and civic career.
A native of Kansas. he came to Colorado and graduated from Colorado College in 1917, after which he served his country as a soldier in
World War I. He ca me to California in 1919, graduated from U.S.C.
Law School and, after a period of private practice, entered the office of
the County Counsel. He was appointed to the Superior Court of Los
Angeles in 1944 but resigned to become a member of the C alifornia
Youth Authority.
He was reappointed to the Superior Court in 1947, and re-elected
in 1948 and 1954. In 1956 he was appointed D istrict A ttorney of Los
Angeles County, retiring from that position at the end of his second
term in 1961.
It is with pleasure that we review the splendid works of our departed
Brother, and we rejoice that he could so ably bring credit and honor to
our ancient and honorable fra ternity.
His loyal devotion will be an inspiration to all of us, that we may
ca rry on with the Masonic and civic path that he has laid out for us,
thereby extending the light of our great country and of our honorable
fraternity throughout the whole world.

Thus we honor the memory of our Brother, William Bryan McKesson.
Maurice B . Ross. To be given the privilege to say a few words at
this time, paying tribute to the memory of a Brother who has contributed
much to both M asonry and the community as a whole. is indeed an honor.
Brother Maurice B. Ross, an active member of the Grand Lodge
Correspondence Committee, was born at Morris, Minnesota, on April
19, 1901, and resided in San Diego, California, for the past sixty-three
years. I am sure that it was a shock to all who knew him when they heard
the sad news of his passing on March 25, 1967. Funeral services were
conducted in the San Diego Scottish Rite Memorial Temple on W ednesday, March 29. 1967, with San Diego Lodge No. 35 officiating.
Brother Ross was a veteran San Diego educator who had been active
in many fraternal. cultural and community organizations. From 1936 to
1943, he was assistant to the Superintendent of the San Diego City
Schools. and from 1938 to 1943 he also served as S ecretary to the Board
of Education. In 1965 he retired from the position as Principal of Sherman Elementary School after serving for twenty-three years.
Brother Ross was initiated and entered as an apprentice Mason in
San Diego Lodge No. 35 on September 12. 1934. passed to the degree
of Fellow Craft on September 28, 1934, and raised to the sublime degree of Master Mason on November 8, 1934. In 1948 he served as
Worshipful Master of his Lodge.
He joined the Scottish Rite Bodies in September, 1936, and was
honored by being coroneted a Thirty-Third Degree Mason on May 26,
1954, at which time he was also serving as Senior Deacon of Southern
California Research Lodge. He also held the distinction of being a member of Commandery No. 25, Knights Templar, San Diego Council;
Royal and Select Masters, San Diego Chapter; Royal Arch Masons;
Imperial Valley Scottish Rite Club; Red Cross of Constantine; Al Bahr
Shrine; Beachcomber Shrine Club and an Honorary Member of the
DeMolay Legion of Honor.
In addition to his Masonic activities, Brother Ross was active in
the San Diego Kiwanis Club, La Jolla Museum of Art, Fine Arts Society.
San Diego Symphony Association and the Globe 400. He served also
on the Board of Directors for the San Diego and State Campfire Girls.
It is evident that with a record such as this, Brother Ross was indeed
a very capable and highly respected man. One who was more than ready
to give of his time and self for the ideals of our fraternal order and for
the betterment of all mankind. His presence among us will be sorely
missed, and I am sure never forgotten.
Rene Canonica. In honoring the memory of those who have gone
ahead, we should not forget Brother Rene Canonica who had a distinguished career in our order.
Brother Canonica, a native of Switzerland, came to California in
1927. He set up his own painting and decorating business shortly there-

after and in 1937 he petitioned La Parfaite Union Lodge No. I 7 for
the degrees of Masonry and was elected. He was initiated in July. 1937,
passed in August and received his Master Mason Degree in November
of the year. Shortly afterward he was appointed to the officer line and
became the Master of La Parfaite Union Lodge for 1946. The following
year he became Inspector for the I 13th Masonic D istrict which he served
with distinction for four years.
He was a member of California Bodies, Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite; Islam Temple of the Shrine; Swiss Societies, and served on
many of the committees of the Grand Lodge.
On January 1. 1967, he suddenly and unexpectedly departed this
life of a heart attack at the age of 62 years. H e is survived by his wife,
a son and a daughter. We have lost a true, devoted and loyal Brother
in the death of Rene Canonica.
In addition to the Brethren named by our Committee members, this
Grand Lodge has lost 441 members. Three hundred eight Lodges suffered losses. Of these 205 Lodges lost one member, 78 lost two members,
21 lost three members, and three lost four members. One Lodge, VeritasJonathan No. 545, lost five Past Masters. Others, known to many of
us. were:
Carroll Trefts, Past Master of Yerba Buena Lodge No. 403, a native
of Stanislaus County. Brother T refts served on the Oakland Board of
Education and the Alameda County Grand Jury. H e passed away at
age 66 - a severe loss to all of us.
Leonel Panosh, Pas t Master of S. W . Hackett Lodge No. 574. veteran
San D iego Masonic leader, Secretary of his Lodge for twenty-three
years. a Thirty-':fhird D egree Mason - an internationally known coin
collector and certainly one of the most beloved men in all of Southern
California. We shall miss him very much.
Gordon Fergus Black, Past Master of Riverside Lodge No. 635.
Gordon moved to the Bay Area in 1942 and there was, there is. no
more dedicated Mason among us. Honored with the Th irty~Third
Degree, he never seemed to tire in his endless Masonic work. All Masons
in this Grand Lodge suffered an irreparable loss when Gordon Black
was called to his rest at 59 years of age.
Edward L. True, a 66 year member of Ophir Lodge No. 33, passed
away shortly before an article about this great and good Mason appeared
in the California Freemason. Ed T rue was ninety years of age. At a
recent Lodge function, 133 were present to honor him. H e was truly
one of California's great pioneer Masons.
George Robert Brockmann, Past Master and one of the founders
of Golden West Lodge No. 455. He served as its Secretary for forty-two
consecutive years. H e founded Mission Chapter, Order of D eMolay.
He organized Golden West Chapter of the Eastern Star. He was one
of the last surviving twelve founders of the Order of Sciots. H e was
truly an honored s on of Masonry.

Fred R.ay Pardee served as Master of Inglewood Lodge No. 421
in 1923. Appointed Inspector in 1926, he supervised all Masonic Lodges
in the Centinella Valley which included Hawthorne, El Segu ndo,
Hermosa Beach, Redondo Beach and Inglewood. He held this office
of Masonic Inspector until 1912. He received his fifty year Masonic
pin on May 4, 1966. During his Masonic career he served as an installing
officer in more than 100 installations. Fred Ray Pardee established a
record of fellowship and service equalled by few and surpassed by
none.
Harry H. Jacobson. Then, too, we lost Brother Harry H. Jacobson,
Past Master of Amity-Seal Rock Lodge No. 370. There was n o o ne
who was held in any higher regard than was Harry Jacobson. He was
completely devoted to the fraternity.
Arthur f. Kahn. As a testimony of the esteem in which he was held,
every elected Grand Lodge officer attended funeral services for our
beloved Arthur J. Kahn, former Assistant Grand Lecturer, who passed
away about a month ago. Art Kahn had given almost all of his adult
life to the craft of Masonry. He was considered to be the outstanding
Masonic ritualist in the State and to know him was to love him. The
Grand Lodge of Masons in California will never, never forget Art Kahn.
The list continues. There are many more for whom this Grand
Lodge can never sufficiently state its devotion and appreciation. These
Brethren were indeed the finest men who lived and had their being
between the snow capped mountains and the sounding sea.
Someone once said, "their story is not graven only on stone over
the native earth, but lives on, far away, without visible symbol, woven
into the stuff of other men's lives."
The human soul is God's highest creation; and from the border
line of light, where history begins, there comes to us the great question
of the ages; "If a man die, shall he live again?" For a Mason, of course,
the answer is yes! We know the spirit rises out of the grave - the
soul cannot be held by flesh alone.

"Beyond the sunset's crimson bars
Beyond the twilight and the stars,
Beyond the midnight and the dark
They have sailed into the dawn of tomorrow,
Where hearts shall find the end of sorrow
And love shall find its own"
And so, my Brethren all, we give you this Committee's words of
respect for our honored dead. I am sure these departed Brothers would
join me in suggesting we honor them by rededicating our lives anew
to the great principles of Masonry and, with the limited time left to
us, establish such a course of conduct that others will find us wort hy of
all imitation!
Then, and then only, have we truly paid the respect due these departed Brethren whom we have paused to honor here today.

During the course of the Annual Communication the Grand Master
called on various distinguished guests to address the members of Grand
Lodge. Each expressed his appreciation for the opportunity to discuss
Masonic subjects of interest. Their remarks were attentively received
and Grand Lodge responded to each with standing ovations.
Following the reception of the distinguished guests, Grand Master
Dayton presented to the Grand Secretary, on behalf of the Grand Lodge
of Japan, a beautifully engraved scroll designating his honorary membership in that Grand Jurisdiction. The scroll indicated the appreciation
of the Grand Lodge of Japan for services which Past Grand Master
Siems had performed through the years for them. Brother Siems requested Brother Kiyoshi Togasaki, Past Grand Master of Japan, to
convey his thanks to the Grand Lodge of Japan.
During the course of the Annual Communication Charles T. Macdonald, Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of the District of Columbia,
presented the History of the Grand Lodge F.A.A.M .. District of Columbia, 1811-1961, to the Grand Lodge of California. Grand Master Dayton
expressed the appreciation of the Grand Lodge for this thoughtful gift
and indicated that it would become a valued addition to the Library and
Museum in the California Masonic Memorial Temple.
An unusual gift was presented by Brother Kenneth W . Hinkle, Past
Master and Secretary of San Francisc~ Victory Lodge No. 360, in the
form of a beautiful. silver fringed apron which had been presented to
his grandfather, William Henry Hill, by Truckee Lodge No. 200 one
hundred years ago. On October 12, 1867, Brother Hill was appointed
Grand Chaplain of the Grand Lodge of California, one of his several
activities in his full Masonic career. The Grand Master gratefully accepted the gift on behalf of the Grand Lodge of California and indicated
it would be placed on display in our Museum.

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE
My Brethren, twelve months ago you entrusted to me the highest
office in Masonry. With the theme of striving to ··increase our candle
power." We then looked hopefully forward together and went our several ways.
Now we are again assembled in annual communication to recount
the experience and efforts of the intervening time, to measure what
progress we have made, and counsel together upon the many things
which bear upon the present and future well-being of Freemasonry in
California and Hawaii.
The hour has also arrived when I must, as my predecessors have
done, account to you for the administration of Grand Lodge affairs
under my direction and to offer for your judgment my acts and recommendations as Grand Master.

It has been a busy year for the officers and committees of Grand
Lodge. The itinerary attached to this message indicates the range and
geographical extent of Masonic events in which the Grand Master, or
others in his behalf, took part. These events took us to almost every
part of our vast jurisdiction and brought us in personal contact with
brethren the length and breadth of the state.
To grasp, in fraternal greeting. the hands of brethren who rarely,
if ever, meet an officer of the Grand Lodge and to share with them an
interval of Masonic fellowship was for me a richly rewarding part of
the year's experience. There was in the eagerness and warmth of their
response evidence that the occasions held a similar meaning for them.
Such occasions serve to draw us closer together and to promote a
more general understanding of Masonic relationships. They can not
help but create a more favorable climate and a richer soil in which our
programs may grow and flourish. I commend to my successors as ex ~
tensive a personal contact with the Craft as time and their particular
situations will allow.
We must look to the reports of the several committees to provide an
overview of activity in the various areas of our interest, and to these
reports as they are presented I invite your undivided and thoughtful
attention.
Many willing and competent hands contributed to the year's work
and this helped to make up for my own limitations. A spirit of harmony
and cooperation prevailed among the officers and committees of Grand
Lodge and their support has been both generous and unreserved. To
each of them I record here my deepest appreciation.
The unfortuante loss, by resignation, of our Deputy Grand Master,
which occurred early in the year, placed added duties upon other

22

PROCEEDIN GS OP THE

officers. Without exception , these additional duties were graciously
accepted and capably discharged .
The burden fell heaviest upon our Senior Grand Warden. who
was called upon to assume those functions which the Deputy Grand
Master normally performs in preparatio n for the new Grand Lodge
Year. In this , he again demonstra ted that dedication to the Craft and
great capacity for work with which we have become so familiar. No
words of thanks on my part can adequatel y express our gratitude.

SEVENTY- FIVE YEAR BUTTONS

It was my unique privilege to present two Seventy-F ive Year Buttons during the year. These constitute d the eighth and ninth such buttons to be presented in the history of our Grand Lodge.
The first presentati on was made on June 19, 1967, at South Gate
Temple, Los Angeles, in the presence of several hundred brethren,
relatives and friends to Brother Horace Scott Seaton, a member of
Charter Rock Lodge No. 410 in Berkeley.
Brother Seaton. whose career as an actor on the stage and screen
spanned a period of sixty-eigh t years, retired at the age of ninety-thr ee.
A letter from Governor Reagan and Resolution s from the California
Assembly and State Senate were read and presented to him in the
course of the ceremony.
Our Brother, Charles Howe Talmage, who will be one hundred
years old on October 24th of this year received his Seventy-F i:e Year
Button at the home of his niece, Mrs. Carl Van Steenberg en, m Long
Beach on the afternoon of August 30. 1967, in the presence of a house
full of brethren, friends and family members.
Brother Talmage was raised in Summit Lodge No. 170 of Fort
Wayne, Indiana. on January 22. 1892. He has been continuou sly a member of Carmelita Lodge No. 599 of Pasadena, since affiliating there in

COMMITT EE RELATION S

It takes a good many committees to carry on the work of Grand
Lodge in a jurisdictio n as large and far-flung as ours. In their varied
functions, they fall into several categories . There are those whose principal work takes place during or in connectio n with the Annual Communication; those whose duties. although performed througho ut the
year , are unrelated to any other; and, finally, those which have or should
develop areas of mutual interest and assistance .
Special attention was given during the year to this latter category.
For the purpose of promoting better acquainta nce among the chairmen.
familiarizing each with the work of the others, and exploring ways in
which they might be mutually helpful, I brought together on one occasion the Public Schools, Constituti on Observanc e, Masonic Education
and Public Informatio n Chairmen . A second group consisted of the
History, Library and Museum, Columbia Temple, Old Los Angeles Hall
and Cemeterie s Chairmen . These meetings proved beneficial in identifying areas of common interest on which cooperativ e action may be
developed . I comqiend to my successor the further pursuit of this idea
as giving promise of useful and constructi ve results.
MASONIC RESOURCE S

There are among the Craft in California many brethren with special
knowledg e and experience in particular fields of Grand Lodge activity,
but who, never having served as Master of a Lodge, are not members
of Grand Lodge and according ly are not eligible for appointme nt to
a Grand Lodge Committe e. They are neverthele ss willing to contribute
their talents. Instances frequently occur in which the services of such
brethren would be useful and would enhance the efforts of a particular
committee. These sources of competenc e and interes t are largely untapped. Their use will extend meaningfu l participati on more broadly
among the Craft and, by augmentin g the skilled personnel available to
them, add to the success of many committee programs. It should be the
policy of Grand Lodge to seek out and, wherever possible, enlist the aid
of these brethren in a consultan t or advisory capacity and I so recommend.

MASONIC COOPERAT ION

Our brethren find outlets for their individual interests and energies
through a number of organizati ons requiring Masonic affiliation as a
condition of membersh ip. All rest upon the same basic foundation , but
each has its own activities and program, and each provides one more
way in which M asons become divided.
Under such circumstan ces, it takes planned and adequate communicatio n to achieve the rapport and spirit of cooperatio n which will
enable us to make maximum use of our vast Masonic resources .
A constructi ve step in this direction was taken during the year when
the Scottish and York Rite Bodies were brought actively into the Public
Schools Week program through contacts with the Public Schools Committee. This served measurabl y to augment the Public Schools Week
program statewide . Those who initiated and carried out this cooperativ e
effort are to be warmly commende d.
There are many areas in which the basis for better communication
and more extensive cooperatio n may be developed , and I express the
hope that in the coming year substantia l further progress may be made
in this direction.
LOOSE LEAF MANUAL

A number of Committe es of Grand Lodge have from time to time
prepared for distributio n to the Lodges separate manuals of guidelines
relating to their particular spheres of activity.
It was felt that a collection of the several manuals in some permanent
form would be helpful to the Lodges and encourage their more extensive

25

use. After discussion over a period of months with various Grand Lodge
officers and committee chairmen, a plan was d eveloped to prepare in
looseleaf form and place in a permanen t binder for each Lodge, the
manuals currently available. The various document s have been made
as concise as their subject matter would permit and dated material has
been eliminated so that each manual should be good from year to year,
except for such additions or modifications as futur e experience might suggest.
Should other committee s develop ma terial suitable for a manual
it is contempla ted that it would be duplica ted and copies distributed
for insertion in the binders .
T~ese manuals are now in your hands and we hope the officers and
committees of each Lodge will find them valuable aids in carrying out
the programs and activities to which the several sections relate. Please
remember that the binder is the permanen t property of the Lodge to be
retained by it as a reference source as needed.
Further comments on this project are contained in the Grand Secretary's report, but I cannot close this portion of my message without
acknowled ging a nd commendi ng the efforts of those who have brought
the manual from concept to reality. In addition to the committee s inv~lved'. important contributi ons were made by the Grand Secretary and
his assistant, the Senior Grand Warden and the Grand Lecturer.
The section on a rrangemen ts for Grand Lodge Ceremonies is the
work of the Grand Lecturer in collaborat ion with the Senior Grand
W arden and the .Grand Secretary. This important feature of the manual
~ay not be applicable to every Lodge but with the continued increase
m requests for cornerston e ceremonie s it is likely to serve a more widespread purpose as time goes on.

DECISIONS

While a number of situations arose which called for the applicati.on
of established law, no questions of law came up during the year wh1c.h
were novel or required interpretations of an original nat~re. It was ~o~s1ble to resolve the problems involved without the formality of a dec1S1on.
Some pending matters are under study. the final determination~ of

TAX ASSESSMENTS

County assessors are presently under the mandate of state law
to apply a uniform percentage of market value in establis~ing the
assessed valuation of real property for tax purposes. In more mstances
than not, this results in assessment figures being revised upward.
There are indications that assessors do not all use the same measure
of market value, particularly with regard to single purpose structures
such as Masonic Halls. This can result in substantial inequities. A local
Lodge or Temple Association is, however, at a disadvantage in seeking
on its own a reasonable adjustment.
The increasing burden of property taxes falls heavily upen Lodge
Halls and is sometimes even a threat to solvency.
.
The interest in this problem is not theirs alone. We have a collective
interest and concern. There appears to be no ready solution but a
thoughtful review based on reliable data may indi~ate som.e .alleviating
course of action in which, as a Grand Lodge, we might partiapate.
I urge the incoming Grand Master to give consideration to a special
study in this field.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

LIBRARY AND MUSEUM

In the years I have served as an Officer of Grand Lodge, I have had
the pleasure of visiting the Libraries and Museums of a number of Grand
Lodges, including those in London, Edinburgh and Dublin. This has
been a s timulating experience. One is impressed with the quality and
extent of both the Libraries and the Masonic Museums in these other
jurisdictions and the great importance attached to them.
We take just pride in our beautiful Grand Lodge Temple but the
space available for our Library and Museum is meager indeed with the
result that these facilities suffer by comparison. It is the one feature of
our Temple which leaves much to be desired. All books available to us
cannot be accommodated and items of historical interest cannot be properly displayed. There is a real and present need for more adequate facilities and this need can only grow as time goes on.
I express the fervent hope that the Temple Board will explore and
in due course develop ways and means of providing library and museum
facilities commensurate with our needs and our status in the Masonic
world.
INDEX -

GRAND LODGE PROCEEDINGS

The 1940 report of the Committee on Masonic H istory called attention to the fact that Brother Mark A. Sawrie, a member of that Committee, was continuing the arduous task of indexing all of the Grand Lodge
Proceedings starting with Volume 1. The work covers every subject, with
proper cross references, and is quite complete up to the year 1953.
Toward the end of 1966 Brother Sawrie sent word to the Grand
Lodge Office that it was his desire to make the card index a vailable to
the Grand Lodge. When the files were picked up by the Grand Secretary,
Brother Sawrie included a number of special volumes which are now in
the Library. In addition to the card index, Brother Sawrie prepared six
loose leaf binders, duplicating cards which are in the index. These have
been most helpful to the Grand Secretary's Office for research purposes.
In his effort to have the work completed and kept current, the Grand
Secretary has prevailed upon the former Assistant Grand Secretary.
Brother Henry D. Oliphant, to undertake the work. It is estimated that
the job will be current by this time next year. When the work is finished,
it is anticipated that there will be in excess of 50,000 index cards used
in the project.
This labor of love on the part of Brother Sawrie, a most competent
Masonic historian, has resulted in a valued addition to the Grand Lodge
Office and Library. The index covers the multitude of matters which have
come before Grand Lodge since 1850 and the records of its actions
thereon. The Grand Lodge of California owes a great debt of gratitude
to Brother Sawrie.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
INTER-JURISDIC TION VISITS

It is our custom to be represented at the Annual Communicatio ns of
neighboring Grand Lodges. Accordingly, during the past year we were
represented by the Deputy Grand M aster at Nevada. the Senior Grand
Warden at Arizona and Idaho, the Junior Grand Warden at Oregon.
Washington and British Columbia, and the Assistant Grand Secretary
at Wyoming. The occasion for our attendance at Idaho was its centennial. Representation at Wyoming's Communication , as well as that
of Idaho's, has been only at indefinite intervals in the past. The Grand
Secretary represented us at the dedication of the new temple of Grande
Loge Nationale Francaise in Paris.
In addition, I had the pleasure of accepting the Grand Master's invitation to attend the Annual Communicatio n of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania , where Mrs. Dayton and I enjoyed the hospitality of a most
gracious host. It is a happy circumstance for us that the Grand Master
of Pennsylvania has found it possible to return the visit and to be our
guest during this session.
Another occasion of special importance was my visit on the evening
of May 6, 1967, to the Grand Master of Baja California. I was accompanied by some 200 of our California brethren. We were met at the
border by a large delegation, presented with a certificate of greeting and
a key to the city of Tijuana, and led by motorcycle escort to the Masonic
Temple where Fenex Lodge No. 10 of Baja Calafornia served as host.
We were welcomed by the Grand Master and brethren in the warmest
fraternal spirit and enjoyed an evening of international fellowship. There
was presented to me a diploma, hand decorated and printed upon sheepskin, which is on display in the Grand Master's office.
No words of mine can adequately describe this wonderful Masonic
experience with our brethren across the border, where we were happy
to learn that Freemasonry is growing and showing great vitality.
It is with personal pleasure that I welcome the Grand Master of Baja
California to our midst.
Twice during the year I enjoyed the distinction of formally receiving
a Grand Master of a sister jurisdiction in one of our Lodges.
On the 21st of January, 1967, the Most Worshipful S. Barry Casey.
Grand Master of Arizona, and I made a joint visit to Eel River Lodge
No. 147 at Fortuna, of which Brother Casey's nephew is an active
member.
On the evening of July 26, 1967, I visited jointly with the Most

EMPLOYMENT BUREAUS

Pursuant to a recommendation of the Board of Control and after a
detailed review of the history and experience of the Masonic Employment Bureaus. I issued under date of March 8, 1967. a directive that
all Employment Bureaus be discontinued as of June 30, 1967.
This was not an easy decision to make. The Bureaus, established
originally to provide employment rather than monetary relief to distressed sojourning Masons and their families, served a most worthwhile
purpose over a long period of years. In the course of time their services
were extended to Masons of this jurisdiction as well as sojourners. Both
in concept and performance these Bureaus exemplified the finest traditions of our Craft and established an imposing record of service.
Placements by the Burea us reached a peak of 18,368 in 1941; the
cost per placement was $1.76 and some 25.000 jobs were being offered
by employers.
Since 1948, however, there has been a steady decline in the number
of placements and of positions offered by employers while the cost per
placement has increased sharply. This decline parallels the rapid growth
and extension of the free state employment service.
During this past fiscal year placements as well as the number of
applicants and positions offered through our Employment Bureaus were
down to their lowest level since the Bureaus were established. Cost per
placement in 1966 ranged from $53.70 in San Francisco to a high of
$261.37 in Long Beach.
A detailed review of the rise and decline of the Bureaus was sent
to the member Lodges of the Boards of Relief affected which showed
clearly that the need for the services of our bureaus has so lessened as
~ make their further maintenance no longer necessary or feasible . The
directive did not, nor was it intended to, preclude Boards of Relief from
making job referrals where available in lieu of financial assistance in
relief cases properly coming before them.
SOJOURNER REL!EP

It has been the policy of Freemasonry in this jurisdiction from the
formation of the Grand Lodge to relieve the distress of sojourning

34

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

Masons and their families. The responsibility for this service has rested
initially and primarily upon the individual Lodges with respect to sojourners in their midst.
In 1856 several Lodges in San Francisco organized among the~­
selves a board of relief as a means of coordinating this relief work. This
voluntary association proved efficient and Lodges in other communities
were encouraged to form similar boards. In the course of time many
Boards of Relief came into existence.
During the earlier years nearly all of the funds contributed by the
member Lodges were disbursed in the form of financial aid. the expens~s
of operating the Boards being nominal. But as time wei:t on the ratio
of overhead to relief increased. The Boards operated with httle or no
supervision from Grand Lodge until. following a study by a special committee. the Board of Control was created in 1926 to supervise and regulate their activities.
Under a system of reciprocity. authorized monetary relief currently
:idvanced by Boards of Relief to sojourning Masons is reimbursed by
the Lodges in the jurisdiction of their membership. The result is that the
principal expense of operating the twenty existing Boards is now a~­
:ninistrative. These are located in the more populous centers where it
may be assumed the great maj ority of sojourners reside. The burden of
supporting the Boards of Relief therefore falls mainly upon the Lodges
in metropolitan areas. Approximately one-half of our Lodges are members of Boards of Relief.
Prior to the legislation which created the Board of Control. Boards
of Relief were clearly voluntary associations operating autonomously.
The present status of the Boards is not as clear. Under the Code the
Board of Control may. with the approval of the Grand Master, create
new Boards of Relief and order a Lodge to become a member of the
Board nearest to it. However, this power appears -rarely if ever to have
been exercised. There are. as a result. instances in which one Lodge in
the same community belongs to a Board of Relief while another does
not. This has given rise to some dissatisfaction.
The status of the Boards is cast under further doubt by the fact
that their paid personnel are treated as employees of Grand Lodge for
the purpose of bringing them under the Grand Lodge Retirement Pia~
and Grand Lodge has made employer contributions to the plan ~n t~e1r
behalf amounting to $46,000 to date. This is done pursuant to legislation
enacted several years ago. And just last year Grand Lodge voted to
pay the employer's share of hospital insurance premiums for employees
of the Boards.
With rega rd to sojourner relief a number of questions occur to us.
What is the present nature and extent of the relief needs of sojourners?
How is the problem distributed geographically? What effect, present or

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

prospective, do such programs as social security. disability and unemployment insurance, and others have upon the problem? W hat are
the proper functions of a Boa rd of Relief? Are modifications in our
present system feasible or disirable? Should these functions be taken
over as a program of Grand Lodge? How should the financial burden be
distributed among the Lodges?
The answers to these and other related questions should eme rge from
a complete and detailed study of the entire subject conducted by a special committee. Since the study will necessarily involve matters of finance,
it seems appropriate to assign it to the proposed committee to evaluate

COVINA ADMISSION P OLICIES

From time to time the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes
is required to pass upon applications for admission to the Home at Covina
on behalf of children residing in California w hose Masonic connections
are in other jurisdictions. This has given rise to the question of whether
admission of such applicants should be limited to a fixed quota or percentage of the residents of the Home.
In his Annual Message Grand Master Breslauer made certain recommendations. one of which proposed that a quota of 20 % be adopted. The
resolution adopted in response to his recommendations did not contain
a specific quota limitation. However. the Board has felt that a limi tation
was implied and in consequence has considered itself obligated to deny
applications on behalf of some children who might otherwise qualify.
Clarification on this point is highly desirable. Making our facilities at
Covina available, in deserving cases, to children of non-California
Masons is consistent with our long standing concern for the welfare of
sojourners and their families .
Our Home at Covina is presently licensed to accommodate up to one
hundred and twenty residents. The present population of the Home is
little more than half that number and the experience of recent years indicates that we are not likely. in the foreseeable future, to approach the
maximum. Under these circumstances, it would not be depriving children
of California Masons of a place in the Home if present admission policies
were to be liberalized.

1875 the Jurisprudence Committee proposed a negative answer to the
question, "whether the petition for degrees of a person who has served
a term in the state prison for grand larceny, even though there were
doubts as to the justice of his punishment, should be received." The
committee's report was adopted. From 1875 to 1957 the test was simply
whether or not the applicant had "served a term in prison." If so, he
could not apply. In 1948 a resolution was presented to Grand Lodge
which provided specifically that anyone "convicted of a felony" could
not apply. This resolution was voted down. The effect was to make the
kind of punishment, not the nature of the crime, the determining factor.
The harshness of this rule, which made no allowance for subsequent
rehabilitation and upright conduct, engaged the attention of Grand
Master Paulsen in 1951 and in his message he recommended that the
rule adopted in 1875 be set aside and "that in the future where a Lodge
is called upon to determine whether or not an applicant is under the
tongue of good report that the question be determined by said Lodge on
the basis of all the facts that exist at the time of the presentation of the
application." The recommendation was strenuously opposed by the
Committee on Policy and General Purposes and was defeated.

RETIREMENT HOMES

In the last few years several Grand Lodges in the United States
have given their attention to projects involving the construction and
operation of retirement facilities for the use of members of their Lodges.
Some have undertaken such projects and at least one now has a facility
of this kind in operation.
The time seemed appropriate to explore this subject on behalf of
our Grand Lodge and for this purpose I appointed a special committee
with M ost Worshipful Ira W. Coburn, Past Grand Master, as Chairman.
The committee conducted an extensive statewide study over a period
of months and assembled a great amount of data which has been placed
on file in the Grand Lodge Office. On the basis of this study, the committee submitted a report addressed to the Grand Master in which it
concluded that there is not a present need in California for a Masonic
sponsored retirement home project. To quote from the report, "it found
there are large numbers of fiscally sound projects in existence which
cater to the most wide variety of tastes and preferences ."
The committee recognized that "Grand Lodge might as a matter of
policy find it desirable to develop retirement home facilities as an opportunity to provide additional service to its members ... even without
a demonstrable need," but pointed out that a feasibility study would
require the services of experts in this field at a cost ranging from three
to ten thousand dollars. The report further noted major problems to
be dealt with involving corporate organization, financing, tax status and
the extent to which the project would be subject to government regulation and control.
I want to take this opportunity to express our sincere appreciation
to the members of the committee for the outstanding service they have
rendered by bringing into focus in .a concise and objective manner the
many questions and problems inherent in a project of this nature and
magnitude.
Further action at this time does not appear to be advisable. The report
will appear in the annual Proceedings and the data accumulated by the
committee will be available should Grand Lodge wish to pursue the
subject further at some future date.
ELIGIBILITY OP APPLICANTS

At intervals over the past twenty years the question of the proper
effect of previous conviction of crime upon the eligibility of a man to

In 1952 it was decided that a person convicted of a felony was
ineligible although he served no time and had made complete restitution.
In 1953 a decision was made that a man was ineligible who received
a commuted sentence for felony and a presidential pardon.
In the same year, on recommendation of the Jurisprudence Committee,
it was held that an army deserter who had served one year in a military
prison was eligible on the ground that imprisonment for more than one
year was necessary to make a federal crime a felony.

In 1955 Grand Lodge gave its approval to a decision that the test
of eligibility was whether the convicted person served a term in a state
or federal prison. On this basis an applicant who had been convicted
when 18 or 19 years old of cattle theft and given a suspended sentence
was held to be eligible.
In 1957, taking note of the fact that there is no uniform designation
of felony offenses among the states and federal government, the Jurisprudence Committee sought to avoid confusion arising out of the word
"felony" a nd declared, "it is necessary to make clear that a person who
has pleaded guilty to or been convicted of a crime morally wrong in itself
is ineligible." To accomplish this, the committee proposed the following:
"Be it further resolved that a person who has pleaded guilty to or
been convicted in the courts of a crime which is morally wrong in itself
is not eligible to apply for the degrees of Masonry." This resolution was
adopted.

38

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

It thus appears that the action taken by Grand Lodge to solve one
problem has created others to take its place.

RECOMMENDATION No. 5

Is service of a term in prison still a test of eligibility? Is the punishment meted out, or the moral nature of the offense, now the controlling
question? Do we now bar from eligibility persons who commit misdemeanors, a number of which involve conduct moraUy wrong? What
effect, if any, should we giTe to judicial determinations that the offender
has rehabilitated himself?
I bring these matters before you once again because one of our Lodges
brought before me a question of eligibility based upon the following
facts: The prospective applicant when 18 years old (an adu lt for
prosecution purposes) pleaded guilty to cattle theft and was sentenced
to state prison. After serving his term he returned to his home community,
where for some thirty years he has continued to reside and has established himself as a law abiding reputable citizen. He is, in fact, now the
local Chief of Police. The court which sentenced him has issued a certificate of rehabilitation in the manner prescribed by law and on this
basis a governor's pardon has been issued.
Yet it appears that under our present law the Lodge cannot consider
his application for the degrees on several grounds, ( 1 ) the crime he
committed was a felony, ( 2) he served a term in state prison, and ( 3)
stealing is an offense morally wrong in itse1£. I felt bound to advise the
Lodge that it could not receive an application from this person.
No one with the interests, integrity and well being of our great
Fraternity at heart would recommend or even seriously entertain the
thought of lowering our standards of admission. No dedicated Mason
would favor any change of policy which would open the door to or be
construed as an invitation to men of evil character or ill repute, whether
such character is a matter of judicial record or otherwise.
However, we subscribe to the belief that a man may redeem himself
and become worthy of associating with us as Masons. for we leave the
door open to future restoration of a member who has been expelled for
conviction of the same crime for which we forever bar an original
applicant.

CODE REVISION

For nearly two years a special committee has been working on its
assignment:
1. To define the duties and responsibilities of the various committees
and boards of the Grand Lodge, including any necessary job descriptions, and
2. To clarify and correlate the language of the California Masonic
Code for the purpose of eliminating duplications, contradictions and
inconsistencies so that it may be easily read and understood by its users,
particularly those without legal training.
Each assignment involved a major task of far-reaching importance.
In the first year, the committee on which I was then privileged to
serve, concentrated its attention upon that part of its charge which had
to do with the structure and functions of committees. Substantial progress
was made but a finished product was not ready for your consideration
at the 1966 Communication.
During the past twelve months this committee, with some additions
to its membership, began work on the second part of its assignment and
in connection therewith reviewed the material it had drafted and
tentatively agreed upon with respect to committees and boards and
various changes were made in the earlier draft. The results have been
submitted to you in a series of resolutions dealing comprehensively with
the structure, titles and duties of committees.
These resolutions serve as a preview of what may be accomplished
to simplif·y and clarify the law. They have been presented at this time

I know we are anxious to get the work finished and it is a temptation
to impose a fixed time schedule upon the committee, but such a ma nda te
might well have a distracting rather than an expediting effect. Patience
is indicated. Let us, instead of setting deadlines, make clear our des ire
that this great task of revision be accomplished as expeditiously a s skillful workmanship will permit.
There are, however, several provisions contained in the resolutions
which might well be implemented now on an interim basis and an
emergent resolution for this purpose will, I understand, be offered for
your consideration at an appropriate time in the course of this communication.
With respect to the second part of the committee charge. it was
stated that .. the objective is not to change the basic law but to express
it in more understandable terms." It thus appears that the committee
was limited to a restatement of present law.
Yet in the course of its deliberations, a number of which I was
privileged to attend, the committee found instances in which it appeared
desirable not merely to rearrange the words but to change the substance
of existing sections of the Code. To propose such changes seemed to go
beyond its assignment and this impeded progress in its work.
We have made over the years significant progress in the organization
of our Masonic law. The Ross Digest was in its time a monumental step
forward. The development of our present Code was a further advance
but experience in its use has revealed certain deficiencies of organization
which it is the purpose of the project now underway to correct.
Some confusion arises in connection with the system of annotations
embodied in the Code.
In the field of public law, the publication of annotated codes is a
common practice of law book publishers. These annotations summarize
court decisions in the application of the particular code section involved.
They are selected and arran·ged by the publishers a s an aid to lawyers
in their search for cases which support their contention. The fact that
they are so published does not make them a part of the code itself and

42

43

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

the court in a subsequent case may by a simple majority of its members
overrule the earlier decision.
The annotations in our California Masonic Code seem to have acquired a different status. Our sovereign Grand Lodge has both judicial
and legislative powers and for this reason it is most important to be
clear as to which power it is exercising when it passes upon the decisions
of a Grand Master.
In performing this function the Grand Lodge is sitting as a reviewing court and it may, by a simple majority. vote to approve or disapprove
a decision. But when we publish the substance of the decision as an annotation to the Code we appear to have given legislative. effect to a judicial act and the vote required for legislation (i.e., a 5/6 vote) is necessary to repeal or delete it. This creates an anomalous situation and contributes to uncertainty as to the law. A system should be devised which
will eliminate confusion as to when Grand Lodge is acting in its judicial
and when in its le~islative capacity.
After giving the matter serious thought and examining the codes of
so me of the other Masonic jurisdictions, I have come to the conclusion
that an entirely new Code. couched in clear and concise language. is
the best way to meet the present day needs of the Craft and that the
current system of annotations should be discontinued. Footnotes under
each code section listing the various annual Proceedings in which the
subject matter was considered should provide an adequate guide to those
who may wish to research the subject in depth. I. therefore, make the following
RECOMMENDATION No. 7
1. That the incoming Grand Master appoint a Special Committee on
Code Revision and that it be directed to prepare a new revised Code for
the consideration of the Grand Lodge.
2. That the special committee be specifically authorized to propose
such substantive changes in the law as it may consider to be in the best
interests of the Craft, such changes being clearly identified as such in
its report.
3. That in the process of rewriting, all annotations representing
Grand Masters' decisions be eliminated and their substance where desirable or necessary, incorporated into the various code sections.
4. That henceforth a decision of a Grand Master be published in
the annual Proceedings only and considered as an opinion, unless the
Grand Master in reporting the same recommends that it be written into
the Code, in which case the Jurisprudence Committee shall prepare an
appropriate resolution for legislative action. Adoption of the resolution
by the required vote will have the effect of amending the code section
involved. If not so adopted, the decision shall stand as an opinion only.

direction have been brought before you. It appeared timely to take a
comprehensive look at our present situation and the various program

Expansion of student aid is a subject of manifest interest to the

The Most Worshipful Leslie E. Wood, Past Grand Master, was
prevailed upon to serve as Chairman but under the pressure of business
and the duties of public office he found it necessary to step down. The
views expressed by him in our conversations, however, were in substantial accord with the conclusions and recommendations hereinafter
set forth .
Everett Houser. a member of the committee. generously undertook
to carry on as Chairman. We are indebted to him and all the members
of the committee for a thoughtful, unbiased and workmanlike performance.
Several alternatives were suggested. to each of which the committee
gave careful and objective consideration. These were:
1. Extension of the Masonic Clubhouse program to other university
campuses.
2. Continued maintenance of the present clubhouses at Berkeley and
U.C.L.A. and development of some new program for other public institutions of higher learning in California and Hawaii.
3. Discontinuance of the clubhouse program and substitution on a
jurisdiction-wide basis of a new approach in serving the present day
needs of students.
In its report to me, which will apear in full in the Proceedings but
for present purposes will be summarized only. the committee expressed
strong belief in the value to Masonry of a successful program for stu~
dents. This is a premise in which I think we may all concur.
The first of the alternatives above listed was ruled out as being
fleither financially feasible nor justified by experience at the existing
clubhouses.
In considering the second alternative the committee made a detailed
review of the history of the two clubhouses which disclosed a steady
decline in student membership and activity over the past ten or more
years. The annual reports to Grand Lodge by the clubhouse boards
indicate that despite intensive efforts to publicize the facilities among the
Craft and the solicitation by personal contact of other students by dub
members. the decline, except for brief periodic spurts, has continued.
A number of factors enter into this result. Student needs in such
matters as the finding of jobs and housing, which the clubhouses originally served, are now met by extensive on-campus services. Whereas the
study rooms at the clubhouses were at the height of activity used many

About this time of year we hear the Masters of Lodges lamenting
the fact that their year is almost over and they h ave accomplished only
a part of the things they had planned. A similar obs ervation may be
made regarding the programs of Grand Lodge. So it should be for, if
our goals were too easily reached, it could only mean that we did not
aim high enough.
There is much unfinished business which it must fall to the future to
complete; a future which will bring into view new a nd higher horizons
with this challenge of new and greater achievement. The experience
of the past year yields convincing evidence that our Craft is and will be
equal to every challenge.
W e stand at this moment somewhat as the god, Janus , of ancient
mythology who faced in opposite directions. Thus he could, at one and
the same time, look back upon the past and forward to the future.
So we pass judgment upon the old year as we prepare also to meet
the new with its hope and promise of greater things to come.
As the hour approaches when the symbol of high office with all its
honor and responsibility will pass into other hands, there comes to mind
those significant words with which the poet, T ennyson, concluded his
"Idylls of the King" ... "And the new sun rose bringing the new year."

Upon receiving the committee's report, I arranged to meet with each
of the clubhouse boards and discuss the recommendations. After full
discussion, a substantial majority of the Board at U.C.L.A. expressed
support for the recommendations. No clear concensus, however, emerged
from the discussion with the Board at Berkeley.
There may be an understandable reluctance on the part of those
who over the years have dedicated their efforts, contributed generously
of their time and expended their energies on behalf of the clubhouses,
to favor bringing an end to what has been one of the bright chapters
in California's record of Masonic service. We owe them a great debt
of gratitude.
In keeping with our best traditions and in the true spirit of service,
the clubhouse program was conceived to meet a then apparent need,
and history will give it high rank in the annals of Freemasonry's achievements. But changing times bring changing needs and it will again be in
the best traditions of the Craft to seek and implement the means of
serving the new and equally pressing needs of the young people of today.

I have dealt extensively with the subject in this message because
I consider the issue raised to be one of the most important and far reaching to come before this Grand Lodge and in making your decision
you should have before you the essential and relevant facts. I believe
the committee has pointed the direction in which we should move and
I make the following
RECOMMENDATION

No. 8

1. That the incoming Grand Master appoint a special committee
to formulate plans for the incorporation of a multi-purpose foundation
under the auspices and control of Grand Lodge to establish and administer a flexible program of student aid and submit such plans for
approval at the 1968 Annual Communication.
2. That the Board of Directors of each Masonic Clubhouse be
directed to take during the interim all necessary steps to discontinue the
clubhouse programs, liquidate the clubhouse properties and make the
proceeds available to the proposed foundation.

A s the Grand Master states, "This Grand Lodge has never taken an
official position for or against the future separation of our Hawaiian
Lodges into a Grand Lodge of their own", and this is obviously because
no such question has ever been presented to it - even were such reference necessary or proper under Masonic law.
Dissemination of written material bearing upon the possibility and
potential costs and problems of separation into a new Grand Lodge by
the several Hawaiian Lodges has been undertaken by a group having
no official status. And the non-availability of readily accessible, impartial sources of factual material and advice, based upon the records and
long experience of this Grand Lodge, has created difficulties for Inspectors, Lodge officers and members in evaluating proposals and statements
by the unofficia l group.
It is the opinion of this Committee that the Grand Master's recommendation is good and timely, especially with the und erstanding that
this creation of a line of communication in no manner evidences any
policy or opinion by this Grand Lodge on the question of possible
separation.

GRAND M A STER

PROCLAMATJON - DEMOLAY WEEK
MARCH 13-17, 1967
It is never easy to grow up .
We know this from our own experience, which should give us the
toleranc e. depth of underst anding and desire to share with the youn g
people of today their adventu re of growing up.
These are days of expand ing knowled ge, but also of question ing.
uncertai nty and change. What sure guidelin es can we offer by which
youth may steer a certain course toward useful. noble manhoo d?
There are around us many who see no clear course ahead and in
confused rebellion are "like one crossing a river who can find neither
ford nor bank."
In its teaching s and precept s the Order of DeMol ay does offer the
needed guidelines. Coincid ing with the great principl es of F reemaso nry,
they provide the standar ds both moral. civic and personal by which each
issue and challeng e confron ting youth can be rightly met.
But it is not enough to proclaim these precept s, or to constru ct around
them an organiz ation for young people. They need us with them! Participation is the key. By gentle guidanc e, by coopera ting with them in the
activitie s of their Chapter s, showing by act as well as encoura ging word
that we really care , ';Ve can help to give the boys of DeMol ay the incentive. the confidence and the courage to build sturdy foundat ion s for the
future. And in so doing we will "increa se the candlep ower" of Freemasonry .
The foundin g of the O rder of DeMol ay by a great Mason was a
most signific ant event in the twentie th century history of our Craft. I t
well deserve s yea rly commem oration on our part, as well as day to day
support of the Order.
Accord ingly, I proclaim the week of March 13-17, 1967, as DeMol ay
Week in this jurisdic tion, and call upon each constitu ent Lodge and every
Mason to evidenc e during this time an active interest in the work of
the Order of DeMola y.
I direct that this proclam ation be read at the next Stated Meeting of
each Lodge and wherev er possible publishe d in Lodge trestleb oards for
March.
Dated: Februar y 6. 1967
Fratern ally yours,
L. E. DAYTON
Master
Grand
Attest:
EDWARD H. SIEMS
Grand Secreta ry
