PROCLAMATION
FORTY-EIGHTH ANNUAL PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK

Enlightened citizenship is the cornerstone of American freedom, and
the Public School is the instrument by which that cornerstone is laid.
Recognizing that, we have from the beginning of our Nation been
committed to the principle of universal public education. Hence today
the public school becomes a major factor in the lives of our children from
the time they are five years old and exerts a continuing influence upon
them during most of their formative years.
As the school population grows, as expanding knowledge and the
advances of science add their demands, and as the patterns of social
change make their impact, the challenge of our public schools becomes
increasing monumental and complex.
We delegate to administrators and teachers the day to day responsibility of making our great public school system equal to the challenge.
We call on them for dedication and professional skill and in laudable
measure they respond.
It is not enough. however, that we place this awesome responsibility
in competent hands. Equally essential is the informed, continuous and
active interest, encouragement and support of the people of each community. This we cannot delegate.
Public Schools Week was initiated by our Fraternity as a means of
emphasizing this role of the citizen to the end that it may effectively be
assumed by each of us. As longtime champions of public education we
should find active participation in the annual recurrence of Public Schools
Week one of our pleasanter duties, for it combines a three-fold interestas Masons, as parents and as citizens.
I hereby proclaim the week of April 24-28, 1967, to be Public Schools
Week in this jurisdiction, and direct that each constituent Lodge in California and Hawaii take an active part in its observance. I further direct
that no Lodge programs or meetings be held during this period for purposes other than this observance, with the exception of stated meetings.
This proclamation shall be communicated to the members of each
Lodge by one or more of the following methods: ( 1) read at the Stated
Meetings for March and April, ( 2) published in the Lodge's trestleboard
for April, ( 3) a copy mailed to every member of the Lodge.
Dated: February 8, 1967
Fraternally yours,
Attest :
L. E. DAYTON
EDWARD H. SIEMS
Grand Master
Grand Secretary

L. E. DAYTO N
GRANO MASTER
PROCLAMATION
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT MONTH

In the things we do for others lie the great satisfactions of life.
This thought has been expressed in many ways and confirmed repeatedly by human experience across the ages. It is a central theme
of Freemasonry, finding practical expression in the two Homes which
the Masons of California and Hawaii provide for our children at Covina
and for our elderly at Union City.
Sharing in the support of these great charities offers us at one and
the same time the opportunity to realize the deep satisfaction of doing
for others, to demonstrate in action the tenet of brotherly love, and to
fulfill a responsibility each of us assumed at the altar.
In accordance with long established custom, I hereby proclaim the
month of May, 1967, to be Masonic Homes Endowment Month. I call
upon every Lodge jn this jurisdiction to seek by all appropriate measures
a new record of contributions to the Endowment Fund, the income from
which is so vitally needed to help meet rising costs.
May the hearts of my brethren be warm with the spirit of generosity
and each contribute according to his means.
I direct that this proclamation be read in full in each Lodge at the
Stated Meetings for the months of April and May, 1967, or published
in the trestleboard, or a copy sent to each member of the Lodge.
Dated: February 15, 1967

Attest:
EDWARD H . SIEMS
Grand Secretary

L. E. DAYTON
Grand Master

PROCEEDING S OF THE

REPORT OF GRAND TREASURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
I take pleasure in presenting my fourth annual report as Grand
Treasurer.
The financial statements and audits of the Grand Lodge, Masonic
Homes of California and the California Masonic Memorial Temple are
a part of this report. Each gives a complete financial history of its individual corporate activity and together they represent the financial story
of the Grand Lodge and all its components . A careful reading of the
several reports. including schedules and exhibits attached thereto, is
strongly urged.
It was again my pleasure to sit in with representati ves of Lybrand,
Ross Bros. & Montgomer y, and with members of the office staff to review the details of the audits. All appropriatio ns and disbursemen ts as
provided in Section 194 C.M.C. were carefully reviewed by the professional auditors. The budget approved at the last Annual Communica tion has been strictly followed.
The fiscal year under review presented a number of unusual items.
Nominal appropriatio ns were authorized. In a few instances they were
insufficient. The Grand Master authorized s upplemental appropriatio ns
covering items totaling $7.235.00. A more detailed statement of budgeted
items compared with actual expenditure s will be presented by the Finance
Committee.
I am pleased to report, however, that as your Grand Treasurer, I
have kept in close touch with this program. The excesses have, in my
judgment, been justified, and are essential. It is also my considered
judgment that some of these are non-recurrin g.
My sincere thanks and appreciation are expressed to our Grand
Master, Most Worshipful Laurence E. Dayton, for his sympathetic
understandi ng and keen interest in the finances of Grand Lodge and
its components ; to my associate, Worshipful Jack F. Bowley, Assistant
Grand Treasurer. for his willingness to discuss financial problems pertaining to our offices; and to our Grand Secretary, Very Worshipful
Edward H. Siems, and his staff for their continuing desire to be of
service at every opportunity , and with whom I have almost daily contacts. Unlimited cooperation is always available.
Respectfully submitted.
PAUL A. PFLUEGER
Grand Treasurer

Referred to Committee on Distribution .

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
I have the pleasure to present my Seventh Annual Report as your
Grand Secretary. It is a reminder that we, as an office staff, have been
under the usual pressure of the volume of work necessary to prepare
for the five days of the l l 8th Annual Communication of this Grand
Lodge. The joy of seeing many old friends and the privilege of greeting
those of you who are here for the first time makes the Communication
a very special Masonic experience.
As we reflect on the activity of this Grand Lodge and the Constituent Lodges during the past several years, we can only conclude tha t
Masons in California generally are doing their full share in upholding
the high traditions of the Craft. We extend to the Officers of the 711
Lodges our thanks for the splendid cooperation we received throughout
the year. The prompt response of Lodge Secretaries to correspondence
has made the work of the office a pleasure. We express our gratitude to
all Grand Lodge Officers, Inspectors and Committeemen for their complete cooperation. The individual effort of each makes it possible for
the Grand Lodge programs to expand and become more effective,
I wish to express my personal appreciation to the great number of
Master Masons, not Officers of Lodges, who have corresponded with
the Grand Secretary's Office to present a thought or an idea which,
in many instances, compliments these programs.

PROCEEDIN GS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNI A

FEES FOR DEGR EES

Withdraw als and Suspensio ns:
This past year we experience d an all time high in withdrawa ls they number 2,670 which includes 484 withdrawi ng and affiliating with
the consolidat ed Lodges. There must be good reasons why this figure
is so high. As an Officer of your Lodge are you concerned about this?
Jt is elementar y that after a man joins the Fraternity every effort should
be made to maintain his interest in it. How can this be accomplis hed?
By giving him a job to do. Maybe it is as a member of the Sick Committee, the Delinquen t Dues Committe e. Program Committe e, Public
Schools or Endowme nt Committe es. There is a place for eveyone. For
the older members, who may be retired, perhaps involvmen t in church,
school, Chamber of Commerce or other programs could be considered .
It does take personal involvmen t.
If the withdrawa ls and suspension s for non-paym ent of dues could
have been reduced by half during the past year, we would have continued our upward trend in membersh ip. Where leadership is evident,
Lodges have more than held their own. The record shows 257 Lodges in
the jurisdictio n with a gain in membersh ip, 421 show a loss and 33 remain even. One of our older Lodges, with over 600 members, raised 38
Candidate s. Out of the total membersh ip they remitted dues for one
member and had only two suspensio ns for non-paym ent of dues. The
annual dues of this Lodge are over $25.00 per year. Where there is
leadership and involveme nt you usually find a healthy Lodge.
Forfeiture of Fees and Contribut ions (Sec. 546) :
Under the provisions of our law where a Candidate taking his Degrees does not complete the work of the Three Degrees within a period
of five years, the Lodge should take action. The Master should declare
the unused portion of the Degree fees and the contributi ons forfeited
unless, by vote of the Lodge, further time is granted. This regulation
gives the Lodge an opportuni ty to alleviate particular ly awkward situations and clear the Lodge records. Properly used it has proven to be a
practical tool. and we do not suggest abandonin g its use.
However, during the fiscal period ending June 30, 1967, our analysis
shows 534 such forfeitures were declared by the Masters. This year
we initiated 5,160 new members which indicates that nearly ten per
cent of the men who sought light in Masonry in 1967 could be lost to
the Fraternity through forfeiture of fees in 1972. In 1962 we initiated
6,426 and our figures show that we actually lost over eight per cent of
the men who started that year. We wonder - were our original investigations of the applicants thorough enough? Did we adequatel y explain
our purposes? Were we slovenly in our coaching and education? Did
we just '"lose track" through carelessne ss? Did we fail to follow up?
Before decla ring the fees forfeited did the Master consult with the recomme:ndors of the Candidate ? Some of these forfeitures undoubted ly were
justifiable but why?

The strength of our great Fraternity has been, and always will be,
determine d by the quality of the men who are permitted to enter our
West Gate. Hence, the decline in membersh ip for the second consecutive year is not too alarming. but it should be recognized ~s part of the
over-all program with which we must deal. The losses m 1966 were
1,014 and there were 1.738 in 1967. A careful analysis of the summary
of statistics on membersh ip should be made by the Officers of each
Lodge. It is a challenge to determine in what way your Lodge is responsible for the over-all figures.
Let us take a good look at some of the segments shown on the summary:
Applicatio ns for Membership:
The number of applicants your Lodge will attract depends in a
large measure upon the personal involvmen t of each member of the
Lodge. What is meant by involveme nt? It means assuming more vigorously your civic, communit y and family responsibilities. In many co~­
munities it is recognized that the leaders are members of the Masonic
Fraternity . Does your membersh i p measure up to that standard? If not,
wh.at are you doing about it?

ACTION BY GRAND LODGE
WITHDRAWA LS, SUSPENSION S AND FORFEITURE S

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
In his report. the Grand Secretary discusses at length the subject of
withdrawals , forfeitures and suspensions and suggests ''the propriety of
the Master appointing a committee to study all withdrawals , forfeitures
and suspensions and make recommenda tions prior to any action by the
Lodge."
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, to which this
portion of the Grand Secretary's Report has been referred, is of the
opinion that the appointmen t of a committee to study all withdrawals ,
forfeitures and suspensions rests in the sound discretion of the Master
and concurs with the Grand Secretary's suggestion.
We therefore recommend that the Grand Secretary's suggestion be
approved and recommende d a yes report.
The Committee on Ritual indicated its concurrence in the recommenda tion.
Adopted.
DUES SURVEY

Analysis of Lodge dues in this jurisdiction has shown an apparent
healthy trend to offset ever increasing costs and meet the necessary
expenditure s of Lodge operation. Since 1957 there has been an average
increase in dues of approximate ly five dollars - from $13.55 to $18.34.
There were 677 Lodges in 1957 and 356 had dues of fifteen dollars or
higher. In 1967 only 52 of the 711 Lodges had dues below fifteen dollars.
At least 35 % require dues of twenty dollars or more per year.
A further review of the record shows that suspension for non-payment of dues in 1957 was 976 whereas there were 1,633 such suspensions in 1967. Reinstateme nt amounted to only 321, which is less than
one in five of the suspensions . Some believe that the increase in suspensions is directly related to the increase in dues. We think not. Rather,
it would appear that it is closely related to leadership. Last year the
Grand Master's recommenda tion, adopted by Grand Lodge, was that
the Delinquent Dues Committee, appointed by the Master, should be
a full-time Dues Committee. Undoubtedl y, many Masters have made
this change, but our contacts with Lodges would indicate that others
have merely reappointed the Secretary, or other members, to follow up
on a spotty or periodic basis. The importance of a full-time competent,
active Dues Committee cannot be overstressed in making an effort

SOJOURNER S

This is a subject for discussion at almost every Grand Secretaries'
Conference. Two years ago the Conference proposed exchanging information on members living outside their jurisdictions. Last year the
program was started by a few Grand Lodges. It is quite simple and this
is the procedure:
Jurisdiction "A" furnishes each Lodge with forms providing f~.r the
name of the member, his address and name of the Lodge. It states: Any
Masonic courtesies extended to him will be appreciated ." The form is
signed by the Secretary of the Lodge. They are forwarded to the Grand
Secretary of Jurisdiction "A" who, in turn, sends them along to the
Office of the Grand Secretary in Jurisdiction "B" or "C", or wherever
the member resides. From there it goes to the Lodge nearest the member's residence. The sojourner is invited to establish and maintain fraternal relations with his Brethren in the community where he lives.
Yes. this is more work for the Secretary. However, if the program
is approved by the Grand Lodge of California, I am confident we could
make the basic information available through the use of data processing
equipment and relieve the Secretaries of the detail work.
Is the main purpose of this program to gain new members by affili#
ation? Not necessarily. There will be some membership gain and perhaps
some loss but primarily it will assist your members to maintain ;nterest
in the Fraternity. It is my opinion that losing contact with 1'. lasonry
is one of the main reasons where there are so many withc1r;:l''' :1ls . I
strongly urge that Grand Lodge approve this program and authorize
the Grand Secretary to determine the best method of implementin g it.
We have already received names of sojourners residing in California

ACTION BY GRAND LODGE
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Grand Secretary advised that two years ago several of the
Grand Secretaries began a program of exchanging information on members living outside the jurisdiction wherein they were members. The main
purpose behind the program was to excite interest in the sojourner to
establish and maintain a fraternal relationship with the brethren of his
community.
This Committee agrees with the Grand Secretary that this program
be approved by Grand Lodge and that he be authorized to determine
the best method of implementing it and therefore moves the adoption of
the recommendation and urges a yes vote.
Adopted.
VETERAN BUTTONS

During the year two Seventy-five Year Buttons and seven hundredforty Fifty Year Buttons were presented to members of California
Lodges. This makes a total of 11.371 Fifty Year and 9 Seventy-Five
Year Buttons presented since the inception of the program.
FRATERNAL VISITATIONS

Your Grand Secretary and Mrs. Siems wish to thank Grand Lodge
for the privilege of representing California at the dedication of the new
Masonic Temple in Paris, erected by the Grande Loge Nationale
Francaise. Also, in company with Grand Master Laurence E. Dayton,
we attended the 250th Anniversary Celebration of the founding of the
United Grand Lodge of England. At the latter event we witnessed the
installation of the new Grand Master of that Grand Lodge, the Duke
of Kent. I have covered the Temple Dedication in Paris in the last issue
of the California Freemason, and by agreement with the Grand Master
he has covered the London celebration in his Message.
In addition to these two official visits, Mrs. Siems and I, on our own,
had about two weeks for sightseeing and touring in Europe. While in
Rome I visited the Grand Lodge Office. I knew in advance that the
Grand Master of the Grand Orient of Italy would not be in Rome. but
he had arranged for me to meet the Deputy Grand Master, Roberto
Ascarelli, who was most cordial and helpful to me.

LODGE MANUAL

In the Grand Master's Message reference is made to the Lodge
Manual which will be distributed to each Lodge during the Annual
Communication. This Manual is the property of the Lodge. Suggestions
as to its purpose and how to use it are set forth under "Guide Lines"
and "General Information."
The items covered to date are: Public Schools, Constitution Observance, Masonic Education, Endowment, Masonic Home at Decato
(Adults), Masonic Home for Children, Public Information, Investments, Ceremonies and Trial Procedures. Each item is printed on a distinctive colored paper and all additions to the material on these subjects
will be printed on the same color paper. This will simplify the replacing
of sheets when a particular section requires updating, revising, etc.
Those responsible for the development of the Manual are certain
that many good suggestions for its improvement will come from Officers
of the Lodges. We sincerely hope so. This Manual is only a guide and
is not to be considered as all inclusive or limiting. but we hope that the
suggestions and ideas included will stimulate the imagination of Lodge
Officers and enable them to improve on programs suitable for their
Lodges.
LIBRARY AND MUSEUM

The importance of the Library and Museum in the Memorial Temple
is emphasized daily by the increased number of visitors who make inquiry
as to its location. It is our sincere hope that sufficient voluntary manpower
will be available so the Library may be kept open daily during visiting
hours. Our sincere thanks to our four mainstays: Brothers Scott,
McMaster, Simpson and Young.
Our special thanks to the Chairman of the Board, David R. Lane. It
is only fak to say that as early as two years ago Brother Dave asked to
be relieved of this responsibility because of his health. At my request, he
told the Grand Master he would remain on in the hope that a successor
would be found. A successor was not found and he has continued as
Chairman to this date. This Grand Lodge owes a debt of gratitude to
Brother David Lane for his outstanding contribution to the growth of
our Library and Museum.
CONCLUSION

I could not dose my report without thanking the members of the
Grand Lodge Office staff for their loyalty and support. It is interesting
to note that the average length of employment is nine and one-half years,
with the shortest length of service approximately two months and the
longest twenty-one years. You can see that ours is not a transient group

T he Committee on By-Laws:
With all seven members present promptly at I 0: 00 A.M. on Sa tur~
day, October 7, 1967, your Committee on By-Laws began its review of
the 133 matters referred to it for report. Since the las t Annual Communication the items shown in the Grand Secretary's Report as " E xhibit
B" were each approved by this Committee and have been adopted by
the Lodges.
The following changes, not ta bulated in "Exhibit B. " were made by
Lodges in adoptin"g the Uniform Code of By-Laws :
Alterna te meeting date changed : 1
Fees increased: I
Fees decreased: 1
Dues increased: 3
Charity increased: 4
The action of two Lodges is disapproved:
La Jolla No. 518 because written notice appears not to have been
given at the next preceding meeting ( C.M.C. Section 365).
Triad No. 81 2 beca use of incorrect provision for an alternate date of
Stated Meeting ( C.M.C. Section 343).
Your Committee commends the fourteen Lodges which have increased the authority of the Charity Committee to a figure more in keeping with present day costs and values. Many of these limits were set in
the now distant past. when the purcha sing power of the dollar was far
greater than it is today. They are now qui te unrealistic. Since the Charity
Committee under our law . Uniform Cod e of By~Laws Article X, C.M.C.
Section 360, consists of the Master and W ardens of the Lodge, there
would appear to be no real risk in enabling these officers to dispense,
when necessary, that charity of which M asonry so much approves b y

80

PROC EEDINGS OP THE

giving them authority at least commensurate with that given their predecessors in the long ago.
The Master of a Lodge is sworn and required to govern his Lodge in
accordance with its By-Laws. The By-Laws of his Lodge are those
adopted by Grand Lodge as the Uniform Code of By-Laws, with the
Lodg e permitted, within limits, to select its time of meeting, fees, dues.
and the authority of its Charity Committee. It seems quite unfair to the
Master , or any other conscientious officer or member of a Lodge, to permit the By-Laws to which he has access in the records of his Lodge to
become obsolete, and therefore misleading as to this law. We therefore
particularly commend Molino Lodg e No. 150 for amending its by-laws
to add the provision with respect to the Annual Communication of Grand
Lodge adopted by Grand Lodge in 1961 . Others with far more obsolete
by-laws would be well advised to follow this excellent example.
Your Committee expresses its gratitude to the Grand Secretary's office for their excellent work during the year, and for their cooperation
w ith this Committee.
Most Worshipful. we move that Grand Lodge approve the foregoing
amendments and resolutions, with the two exceptions above stated , and
that the charters of the Lodges moving their places of meeting to another
city or place be amended in accordance w ith C.M.C. Section 373.

TRIAL RECORD No. 1863
A member of San Francisco-Victory Lodge No. 360 made application to the Lodge in 1952. He answers "no" to question 12 of his application which at that time asked if he had any knowledge of any legal or
J]loral reasons which would prevent him from becoming a Freemason.
In so doing he concealed three convictions between the years 1933 and
1941 . The first two were for stealing of poultry and the last for forgery
for all of which he served time. In 1965. after he had been a member of
the Lodge for thirteen years, his derelictions were discovered and he
was charged, admitted the circumstances , but claimed he felt that he had
served his time and had been rehabilitated and therefore could properly
answer the question " no".
The accused admitted freely the truth of the charges and decided not
to have a trial. He was expelled from the Lodge and the proceedings were
reviewed and affirmed by this Grand Lodge in 1965. In 1966 and again
this year he has applied for restoration. He has presented numerous letters and evidence as to his good conduct and rehabilitation both before
and since his application and election to membership to the Lodge.
Your Committee feels, however, that had he disclosed his derelictions
at the time of his application he would not under our law have been eligible and it is felt that this Committee cannot recommend the restoration
of someone who would be ineligible under our existing law.
We therefore present the following resolution and recommend its
adoption.
RESOLVED, that the application for restoration in Trial Record
No. 1863 be denied.
Adopted.
TRIAL RECORD No. 1911
A member of Unity Lodge No. 368 was charged with four counts of
wilfully and knowingly filing false and fraudulent income tax returns.
He had entered a plea o f "nolo contendre" in the Federal Court, had
been found guilty, fined, sentence suspended and placed on probation.
He plead not guilty to the Masonic charges and a trial was held. The
accused offered no evidence on his behalf but relied on his counsel's
argument that the plea of "nolo contendre" was not an admission o f guilt.
The Trial Master correctly admitted the plea into evidence but improp ~
erly allowed counsel to argue that it was not a plea of guilty and the

PRO"EEOINCS CW THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

commission should not consider it as such. The commission found the
accused not guilty.
The committee feels that as the accused offered no defense the com.
mission was bound to find him guilty. We have many times in the past
ruled that in our Masonic law a plea of "nolo contendre" is admissible
and is construed to be an admission of guilt. The crime of wilfully and
knowingly filing false income tax returns is one involving moral turpitude. No explanation was offered, therefore the verdict should have been
one of guilty.
We offer the following resolution.
RESOLVED. that the finding of not guilty in Trial Record No. 1911
be reversed and the matter remanded for a new trial.
Adopted.
TRIAL RECORD No. 1924
A member of Welcome Lodge No. 255 was accused of overcharging
patrons at the Post Office at which he worked and pocketing the differences. The charges were observed by postal inspectors. He was charged
in the United States District Court for violation of U.S. Code Section
I 726, unlawful collection of postage and charges were subsequently
filed against him in his Masonic Lodge. He wrote a letter to the Secretary in which he plead guilty to the charges as set forth in the specifications. The Trial Master found him guilty of embezzlement and fixed
the penalty at expulsion.
The accused has filed an appeal. There is no question as to the facts
or the procedure. However, the finding of embezzlement is technically
not correct since the charges preferred were the unlawful collection of
postage under a specific U.S. Code Section. The Committee does not
feel. however. that this technicality should be allowed to upset the finding of guilt by the Trial Master after a plea of guilty to the charges
which certainly involved moral turpitude. The procedure otherwise was
in all ways correct.
Your Committee therefore believes that the proceedings and penalty
of expulsion should be affirmed and offers the following Resolution.
RESOLVED. that the finding of guilt of unmasonic conduct and the
penalty of expulsion in Trial Record No. 1924 be approved and affirmed.
Adopted.

to state what particular act was committed and therefore a plea of guilty
to the charge was not necessarily a plea of guilty to unmasonic conduct.
Contributing to the delinquency of a minor under the Welfare and Institutions Code embraces a number of offenses, many of which would not
constitute moral turpitude. The record does not inform us as to the
nature of the act.
We therefore feel the accused should be retried with the charge of
unmasonic conduct made more specific and offer the following Resolution.
RESOLVED. that the finding of guilt and the suspension in Trial
Record No. 1927 be revised and the matter remanded for a new trial.
Adopted.
TRIAL RECORD No. 1928
The accused, a member of Blackmer Lodge No. 442. was charged in
the Criminal Courts with indecent exposure but allowed to plead guilty
to a charge of disorderly conduct. He was sentenced to serve 90 days
in the City jail and placed on probation subject to obtaining psychiatric
treatment. Charges were filed in the Lodge and he wrote a letter to the
Secretary. admitting that the charges were true and pleading guilty but
stating that he was in need of psychiatric treatment. The Master found
him guilty of indecent exposure and unmasonic conduct and fixed the
penalty at suspension.
The procedure was in all ways correct. Your Committee. however.
after having considered all of the evidence in the record is of the opinion
that the penalty should be raised to expulsion.
We therefore' offer the following Resolution.
RESOLVED. that the finding of the Master in Trial Record 1928
be approved but that the penalty be raised to expulsion and that the
accused be expelled from all of the rights and privileges of Masonry.
Adopted.

REPORT OF THE GRAND LECTURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The duties of the Grand Lecturer are prescribed in Section 156
of the California Masonic Code, and the specific duties are contained
within six numbered paragraphs under that Section. This report will
recount the activities of the Grand Lecturer, with the assistance of the
Assistant Grand Lecturers, in the discharge of those duties.
Paragraph First: In order to supervise and direct the Assistant
Grand Lecturers and the Inspectors in the performance of their duties,
and to require conformity with the adopted Ritual and work, the following meetings and conferences were held during the year:
In December, the Ritual Committee held its annual meeting for the
express purposes of reviewing and exemplifying the entire Ritual and
lectures of the Three Degrees with the Assistant Grand Lecturers filling
the various stations during the work. This was particularly helpful to
the newly appointed Assistant Grand Lecturers.
The usual Spring conferences of Inspectors were held as follows:
Divisions I and III, at Clear Lake, April 21-23, 1967, conducted
jointly by Worshipful William F. Poynter and Worshipful Ulysses
G. Patropulus, Assistant Grand Lecturers;
Division II. at Bijou, Lake Tahoe, June 16-18, 1967, conducted
by Worshipful Frank P. Lemen, Assistant Grand Lecturer;
Division IV, at Sonora, June 2-4, 1967, conducted by Worshipful
Wallace H. Fiske, Assistant Grand Lecturer;

93

DiVision V, at San Diego, May 19-21. 1967, conducted by Worshipful Burton Meyer, Jr., Assistant Grand Lecturer;
Division VI. at Indio, March 31-April l, 1967, conducted by Worshipful William H. Price, Assistant Grand Lecturer.
At these conferences the work of the more recently appointed lnpectors was particularly noteworthy, and reflected the continuing
~rogress directed toward uniformity and conformity to our established
Ritual.
Also, during the year, the Assistant Grand Lecturers conducted
a series of schools of instruction for the Inspectors in the various divisions. The Inspectors, in turn, conducted schools of instruction for the
officers of their respective Districts.
Last Spring, I directed Assistant Grand Lecturer Frank P. Lemen
to Hawaii to conduct the Annual School of Instruction for the Inspectors
and Officers' Coaches of the Lodges located in the Islands. He also
conducted a special school of instruction for Candidate Coaches. His
report indicates that we are making real progress in raising the standard
of ritual in the Islands. The three Inspectors in the Islands and the
Officers' Coaches of the various Lodges deserve the highest of praise
for the results that are evident in the work there.
Paragraph Second: The duty of examining the Assistant Grand
Lecturers. on receiving notice of their appointment by the Grand Master,
became necessary on three occasions during the past year. After fifteen
years of highly commendable service in Division I, Worshipful Clare
B. Campbell tendered his resignation, to become effective at the close
of our last Annual Communication. Brother Campbell endeared himself
to the brethren throughout our jurisdiction and was a source of strength
in the deliberations of the Ritual Committee. Also, upon the election
of Worshipful Robert A. Crigler, Assistant Grand Lecturer of Division V, to the office of Junior Grand Warden at our last Annual Communication, a vacancy occurred in that Division. Brother Crigler's outstanding work in his various assignments in Masonry merits the accolades of his many well wishing friends and brethren. More recently,
the Worshipful William F. Poynter, Assistant Grand Lecturer of Division I, asked of the Grand Master that he be relieved of his duties,
mentioning that he had accomplished most of what he had set out to
do when he was appointed to the office more quickly than he had antipated. When Brother Poynter assumed the Assistant Grand Letcurership, he stepped into a responsibility in a far flung Division, and his
work in various areas of that responsibility, particularly in the smooth
transition from a large geographical Division to two separate entities
of a more compatible makeup, has been greatly appreciated. We know
that he will continue to serve Masonry in various capacities, and we
wish him well in all his future endeavors.
Following the close of our Annual Communication a year ago, a

In addition to the foregoing resume of activities during the Year,
the following account of additional activities should be noted :
At the One Hundred Seventeenth Annual Communication held last
October, a resolution was adopted which authorized the preparati011
of a suitable memorial copy of the Masonic Funeral Service for presen.
tation to the widow or next of kin. By direction of the Grand Master
and the terms of the Resolution. the Ritual Committee prepared a format
for the printing of such a memorial copy of the Funeral Service. During
the year, it was printed and made available to the Lodges of the jurisdiction.
Also, the Ritual Committee has prepared a supplemental page of
instructions to be applicable to adapt our Funeral Service to a memorial
service. This was accomplished in accordance with the observations
made by the Committee on Policy and General Purposes in reporting
on the defeated resolution entitled "Optional Funeral Service- Memorial." The supplemental instructions will be made available to Lodges desiring them.
The Grand Lecturer and the Ritual Committee have, for some time,
been considering the preparation of a book of instructions or handbook
to guide the Inspector in the discharge of his duties. Much of the material has been in the hands of the A ssistant Grand Lecturers for some
time, and is now being prepared for use by the Inspectors. We feel
that the more detailed instructions and guide lines will be instrumental
in maki ng for more effective service by the Inspectors in the va rious
parts of our jurisdiction. Two years ago. reference was made in my
Annual Report to a part of such a book of instructions pertaining to
Grand Lodge ceremonies. covering all details with regard to advance
planning. the opening of Grand Lodge, and the actual ceremony itself.
This has been most helpful to the Assistant Grand Lecturers in assisting the Inspectors and Masters of Lodges in preparing for s uch a ceremony. and because of the increasing number of Lodges becoming involved in such ceremonies in recent years, the Grand Master deemed
it appropriate to include this portion of the proposed Inspector's Handbook in the looseleaf booklet about to be distributed to the individual
Masters or Lodges.
Through the years the Inspectoral Corps has performed admirably
in the various areas of responsibility assigned to the Inspectors, and
we are all deeply indebted to this fine group of brothers who have given
of their time, energy, and talents year after year. Today [ want to express my appreciation and thanks to all who have served. and particularly so to those whose tenure has extended over a period of time and
who have now stepped aside to allow others to share in the pleasure
of service in this capacity. Twenty-nine of this group have retired during
this fiscal year. and twenty-nine new Inspectors are now actively engaged
in building on the experience and service of their predecessors, and in·

ectfng new ideas and enthusiasms in this important phase of our Grand
loctge activities.
In commending the Inspectoral Corps, I am not unmindful of the
sf nificant contributions to its stature by my predecessors in office, Very
Jorshipful Elbert W . Davis and Very Worshipful Donald G. Campbell. Past Grand Lecturers, and the invaluable counselling and iniration they have afforded me in the discharge of my duties.
sp In accordance with custom followed in previous years. the request
for budget appropriation for the Inspectors' various expenses. the Ritual
Committee, and the Grand Lecturer, has been submitted to the Finance
Committee for consideration. Basically, this year's request is consistent
with previous years, with the exception of two non-recurring items.
The aprons assigned to the Assistant Grand Lecturers and the Grand
Lecturer have been in service for a good many years. and their deterioration in appearance has become quite noticeable. We have, therefor, asked that the sum of $400.00 be included in the appropriation to
cover the purchase of "travelling" aprons for the six Assistant Grand
Lecturers. and apron and collar similar to those of the other elective
Grand Lodge officers for the Grand Lecturer. Also, we have asked that
the sum of $200.00 be included to cover the cost of re-producing the
book of instructions for the Inspectors referred to previously in this
report.
In closing. I desire to express my personal thanks and appreciation
to the Grand Master for the numerous courtesies extended throughout
the year; to the Grand Secretary and his staff for their continued assistance and concern; to the Assistant Grand Lecturers for their unswerving loyalty and cherished friendship; and to you. my brethren,
for th.e opportunity you have afforded me to be of service to you and
to our beloved fraternity.
Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES OF THE
MASONIC HOMES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M . of California:
In reporting to the Grand Lodge your Board of Trustees of the
Masonic Homes is fully cognizant of the faith and confidence which the
brethren have reposed in this Board. This marks the 75th report to the
Fraternity and also marks the 50th Anniversary of the dedication of the
Home for Children at Covina. The Masonic Homes are the embodiment
of those truly Masonic tenets of Brotherly Love and Relief and should be
the source of our greatest satisfaction as men and as Masons.
The Board met in San Francisco on October 14, 1966 for the purpose
of organizing. The election of John F. Porter, Deputy Grand Master.

COVINA

Our new Superintenden t at Covina since June of 1966, Brother James

C. Blaine of Lexington Lodge No. 104. has fully met the expectations
of the Boa rd. H is untiring enthusiasm , his deep understanding of the

needs and aspirations of our children and young people, and his leadership of the splendid staff. have meant a continuance of the fine work of
the Covina Home. His wife, Dorothy. and the younger Blaines, have
a ll entered into the life of service and have donated of their time and
talents to the benefit of the Home.
The population of the Home has increased from 58 in June. 1966 to
67 at the close of June, 1967. This is, in part, due to applications from
within this Jurisdiction and, in part, due to the acceptance of next of kin
of Masons of other Jurisdictions as approved by your Grand Lodge in
1961. While our concern for a ll children is great, our responsibility to
California and Hawaii Masons, and their children. must, of necessity,
come first and it has become necessary to limit admissions from other
Jurisdictions for the time being.
We can report to you important decisions bearing on our Children's
Home. For several years the Board has been considering the possibility
of moving from our present location, both to seek new surroundings and
to modernize and update our buildings. A study, in depth, of the pros

99

d cons of such a move and a review of the physical plant has led the

111

cl to conclude that from every standpoint we will be better and more

~omically served by remaining at Covina. The environment, the public

:d° cation facilities, the health and recreational facilities which we already

la ~e. would be both costly and difficult to duplicate in another location.
a The pressing need is for the replacement of the present fifty~year old

dOf!llitories wi th modern cottageAype units. Further, studies are to be
ade in evolving a master plan of replacement of these buildings, to pre~
:rve the e~sentia.l community of. t~e Hom~, but to subs~itute sa.fe ~nd
lllodern livmg units for those bu1ldmgs which have outlived their time
and usefulness.
We reported to you in 1964 the acquisition of a beautiful camp at
Big Bear. This site on which the leasehold and buildings were transferred
to the Masonic Homes. was the generous gift of a non-Mason , Mr. Lewis
J. Smith. Mr. Smith has since passed away but the thoughtfulness of
the man and his gift are memorialized for future generations by a plaque
set in the stone which marks the entrance to Camp Masonic.
At the time of acquisition, the lake bed had receded to such a point
that several hundred yards separated our dock from water's edge. Replenishment of the lake has brought the level back and the dock now
stands in seven feet of clear water. The camp, both for winter outings
and summer camping, is bringing new experiences and great joy to our
young people.
The Order of Rainbow for Girls made a generous donation to outfit
a camp infirmary. This donation has been used to convert, with the proper
plumbing and sewer connections , a fine mobile home into a permanent
infirmary installation. The mobile home was acquired from a Decoto resident. It has been suitably inscribed to designate its donors and is an
important part of the camp program. Thoughtful gifts such as these attest
to the fact that we are indeed one Masonic family.
DECOTO

While both Homes are under the regula tion and licensing requirements of the California Department o( Social Welfare, the brethren must
understand that because of the infirmities of age, these res trictions bear
most heavily on our admissions to the Home at Decato. For several
years, we were prohibited from accepting anyone who required a cane
for assistance in walking and those guests who might later need a cane
were required to be quartered in a separate unit. Through the excellent
work of your Board's president and secreta ry, and after many meetings
with the Welfare Department representatives , this rule has been somewhat modified. A cane is permitted w hen utilized only to assist balance,
but the Department's rules of admission still bear heavily. With an a verage admission age in excess of 80, more detailed physical examinations
are a necessity. The Board, guided by Dr. Hopp, our Board member and

100

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

C. RAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

present Senior Grand Warden. is moving toward a more enlightened
and helpful policy on pre-admission physical examinations.
The first year of Medicare has brought some rather substantial reduc.
tions in outside hospital and surgical care costs. It must be remembered,
however. that this program has no effect on our own hospital costs. With
a 131-bed hospital, supplemented by the licensing of 36 beds on the fifth
floor in Adams Hall. giving 2'1-hour bedside attendance, our costs are
following the inflationary trends of other like institutions. The substantial salary increases of a year ago were repeated in great part this summer. To maintain the quality of care which the Masons of California
rightly demand for our Decoto guests requires us to meet the competition
of other hospitals for competent personnel. We are sure that you understand and support us in this.
There had been no increase in the amount of the monthly grant to
guests for pocket money since 1956, when it was set at $12.00. This year
the Superintendent recommended, and the Board concurred in, an increase to $15.00. This small increase is offset in the total by the decline
in the number of guests of some 70 from the peak in 1962.

tttJStS and the Endowment Fund. The establishment of computerized
.records has assisted greatly in your Board's keeping current on expense
iteJJlS· A monthly report. in great detail, permits the pinpointing of cost
changes and permits close and constant scrutiny, not only of present
needs, but of future budget requirements.
The Board owes a very considerable debt to Brother Siems. His untiftng devotion and his willingness to furnish each detail of information
are most appreciated. With his burdens ever mounting, we look forward
to their lessening by adequate assistance. To him and his staff go our
heartfelt thanks.

FINANCES

The cost increases reflected in our hospital are but a part of the continuing spiral which affects our whole operation. Salaries and wages in
all phases of endeavor, whether government or business, have lifted
budgets to an all-time high. Although the Board, both in preliminary
committee meetings and working as a whole, has pruned and pared, the
1967-68 budget is the highest in the history of the Homes. With quality
care demanded, the Board constantly reviews expenses and requires
economy in each field of operation.
Were it not for the Endowment Fund built up through the work of
the Endowment Board and the careful investment of these funds by your
Investment Committee, our per capita would surely increase. Adding to
the bright side of the picture. in addition to your generosity. is the everincreasing source of gifts and bequests.
With the projected modernization program of our Covina Home, encouragement should be given to the direction of bequests to capital funds
to become a part of this heart-warming endeavor. The inclusion of the
Masonic Homes in giving need not be limited to Masons alone, as witness
the splendid gift of Camp Masonic referred to earlier.
Because of your generosity through the Endowment Fund. and because gifts continue to show the spirit of Masonic charity, we can report
to you that no increase in per capita for the Homes is required. We,
therefore. recommend a continuance of the $1.50 required in 1966.
ADMINISTRATION

Our Secretary has labored over the years to modernize the office
which he so ably manages. The bulk of financial transactions and investment records arises from the administration of the Homes. the various

101

CONCLUSION

This report could not be properly concluded without tribute to the
long and faithful service of our two retiring Trustees.
Brother "Pete" Anderson was first appointed a Trustee in 19'18 and
served until he became Grand Master in 1956. Again appointed in 1958,
he has served with great devotion since. Pete's particular love has been
the Home at Decoto, and the hospital and new wing, dedicated to and
named after our two beloved Charlies, Wollenberg and Adams, are
monuments . too, to our President Pete and his love of Masonry.
Brother Ned Stewart was first a member of the Board as Junior Grand
Warden in 1952, serving until elected Grand Master in 1955. Reappointed to the Board in 1958, Ned served the Board as its President,
succeeding P.G.M. Arthur M. Warren, until October, 1965.
As they leave our Board, both their names are being added to that
list of names of those Brethren who have devoted and continue to devote
an ever increasing ~mount of time for the benefit of the guests at our two
Homes.
Service to an ideal is of more lasting honor than any other. California
Masonry and the Board, as well as our Decoto guests and Covina children, will continue to draw inspiration from the loyalty and dedication
of these good brothers.
While a wise constitutional provision, limiting a trustee's service to
three consecutive terms, provides for a fresh infusion of talent and interest, we on the Board will miss our President and Vice President and wish
them Godspeed in their retirement from this activity.
Respectfully submitted,
BOARD OF TRUSTEES

REPORT OF SUPERINTENDENT
MASONIC HOME AT UNION CITY

Saturday, August 20. 1966, was another important day, it being the
annual visitation of the East Bay Past Matrons' Association and their
reception for the Grand Matron of Eastern Star. This is also the annual
"Jam and Jelly Day", on which they bring s ufficient jams and jellies
for the year's supply, along with many other items. Our sincere thanks
and appreciation to this group.
Another highlight in the history of the Home was Wednesday,
October 12, 1966. when about 1.450 M asons and their wives visited
the Home and were served lunch. This is one day of the year a ll the
residents look forward to with anticipation.
Many groups have visited the Home this past year. Our thanks and
appreciation to those who have taken time to entertain our residents,
such as De Mclay, Job's Daughters . Rainbow Girls, Order of Eastern
Star, Masonic Club House. Masonic Lodges and the San Leandro Musicians' Union.
Our heartfelt thanks to all the Lodges for their generous contributions and support to our Christmas Fund. This enables us to give every
resident a "very Merry Christmas". We express our thanks to various
groups and individuals for gifts of TV's, radios, clothing, etc. Two
items in particular we would like to mention, one being a Sony tape
recorder given by the Ladies Auxiliary of Ashland Lodge No. 798 in
San Lorenzo. and the other, the delivery of $100.00 per month of merchandise from Brother Warren M ooney of Standard Lodge No. 440,
Oakland.
Our register was signed by 3,701 visitors. representing 501 Lodges
in California and .Hawaii, 9 other jurisdictions, 7 foreign countries and
28 states.
We have had an extensive maintenance program this past year and,
with preventative maintenance action. we have been able to keep ahead
of many breakdowns.
We replaced much of our equipment in the kitchen with stainless
steel; such as tables. carts. etc.
To all our employees, I wish to express my personal appreciation
for their cooperation in caring for our residents in the Home and Hospital. Thanks for a job well done.
To all the residents . on behalf of the staff, we express our thanks
to you for your cooperation and assistance in helping to make this a
better home for you.
My persona l thanks to each Trustee for his confidence and helpful
guidance. Each one has a sincere personal interest in the Home and our
residents. For this. each is to be commended for his work on the Board.
It is a great pleasure to continue to serve the Board of Trustees and
the Masonic Fraternity as Superintendent of the Masonic Home at
Union City.
Fraternally yours,
GAIL H. DAVID, Superintendent

On June 30, 1967 there were 106 patients in the hospital, of which

the fifth floor of Adams Hall, which is also under the supervision of
the hospital. and these patients are considered permanent.
The Palo Alto Medical Clinic is supplying medical care to our residents here at the Home and the Palo Alto Clinic, as well as the Palo
Alto-Stanford Hospital.
We have been under plans "A" and "B" of Medicare since July 1.
1966. This has reduced our hospital bills considerably. and will help
with the medical portion. It will take a year or so of experience to realize
the full benefit.

the Home and the welfare of our residents.

year. One important occasion was the celebration of the 101 st birthday
of one of our lady residents. Another special occasion was the annual
meeting of the Board of Trustees a t the Home on Saturday, January 7,
1967 with a reception for our Grand M as ter by the residents that evening.
During the year many of the Trustees have visited and inspected the
Home, and talked with the residents.

REPORT OF THE SUPERINTENDENT-CO VINA HOME

Masonic Homes Trustees. We are looking forward with great anticipation to our re-dedication ceremonies to take place at Covina on September 10, 1967. This ceremony will serve to remind us that we will have
completed fifty years of Masonic service at Covina, having served some
twelve hundred plus children and that we are re-dedicating our interest
and efforts to continue to serve the children of our worthy Brethren.
Special thanks to the Board of Trustees and the Masons of California
and Hawaii whose continued interest and generosity make possible the
work of the Home for Children.
Respectfully submitted,
JAMES C. BLAINE, Superintendent

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
It is with great pleasure that I submit my second annual report as
Superintendent of the Masonic Home for Children for the year ending
June 30, 1967. This year's end showed a population of sixty-two children, consisting of thirty-six boys and twenty-six girls.
The year 1967 saw three of our Home family graduating from High
School. Marsha Fitzgerald, who will be attending a northern college
in September, Brenton King, who will be enlisting in the Armed Services,
and Steven Archinal. who will be attending college on a Masonic Home
scholarship. We wish them good luck and Godspeed.
The past year has seen many changes at Covina. A coat of paint on
all the buildings has helped their appearance. The planting of cut flowers
and the removal of several high hedges, plus the addition of sidewalks
in front of our property have enabled our children to feel closer to the
community. All dormitories have had improvements including such things
as new rugs, curtains, furniture, bedspreads, etc.
Summer camp will be enjoyed on a co-ed basis. All children will
enjoy an extensive stay in the mountains: part of the time being spent in
"back-packing" into the wilderness areas of Southern and Central California. The remainder of the time will be spent in residence at Big Bear
with periodic overnights and weekends at the beach.
Our Masonic Home Family has enjoyed relatively good health this
past year. We have experienced our customary summer and winter colds,
one tonsillectomy, and the expected number of summer cuts and bruises
that are found in every family.
It is certainly gratifying and heartwarming to observe the continuous
benefits presented our children through the dedicated efforts of the many
affiliated individual members and the groups. As a result of these donations our boys and girls have received special sports equipment, interesting and valuable stamps, coin collection items, tickets to outstanding
events (i.e., plays. movies, sports events, circuses, etc.), ponies for riding
enjoyment, parties with clowns, puppets and specialized entertainment,
plus innumerable food treats for those with a "sweet tooth." All these
contributions being geared to provide special and memorable happiness
for our youngsters.
In May, one hundred twenty-eight Alumni enjoyed dinner and dancing in the Home dining room. A wonderful evening was spent reminiscing and sharing fond memories. It is hoped that a similar type of reunion
can be planned for years to come. The weekend prior to Grand Lodge,
the Northern California Alumni met for dinner in San Francisco. A similar fete is planned for October, 1967.
Pla.ns for the future of Covina will be found in the report by the

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON RETIREMENT PLAN

To the. Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
In 1954 the Retirement Pension Plan was inaugurated for employees
of the Masonic Homes of California, the Grand Lodge of California and
affiliates, to provide a retirement income for employees in addition to
Social Security benefits. The Retirement Plan Committee proposed certain revisions at the last session of Grand Lodge in October, 1966, which
were adopted. These were substantial improvements to the plan and are
contained in the report submitted last year.
As of January l, 1967, 96 employees had membership in the plan
from the Masonic Homes and 23 had membership in the plan from Grand
Lodge and Grand.Lodge components. The number of retired members
of the Masonic Homes was 17 while there were 10 retired employees
from Grand Lodge and Grand Lodge components as of that date.
Your Committee has conferred with the representatives of the Wells
Fargo Bank, who are the trustees for the plan, and we are pleased to
advise that as of August 8, 1967, the market valuation of the fund was
$931,467.39 which had previously been carried at $927,749.34. The
investment policies of the trustee were reviewed and confirmed by the
committee. The plan has been reviewed periodically with the employees
of the Masonic Homes as well as the employees of the Grand Lodge
and its components. There has been general approval to the improvements made last year. Certain minor improvements were considered by
the committee but it was thought best to hold these over until next year.
Respectfully submitted,
L. HAROLD ANDERSON, Chairman
ALFRED F. BRESLAUER
PHIL N. MYERS
PAUL A. PFLUEGER

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

IN GRAND LODGE

We are happy to report that 644 of the Lodges in California attained
the Honor Roll this past year, and that 435 Lodges went on to the $3.00
figure or higher. To all we extend our congratulations and sincere thanks.

MORNING SESSION-TUESDAY, OCTOBER 10, 1967

Grand Lodge was called on at 9:30 a.m., the Grand Master presiding.
This session was raised by Worshipful Wiley T. Killingsworth, Master
of Bixby Knolls Lodge No. 699. The invocation was delivered by the
Grand Chaplain. The minutes of the morning and afternoon sessions of
Monday, October 9, were read and approved.

ANNUAL REPORT OF THE
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD
The Homes Endowment Board takes pleasure in presenting its annual
report for the fiscal year July 1. 1966 through June 30, 1967.
INCOME FROM THE ENDOWMENT FUND

Because of the continuing generosity of the Masons of California
the income from the Endowment Fund continues to grow and work for
our Homes. The income from the Endowment Fund this year was
$765,284.28 and that amount has been transferred to the operating
expense account of the Homes.
GIFTS AND BEQUESTS

Our sincere thanks go to those who have remembered the Endowment Fund during the past year with gifts and bequests amounting to
$268,265.94. Another $754,879.36 was received directly by the Board
of Trustees without going through the Endowment Fund, making a
total of $1.023,145.30 from gifts and bequests. We are certain you can
understand the importance of gifts and bequests and why we continue
to mention them.
CONTRIBUTIONS THROUGH LooGES

Contributions by the members of the Lodges amounted to $855,116.02
this past year, which means that 116, 409 brethren had a part in this,
with an average of $7.35 per contribution. The average amount per
member in all Lodges was $3.52.
We are very thankful to the many brethren who saw fit to make
sizeable gifts to the Endowment Fund, especially the late Brother
Duncan A. McLeod of California Lodge # 1 for his gift of $10,000.00.
We feel. however, that part of the joy and privilege of being a Mason
is for each of us to share in the opportunities that are presented to us.
Having a part in building the Endowment Fund is one of these opportunities. The size of the gift is not as important as the satisfaction one
:receives by having a part in this endeavor which lies so near to the
heart of Masonry.

CONCLUSION

As chairman of the Endowm ent Board I wish to express my thanks
to the members of the Board for their efforts on behalf of our Homes
during this past year. Seeming ly nothing has been too difficult for them
to do.
Every member of the Board in turn is grateful for the privilege of
serving Masonry in Californ ia.
We would also like to express our thanks to the most Worship ful
Gra nd Master, Laurence E. Dayton, and each of his officers for their
assistanc e to us. The Assistan t Grand Lecturer s and the Inspecto rs have
been helpful in every way in lighting a path for us and making our work
easier.
To the Masters , Warden s, Secretari es, and Endowm ent Committee~
men of the Lodges and members, we extend our thanks because, finally,
Brethren , it is you and your belief in our Masonic teaching s who make
this program possible.
Respectf ully submitte d,
THE MASON IC HOMES ENDOW MENT BOARD

REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES
CALIFORNIA MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F . & A. M. of California:
This is the Thirteenth Annual Report of the Board of Trustees of
California Masonic Memorial Temple.
At the close of the 1966 Annual Communication of Grand Lodge the
California Masonic Memorial Temple Trustees met in Annual Meeting.
The President, Ralph H. Head, reported the election of John F. Porter
as Deputy Grand Master, Eugene S. Hopp, as Senior Grand Warden,
and Robert A. Crigler as Junior Grand Warden. H e also announced the
appointment by the Grand Master Laurence E. Dayton of Fra nk F.
Goodman and Carl U . Zachrisson to the Board of Trustees.
The terms of the appointed members of the Board were as follows:
expiring in 1967, Samuel I. Jacobs and Howard H. McKinley, expiring
in 1968, Lyle E. Patton and Ralph H . H ead, expiring in 1969, Frank F.
Goodman and Carl U. Zachrisson.
All human history, H. G. Wells once observed, is in essence the
history of ideas. Idea~ have ruled the world since the beginning of recorded history, and although every age has had its tyrants and its benefactors, in the long perspective of time, men have only been implements
for transferring ideas into action. Where the people have prospered
most they have produced the greatest number of outstanding ideas. In

131

Western civilization the greatest concepts have been those which made
the greatest contribution toward the security and freedom of men.
In 1947 men of vision conceived the idea of a Memorial Temple
which would be dedicated to those Masons who had given of their lives
to the cause of freedom in World War II and now, twenty years later.
that idea has been consumated in a Temple free from debt and standing
as a symbol of security in an ever changing world.
The role of the Board of Trustees of Memorial Temple has already
gone through two phases : the first role was that of being builders. The
second responsibility was that which brought financial stability and
elimination of debt. Now it would appear that the Board enters into
the third and presumably the permanent stage of responsibility: to protect, maintain, and keep in balance the economic condition of the Temple.
The statement of assets and liabilities as of June 30. 1967, and which
by reference becomes a part of this report shows assets of $5.995,556
and total liabilities of $1.287.00 ClS of the end of the fiscal year, June 30,
1967. The most significant item in the statement is the establishment of
a depreciation reserve on building, equipment, furniture, and fixtures
totaling $559,782. This charge for depreciation covers the life of the
Temple to date and is in line with good and sound a ccounting practices.
It results in the placing of realistic values in the financial statement.
During the fiscal year the income from the rent of the auditorium,
the exhibit hall. and the garage reached a new high, and, combined with
other income, produced, after the deduction for operating and general
administration expense, an operating profit of whot might be termed a
cash flow of $55.943. The depreciation charge-off for the year amounted
to $62,999 and thus a book loss of $7,056 resulted.
Beyond the cold statistics of the financial statement are the more interesting fi gures which show that approxima tely 246,000 residents of and
visitors to San Francisco were entertained and enlightened in the beautiful auditorium of the Temple. The exhibit area was host to eighty-two
different orga nizations w hich used its facilities. Stockholders of some
of the country's leading business and industrial corporations have attended annual meetings in these halls. For all this and more, California
Masonic Memorial Temple has served as a showcase for the principles
of Freemasonry before the cross section of America who have been our
visitors. The expanded use of the Temple has made it possible to provide
a new maplewood s tage and a vastly improved loud speaker system.
All of this activity has been under the direction and charge of the
Manager of the Temple, George D. Gavin. The Trustees are grateful
to Brother Gavin for his dedicated, efficient, and imaginative service to
the Temple and thus to its success. We a re sure that the members of
Grand Lodge will concur.
In the early planning of Memorial Temple it was established that

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CAUPORNIA

California Masonry's two great Homes at Union City and Covina w~uld
be the ultimate beneficiaries of any financial rewards the Temple might
produce. That pledge was realized by Board action on May 18, 1967,
when the first contribution dividend in the sum of $10,000.00 was authorized for payment to the Masonic Homes of California.
Thus the cycle is beginning to complete. The idea of twenty yea~s
ago has become a symbol of freedom and security. California Masomc
Memorial Temple is now a landmark, not only on Nob Hill in this City
by the Golden Gate, but in the history of California Freemasonry.
Respectfully submitted,
RALPH H . HEAD ( 1968)
President
Officers and Trustees :
SAMUEL I. JACOBS , Vice Pr-esident ( 1967)
PAUL PFLUEGER, Tr-easurerEDWARD H. SIEMS , Secretary

Referred to Committee on Finance. (Budget allocation)

Our appreciation to Inspector Edward C. Lohmeyer and our Tour
Committee, for continued help in greeting and lecturing to various
groups. Daily we welcome members of Blue Lodges, DeMolay, Rainbow for Girls, Job's Daughters. and many others. Visiting hours remain
Monday through Friday. 8:45 A .M . to 4:45 P .M . ; Saturday and Sunday, 12 Noon to 4:00 P . M . The weekend opening has given travelers
passing through San Francisco an opportunity to visit. Masons active
in their home jurisdictions are impressed with our bea utiful Temple and
are most generous with their compliments.

REPORT OF THE MANAGER
To the Trustees of the California Masonic M emorial Temple
Brethren:
At the last Annual Communication of Grand Lodge we witnessed
the burning of the Temple Mortgage which was an important milestone
in the life of our California Masonic Memorial Temple. There are
summarized below the important activities and changes made during
the last year.
TOURS AND VISITATIONS

Each year we look back on our register of visitors and are amazed
by the number who sign and note the distances from which th.e?' travel.

MAINTENANCE AND IMPROVEMENT:>

This is our ninth year of operation. Concerted effort is being put
forth to maintain the high standards which we have established in the
upkeep of our physical and mechanical properties.
Our ventilating and heating systems have been overhauled and
controls replaced where necessary. A series of valves were added to
the overhead water lines to the coolers for improved efficiency and
economy. We have a continuing routine of washing the walls to reduce
painting requirements. We have stripped and resealed the outside and
inside terrazzo as well as the tile floors. Modern lighting has been
installed in the Garage on A and B decks and a portion of C deck. It
is hoped the remaining floors of the Garage may be completed early in
1968.
The flooring on the stage of the Auditorium, which was badly
splintered, has been replaced with maple. This will make it more
attractive to the producers of high type cultural events.
INCOME

The gross income for the Temple operation for the fiscal year
amounted to $193,666, which was an increase of 11.8% over the increase shown in 1966.
The Garage income reached an all-time high for the year and had
the highest month of income since the Garage was opened for business.
It reached $11,450 in a single month.
We are continually faced with increased costs of outside services
and materials. Every means is devised to effect a more efficient operation and to be constantly conscious of the need for economy in operation
to off set these increases.
CONVENTION AND AUDITORIUM DEVELOPMENT

Convention business in San Francisco has grown faster than accommodations to handle them. In consequence, much new housing, cultural
and exhibit facilities are being built or are on the planning boards.
The Hotel Hilton has completed two major additions to their facil~
ities to handle conventions.

The South of Market Y erba Buena Center is still a good possibility.
Mark Hopkins Hotel has changed ownership and the rooms have been
extensively remodeled. Stanford Court Apartments have been purchased
by a large hotel chain and a new hotel and convention center will replace
the older building.
Japanese Cultural Center in the Western Addition is nearing completion. Rockefeller Center is planned for the Golden Gateway with
several high rise buildings which will include theaters and hotels. Several
other major hotels have reported proposed room expansion. All will
have an effect on our facilities for rental purposes.
San Francisco is installing new street lights on California Street
from Kearny to Van Ness Avenue. Electric stop and go signs are also
being installed at Taylor and at Jones Streets. Contracts for the paving
of Taylor Street. between Pine and California Streets, have been let.
All will have a direct bearing on the Temple property.

We were selected for important business meetings, which included
Moody's Investment, and Manhattan Fund; a series under the heading
of Continuing Education of the Bar. and Miranda Plus Thirty.
We were favored with the California Canners and Growers annual
meeting, the Bank of America, and the General Telephone & Electronics
Stockholders meetings.
IBM made an outstanding presentation to their I 00% Club and
Golden Circle. Their messages were delivered to their employees
through the use of 26 slide projectors, and two moving picture cameras,
operating simultaneously when required.
The Printing Industry Convention had an overflow from the Exhibit
Hall to a portion of E deck in the Garage. This meeting was followed
by the Western Franchise. The State Board of Accountancy and the
State Bar Examinations were conducted in the Exhibit Hall.
Stanford Graduate School of Business presented a meeting for
business men with a group of speakers of international stature. They
attracted a very prominent audience.

134

OCCUPANCY

The occupancy of our facilities has increased over last year. We
have maintained a diversity of usage to assure income when rentals in
one or more areas are in slack periods. We had many very delightful
concerts and are gratified when nationally known groups repeat their
performances here year after year.
Glenn Yarbrough filled our Auditorium for two shows in one evening.
Clancy Brothers and Tommy Makem, Fred Waring, Jose Greco, Ferrante & Teicher, Andres Segovia. Peter Paul and Mary. and several
others were on the repeat list.
We were also favored with a Sacred Music Concert. American
Society for Eastern Arts. Ramsey Lewis. Lou Rawls, Min-On. and
White Heather Concert.
Also featured were Dennis Day, Mort Sahl. Barbara McNair, Bob
Hope. and Jonathan Winters.
Both the Houston and Melbourne Symphonies gave well received
performances, as did the Moscow Chamber group. This year. in addition to our Miss Chinatown U.S.A. contest, the Coronation was held
in our Auditorium.
The National Auto Dealers and the American Bankers Association
had Fashion Shows for their conventioners. The Ebony Fashion Show
repeated its always entertaining and delightful presentation in December. Macy's Teen Fashions was a huge success.
The Annual San Francisco International Film Festival was held
in October. They will return for the third year.
Five San Francisco High Schools rehearsed and graduated with
2.365 students participating. Three high schools had their mid-term
graduations, with 706 receiving diplomas.
Also in the Auditorium the Salvation Army had its graduation exer-

PROJECTION

We have substantial bookings for the next several years. The
months immediately ahead are heavily scheduled. We will have annual
stockholders meetings and the German Consul in San Francisco is
bringing in "Spotlight on Germany" for two weeks.
PUBLIC RELATIONS

We are conscious of the need for good public relations. We endeavor to keep in close contact with civic affairs, and groups who might
affect the occupancy of our facilities.
We have again accepted Directorship on the San Francisco Convention and Visitors Bureau Board, also the Nob Hill Association.
Satisfied tenants are one of the best means of promoting the use of
our Auditorium and Exhibit Hall. It is always our aim to add helpful
services which make the beautiful Temple facilities that much more
desirable.
We quote from a few letters received recently. which emphasize the
desirability of this phase of our work.

your staff during our stay at Masonic Temple.''

Two valuable and reliable members of our small staff reached retirement age and have decided to take their well earned rest. Our best

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
RECOGNITION OF FOREIGN GRAND LODGES
To the. Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Recognition of Foreign Grand Lodges has had
under consideration several requests for recognition. as well as other
information from foreign Grand Lodges, and submits the following
report and recommendations:
As information, we report that an unfortunate difference has developed between the Supreme Council of the Ancient . & Accepted
Scottish Rite of Turkey and the Grand Lodge of Turkey. It appears
that the difficulties have grown out of the previous relationship between
the Supreme Council and the Grand Lodge, the former having for
many years dominated the latter by various means, one of which was
to insure that an office holder of the Supreme Council was always
elected Grand Master. Prior to our recognition of the Grand Lodge
of Turkey, this relationship had been terminated and each body declared its independence of the other. The efforts of the Grand Lodge

140

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

to become truly independ ent and to bring its ritual and practices into
conform ity with what is more nearly world practice in Freemas onry was
apparent ly deeply resented by the leaders in the Supreme Council. who
took advantag e of what appeared to them to be irregular ities in the
part of certain officers of the Grand Lodge. and suspende d Past Grand
Master Efrem Tok to temporar y exclusion from Freemas onry for one
year. and sentence d to permane nt expulsion the reigning Grand Master,
Dr. Enver Needet Egeran. Needless to say, such action was condemn ed
by the Grand Lodge as illegal. arbitrary and a derogati on of its sovereignity. Each side has issued statemen ts justifyin g its actions but
the fact remains that all relations between the two bodies have been
broken off. Since then there has been a defection of members from
the Grand Lodge of Turkey, and a new Grand Lodge called " The
Grand Lodge of the Masons of Turkey" has been formed which has
eight or ten subordin ate Lodges.
A similar and equally regrettab le situation has develope d in Peru.
where a schism has occurred between the Supreme Council of Peru
and the Grand Lodge. which has resulted in the formation of a Grand
Lodge sponsore d by the Supreme Council named "The Most Serene
Grand Lodge of Peru."
Informed Masonic opinion holds that neither the Grand Lodge of
Peru nor of Turkey is responsib le for the difficulties with which it has
been confront ed.
A happier report can be made on the Masonic situation in France,
where regular Masonry is stronger today than ever before. As many
of you will recall, for many years we recogniz ed both the National
Grand Lodge of France and the Grand Lodge of France, but at the
l 962 Commun ication we withdrew our recognition from the Grand
Lodge of France, the reason being that in spite of promises and avowals
to the contrary , the Grand Lodge was drawing closer to the Grand
Orient of France, whose irregular ity is notoriou s. This reapproa chment
was signalize d in Septemb er l 964 by the negotiati on of a Treaty of
Alliance between these two Bodies. This action impelled many Masons
of the Grand Lodge of France, who valued regular and tradition al
Freemas onry, to seek asylum in the National Grand Lodge. A District
Grand Lodge was organize d to cover the period of transition , which
included negotiati ons and experime ntal trials. The result has been that
the stature of the National Grand Lodge has been enhanced as the
only regular Grand Lodge in that country. Over ] .000 former members
of the Grand Lodge, grouped into thirty Lodges. have come over to
the National Grand Lodge, and of the thousand new members who
have been raised, 850 are native French, which indicates that the National Grand Lodge is becoming more represen tative of France.
The situation in Cuba remains perplexin g. As we reported in 1962.

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORN IA

141

the Grand Master, Dr. Juan Jose Tarajano , was forced by the Castro
Governm ent to flee to Florida where, with the permission of the Grand
Lodge of Florida, he set up the Grand Lodge of Cuba in Exile, and
performe d outstand ing services to the many refugee Masons from
Cuba by helping them reestabli sh themselves Masonic ally and economically in the United States. However , on Decembe r 31, 1966, Dr.
Tarajano relinquis hed his powers as Grand Master and declared that
the Grand Lodge of Cuba would enter a period of complete recess.
He also urged that Cuban Masons in exile affiliate with regular Lodges
in the places they now reside. However , in March l 967, the Grand
Lodge of Cuba in Exile in Florida was called to labor. and a new
Grand Master, Laureano Pino was installed .
The Grand Lodge of Cuba in Havana. of which Dr. Valdez Castello is Grand Master, is still working, and claims not to be dominate d
by the Castro Governm ent, although it admits it is facing difficult, trying
times. Most of its external affairs are in charge of Pa~t Grand Master
Carlos Manuel Pineiro, who is also an ex-Presi dent of the InterAmerica n Masonic Conferen ce. and a member of its Commission for
Informat ion for Recognition, and who resides in Puerto Rico. At present
there are delegatio ns in Californ ia accredite d by each organiza tion,
and prelimin ary work has been done to determin e the position of Grand
Lodge under the pertinen t Masonic law.
We have under consider ation requests for recogniti on of the Grand
Lodge of Pernamb uco and the Symbolic Grand Lodge of Brasilia, both
in Brazil. We regret to say that these requests have been pending
before your Committ ee for sometime but we have not been able to obtain the facts and informat ion concerni ng the organiza tion and tenure
of these Grand Lodges. The Grand Lodge of Brasilia was constitut ed by
the Grand Lodge of Goias, which neither we nor any other Grand
Lodge of the United States, except Michiga n, recognize; and the Grand
Lodge of Pernamb uco is only recogniz ed by Kentuck y and Missouri .
For this and other reasons, we suggest that the said requests be put
over for further investiga tion and study.
We. therefore , move adoption of this report and its suggestio ns.
Respectf ully submitte d,
WILLIAM RHODES HERVEY, JR•• Chairman
