REPOR T OF COMM ITTEE ON COMM ERCIA LISM
To the Most Worship ful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Commercialism submits herewith its report for
the year just ending.
No infractio ns of our laws, rules and regulatio ns requiring serious
action on the part of this Committ ee have come to our attention and

142

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

because of this the report will be brief dealing mostly in generalities.
Our Symbolic Lodges have presented no difficulties that were insurmountable. The Scottish and York Rites have likewise been no
problem. It was only among the appendant or pre-requisite organizations
that there was any a ppreciable amount of counselling necessary. This
required quite a bit of correspondence on occasions, while with others
a phone call or a meeting s traightened matters out. The trouble here
is that the outgoing officers fail to brief the incoming officers on the
Regulations Governing Organizations subject to the Juri~diction ~f
this Grand Lodge as printed in the appendix to the California Masomc
Code and it thus becomes a matter of education.
Generally speaking the Shrine has kept pretty well in line though
there are still several items that must be closely watched so as to prevent
violations inadvertently.
The philanthropic image of mankind in connection with the Shrine
a nd its hospitals over the past years has built in most people's minds
a picture all tied around the hospitals and the good they do so that
certain other endeavors are sometimes misinterpreted. This matter has
our attention and in due time a recommendation will be made to the
Grand Master.
There have been a few instances where certain Masters have been
a pproached in an endeavor to sell Past Masters Jewels which indicated
the use of a Masonic roster but our investigations found such was not
the case.
Also there have been a few insta nces where business cards have
turned up carrying the square and compasses and on contact have
ascertained that the person involved was either not regular or a sojourning member; in every instance so far, correction has been promised.
The lack of complaints apparently has been brought about by education over the period of years and the fact of this committee's existence
which gives members of the craft and prerequisite bodies a place to ascertain the facts and to look before leaping. If for no other purpose,
your committee is happy to serve.
On occasion we have found it necessary to contact certain of the
Grand Lodge Officers who have been most helpful. To our Grand
Secretary and his staff our sincere thanks.
T o our Grand Master for his kindly counsel and advice on a
number of occasions, our special thanks. It has been a pleasure to have
served under him.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON LODGE FINANCING
To the. Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M . of California:
The Committee on Lodge Financing respectfully submits for your
approval and adoption this report indicating its activities and tr~n~ac­
tions relating to the fin ancial matters of Lodge and Temple Assoc1at1ons
operating Temple properties within its jurisdiction for the past year. An
analysis of the report reveals continuing and definite progress in the
construction, maintenance and operation of Masonic Temples throughout the jurisdiction. During the year, 305 Temple Associations and
Lodges have submitted to the Committee for its information, study
and review, statements of the financial status of their transactions and
other matters relating to Masonic T emple processes and controls. This
is in conformity with the requirements of Section 200 of the Masonic
Code. These financial statements disclose that each year more and
more interest is being taken in the efficient conduct of the business and
financial affairs of Masonic Lodges. The increasing and continuing
success of the financial operations of M asonic T emples gives cause for
the Committee to again recommend that the Lodges owning T emple
properties (who have not as yet done so) form non-profit Temple A ssociations to conduct the business and financial affairs of their Lodges. During the past year the Committee acted upon 74 applications relating to
the purchase of property, construction a nd maintenance of Lodge facilities. The Committee approved 19 applications for the transfer of
funds from the Lodges to the Temple Associations for use in matters
relating to Temple construction , operation and maintenance; 11 re~
quests for the p"urchase of property for future Temple sites; 3 requests
to enter into contracts for the construction of new Masonic Temples;
19 requests for capital improvements, expansion, renovating and repairs; 4 requests to borrow funds; 11 to form Masonic Temple Associations for the purpose of conducting the fin ancial affairs of the Lodges;
3 requests to enter into satisfactory leasing agreements: I 6 requests
to invest in Temple Association stock, and other various items. Full
details of all the transactions are contained in the Grand Lodge files.
These. with other miscellaneous requests, required necessary action
of the Committee in approximately 115 proceedings. During the year
numerous visitations were made to Lodges throughout the jurisdiction
to advise and counsel with the brethren concerning problems affectin!'.f
Lodge and T emple Association properties. These visitations, made upon
the invitation of the Lodges, were most satisfactory and in almost every
instance problems confronting the Lodges were resolved.
It has been most gratifying to note the increasing interest of the
Lodges in keeping their Masonic Temples in proper order and repair.
This is most important, as the image of Masonry created by good
housekeeping, both within and wihout the Temple, must be maintained
in order that the fraternity may continue to enjoy the regard and re-

144

145

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

spect of their respective communities and the s tate. Elevators, heating
and cooling systems, and other accommodations a re being installed,
which result in great benefit to the brethren and to the comfort and
enjoyment of all others who have the privilege of using the Lodge facilities. Continued neglect in maintaining the Temples in proper order
can only result in their obsolescence. Self-content , apathy and neglect
are as sinful and destructive as enthusiastic endeavors are virtues. When
enthusiasm and interest are lost, neglect takes over and Temple buildings gradually become decadent and obsolete.
There is no substitute for earnest enthusiasm if we are to conquer
the threat of obsolescence. It takes little time, little financing and little
effort, but with continuing perseverance to keep Temple properties up~
graded, we will keep pace with the growth of the community, thereby
maintaining the high image that our fraternity deserves.
If every Mason would contribute but one hour per month to the
benefit and welfare of his Lodge, you can well imagine the terrific im~
pact this would have on the strength and growth of Masonry in California.
Neglect in attending your Lodge meetings. failure to support Grand
Lodge programs. neglect of the obligation you must have to yourself.
can only result in a diminishing and damaging lack of interest in the
entire membership.
The Committee continues to recommend that the Lodges and
Temple Associations constantly review their insurance program in order
to be certain that they are properly insured in all requirements necessary
to protect their property and their members. Also, occasional review
should be made as to their status relating to tax requirements of all
local, state and federal agencies. The requirements as to tax exemption
should be adhered to in order that the Lodges and Temple Associations
conform to all existing laws regarding tax matters.
The Committee on Lodge Financing expresses its appreciation for
the assistance and encouragement given by our Grand Master, Laurence
E. Dayton, and other officers and members of Grand Lodge. We are
also extremely grateful for the help and assistance given us by Grand
Secretary Ed Siems and his most efficient and accommodating staff,
for without their splendid cooperation, the Committee could not carry
out its functions. With such assistance, cooperation and encouragement
from everyone concerned, the privilege of serving Grand Lodge on this
Committee is most gratifying and rewarding.
Masonry is growing stronger in California and its strength will
continue to grow so long as its members have the enthusiastic endeavor
and determination to build and maintain Temples creditable to the fra-

ternity; Temples where they may commune together with their brethren
in harmony to dedicate and re-dedicate themselves to be diligent in
their work, to live creditably and act honora bly by all men.
Respectfully submitted,
MARK A. GREEN, Chairman

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON
PROGRAMS FOR STUDENTS
T o the M ost Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California:
The members of the committee commend you for giving attention to
the subject of programs for students. We believe that a successful program is vital to the Fraternity and the continued progress of Masonry.
Each member also expresses his appreciation for being named to the
committee and for the opportunity to contribute toward the welfare of the
youth of California.
The Masonic Home at Covina, splendid as it is. is not suitable for
implementing a program for students past the high school stage.
In the latter area the Fraternity has made a notable contribution in the
erection of the Masonic clubhouses at Berkeley and Westwood aimed a t
the welfare of college students. The history of the clubhouses commences
around 1920. They have required financial support from Gra nd Lodge
at a rate which now approaches $50 ,000.00 per year. A total of over
$ 1.000,000.00 has been appropriated by Grand Lodge for the clubhouses
since they were built.
Large as these figures are, an investment of this kind is well within
the capacity of California Masonry provided the intended benefit to
students is being achieved. Unfor tuna tely, the clubhouses are no longer
serving their intended use. A chronological history of the rise and fall
of the clubhouses is attached hereto. marked "EXHIBIT A."
Profound social and scientific changes have taken place during the
last forty years which militate against the usefulness of the clubhouses.
Transportation and communication have so improved that students are
in close touch w ith their homes and other parts of the state. T he original
need for study and social areas has been compensated by the magnificent
library. student union, auditorium and other buildings erected on the
campuses at public expense, with which we cannot and do not care to
compete.
The second principal factor which has changed during the same
period is in the structure of institutions of higher learning. The original

146

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

clubhouse at Berkeley was planned at a time when that was the only
s tate university. The building at U.C.L.A. was added when that university was known as the "Southern Branch." However, the university
now has eight branches with still others planned and the state colleges
have advanced in importance and attendance. In addition, the junior
college or city college has developed until they are as common as high
schools used to be. Late figures list 253 institutions of higher learning in
the State of California.
By maintaining clubhouses at Berkeley and Westwood we are at best
providing facilities for less than 7'/c of all university and college students
in the state. We are servicing two institutions of higher learning and
neglecting the other 251. Additional comments in the nature o f supplementary data regarding the Ma sonic clubhouses are attached hereto,
marked "EXHIBIT B."
It is the firm conviction of the special committee that the Masonic
clubhouses should be sold and that the struggle to keep them in operation should be given up. It is wasteful to appropriate large sums of money
annually to purposes which no longer have popular appeal to young men
and women . It is unfair to other institutions of learning to concentrate
our efforts on two campuses when there are so many others scattered
around the state.
These findings were carefully considered both in committee meetings
and by individual members of the committee who investigated independently, and now recommend that the clubhouses be sold and converted
into cas h. Real estate appraisa ls w hich we believe to be reliable indicate
that a total o f $1,000,000.00 may be realized by Grand Lodge from the
sale of the two properties.
The termination of the clubhouse program will leave Grand Lodge
without any activity in behalf of the young people of college age. The
second phase of our study has therefore concerned itself with the best
possible program we can devise for the assistance of students.
The committee sponsored by the National Association of Secondary
School Principals came to the conclusion that probably close to half of
a ll high school students should be given some kind of vocational education, whereas only 13% are at present. They recommend that the range
of courses should be broadened, classifying such courses as follows:
"Occupational education - training for the simpler jobs such as
food service, nurse's aide, gardener, furniture repairman. These jobs,
says the committee, will increase in number despite a utomation and so
offer the best hope for young people with limited ability.
"Traditional vocational education - training for jobs in agriculture,
business. trade, home economics. These include jobs as auto mechanic.
appliance repa irman, sales. clerk and office machine operator.
'Technical education ...\; training for such jobs as draftsman, computer systems programer, tbol and die technician, technical writer, dental

hygienist. These jobs would in most cases probably require one or two
years of post-high school training."
Other authorities have declared that the greatest need in the educational picture is more vocational and trade schools. A d isproportionate
amo unt of attention has been focused on the young man and woman of
exceptional ability, the " Grade A" student. College courses generally
are designed with such students in mind, and scholarships are provided
so that in cases of need the gifted young person will obtain the needed
education. It would seem that no one cares about the mechanical or
average student. We have forgotten tha t "a good plumber is better than
a poor philosopher."
Another point to be considered is that those who decide to acquire
skills in the vocations and trades often come from disadva ntaged families
and are therefore in greater need of financial help than those w ho pursue
the liberal arts and sciences. They also may look forward to profitable
employment so that it is the belief of the committee that there is no need
to make outright gifts to such students, but only to advance them needed
funds on a loan basis to be repaid in easy installments when employment
is obtained. We believe this is in the best tradition of America and the
Fraternity.
The committee favors the establishment of loan funds for the assistance of students interested in vocations and trades. We should remember that our Fraternity sprang from an operative art. Our founding
fathers were the skilled mechanics of their day. They had gone through
a period of apprenticeship and training. They had mastered the secrets
of their day. They had the proficiency which today wou ld be taught in a
vocational or trade school. It therefore seems fitting and proper that we
as Masons s hould encourage young people to become the Master Masons
of the twentieth century in vastly more sophisticated fields.
Individual loans need not be large in size. The ra ther sparse funds
available for this purpose are usually in amounts from $25.00 to $300.00
per year. A more realistic basis might range from $100.00 to $1,000.00
per year.
In speaking of voca tional and trade schools we do not refer to commercial trade schools but to some sector of the public school system. They
a re operated by high schools or junior or city colleges. Such schools have
departments aware of the financial problems of the students, and this information s hould be sought out and used when the Grand Lodge program is instituted. However, we do not thi nk that the selection of applicants should be left entirely to school officials. W e have Masons in all
parts of the jurisdiction and with a little organization, they can be put in
a position to screen the recommendations of school authorities.
The committee has been impressed by the critical need for vocational
and trade assistance and has reported accordingly. Educational studies
are pointing to the same glaring lack in our system. It is therefore likely

147

148

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

that the imbalance will be corrected in the course of a few years or a
decade. Other needs will doubtless appear such as the likelihood that
tuition will be charged in state schools.
We would not want our funds channeled rigidly into one phase of
education when needed in some other phase. Many scholarships go begging because there is no flexibility to their requirements. Masons a re
interested in the public schools and in higher education. They want their
funds used where they will do the most good . If we can limit our loans
to vocational and trade purposes we will be selecting a single channel
to meet the need of the moment. That was done when the clubhouses
were built. The need gradually disappeared but the clubhouses could not
adapt to changing needs.
We favor a flexible s tatement of purposes so that the funds of G rand
Lodge may be used to best advantage. Outright grants or gifts in the
form of scholarships should be possible in addition to loans and academic.
technical and professional subjects come within the jurisdiction of the
committee or commission administering the fund.
The possibility of augmenting funds available for the educational purposes covered by this report by means of gifts and bequests should not
be overlooked. We have well-to-do members interested in young people
and anxious to help. who have been frustrated by a lack of a Masonicoriented program for students. It is our belief that substantial funds will
be forthcoming if a program of the type we envision is established and
it is given adequate publicity and a reasonable period of successful operation.
A permanent, single fund is needed so that a clear designation may be
made in wills written today and which may not be probated for 10 or 20
years. One suggestion to designate the fund is Masonic Grand Lodge
Educational Foundation. It is likely that a separate non-profit corporation
should be formed under the title selected. thus giving identity to the work
and protecting the name of the foundation from infringement. Care should
be taken to keep the non-profit corporation under the control of Grand
Lodge to see that the corporation has tax-exempt status and that
transfers o f money or property will enjoy exemption from gift. inheritance
and estate taxes.
'
The recommendatio ns we make to carry out the various items in this
report are as follows:
1. That the operation of the Masonic clubhouses a t Berkeley and
Westwood be discontinued, the properties sold and the proceeds turned
over to Grand Lodge.
2. That the proceeds of sale be used as the nucleus of an educational
foundation, the income and as much of the principal as seems desirable
to be used for the education of young people.
3. That a name be selected for the operation. such as Masonic Grand
Lodge Educational Foundation, and that an appropriate legal form be

adopted such as a non-profit corporation having perpetual existence, all
subject to the ordinances of Grand Lodge.
4. That the annual appropriations formerly devoted to the clubhouses

Student Programs with authority to act fo r him in screening applications

EXHIBIT B
SUPPLEMENTARY DATA REGARDING MASONIC CLUBHOUSES

Many changes have occurred since the Clubhouses at Berkeley and
U.C.L.A. were established.
1. Services initially provided at the clubhouses, and which were then
lacking on Campus (such as the finding of jobs and housing for students)
are now adequately provided at the University.
2. Since the clubhouses were founded, the number of campuses of
the University of California has multiplied, the state college system and
junior college program have come into being, and the students from
IV!asonic families distributed accordingly. In addition many such students
attend private colleges and universities.
3. Grand Lodge now has no program for the benefit of students not
attending the two campuses at Berkeley and U.C.L.A. Numerous inquiries have been made regarding this situation.
4. The experience at Berkeley and U.C.L.A. indicate that a clubhouse is no longer the best way of helping students, either there or elsewhere. And in any event, the cost of new clubhouse projects would be
prohibitive.
5. If the two clubhouses are continued. with an outlay by Grand
Lodge of about $50.000 a year. representing a per capita tax of more
than twenty cents, the Grand Lodge will be without financial means to
inaugurate or implement new programs.
6. Recent appraisals indicate that a net of $1,000.000.00 may be
anticipated from the sale of the two clubhouse properties. Returns on
the investment of such a sum. together with a continued appropriation of
$50,000 a year by Grand Lodge would make available approximately
$100.000 a year for scholarships or other types of aid to students.
7. The bequests left to our Home at Covina for students aid suggest
that a foundation administered for the benefit of students, both Masonic
and non-Masonic, would attract considerable new money ove.r a period
of time and expand the opportunities for service to youth.
8. The experience at this year's receptions for the Grand Master, at
the two clubhouses, confirms the declining membership and use of the

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON
MASONIC RETIREMENT HOME PROJECT
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your special committee on the Masonic R etirement H ome Project
held a series of meetings of all the members of the committee and add itional meetings were held by the committeemen in the north and south.
A great number of existing retirement projects were surveyed in some
depth by the committee. These projects ranged from complete care
medical homes to minimum care apartment type residences. Your committee was impressed by the many complex factors disclosed by its investigations.
The Grand Mas ter's directive was for the committee to make a study
of the need, desirability, problems, and type of facility. The committee
addressed its attention to these points.
The committee agreed that the need for a retirement home project did
not exist. It found there are large numbers of fiscally sound projects in
existence which cater to the most wide variety of tastes and preferences .
The committe agreed Grand Lodge might as a matter of policy find
it desirable to develop retirement home facilities as an opportunity to provide additional service to its mem bers. This service might be considered
desirable even without a demonstrable need.
The committee considered many problems discovered as a result of
its investigations. The committee agreed that some of the major problems
requiring additional attention should the project be considered desirable,
include:
Corporate Organization. The problem of determining if the home
should be independent or a subsidiary of Grand Lodge and
whether it should be a profit or non-profit enterprise.
Financing. The problem of providing the considerable financial
requirements involved, the extent of which depends on the corporate organization and type of facility.
Tax Status. The problem of the possible effect on the non-profi t
status of Grand Lodge itself.
Government Control. The problems involved with the supervisory and regulatory control over such a home by such agencies

156

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

as the Internal Revenue Service and the California Department of
Social Welfare.
The committee considered the many types of facilities in existence
such as urban or suburban, guaranteed life care or medical group insurance, separate residential or community and others. The committee
agreed it could not make recommendations on a type of facility without
first determining membership interest and other information.
As a result of its extensive studies, the committee concluded that
should such a project be considered desirable, expert professional advice
would be essential. Such experts in the field of retirement homes are
available and the committee understand a feasibility study would cost
from three to ten thousand dollars.
All records and data assembled by the committee together with the
minutes of its meetings have been collected and are available.
This assignment has been a most enlightening experience to all the
members of the committee and the opportunity for them to serve is deeply
appreciated .
Respectfully submitted,
IRA W. COBURN, P.G.M .. Chairman
w. STANLEY DAVIS
ROBERT VAN HEEKEREN

REPORT OF COMMIT TEE ON
CONSTIT UTION OBSERVA NCE
To the. Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
Some 180 years ago the thirteen fledgling states chose from among
their community leaders some .6.f~-flve delegates to attend a Constitutional Convention. Of this number, approximate ly one-half are said
to have been Masons. Among the active leadership of the Convention
were men well-known for the part they had already played in creating
this new nation-men who in many instances were also known as
leaders of the Mason.ic Fraternity of their day. George Washington ,
the presiding officer of the Convention and hero of the Revolution,
who was later to be our first President, had been Master of his Lodge
in Alexandria, Virginia. Benjamin Franklin, known to all as perhaps
the greatest intellect of the day, had served as the first Grand Master
of Masons in Pennsylvan ia.
The interest o! Masons and Masonry for the political wellbeing
of our nation is, therefore, well established and dates back to our
founding fathers. Against this backdrop, what could be more natural
than for the Masonic Fraternity of today to be among the leaders in
promoting an awareness and appreciation of the Constitution of these
United States. which document delivers into the hands of its citizens
the right of democratic self-determination and guarantees to each citizen those basic rights desired by all mankind, and reserves to the
people the power and responsibility for government .
In spite of this historical position of Masonic leadership in community affairs, far too many of our Brethren today suffer from the
same apathy which prevails among our citizenry as a whole. Your
Constitution Observance Committee, therefore, has a two~fold job-it is not only necessary to alert the public as a whole to the splendors
of that great document of freedom given us on that immortal daySeptember 17, 1787- but it is also necessary for us to wake up our
own "sleeping" Brethren, and to remind them of the many blessings
we enjoy in this country because of our Constitution.

158

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

In attempting to fulfill this two-fold roll, the members of your ~on­
stitution Observance Committee have actively encouraged the various
Lodges of this jurisdiction to hold appropriate ceremonies commemorating Constitution Day. These efforts have met with varying deg.rees of
success. In many instances the Lodges have be£n most cooperative and
most appreciative of the efforts of the Committee, and have responded
with vigor to the Proclamation as promulgated by our Grand Master.
Many excellent programs were prepared and presented within the
confines of the States of California and Hawaii. Many Masons spent
many hours in preparing suitable programs for presentation to their
Brethren and their neighbors. These Lodges and these Brethren should
be commended for maintaining this position of leadership which has
been traditional among Masons. It is the opinion of this Committee
that the quality of the programs which have been presented during
the year 1967 has continued to improve, however, the same basic complaint of lack of attendance and general apathy still prevails.
Unfortunately. too many excellent programs were poorly attended.
both by Masons and by the community as a whole. It would appear
that continued emphasis must be given to co-sponsorship with other
community organizations; to increased publicity; and to programs
which can be presented to an audience already gathered for some other
purpose.
your Committee is encouraged in that the Masters of the Lodges
in the jurisdiction seem to be increasingly aware of their obligatio~ to
present a suitable Constitution Observance Progr~m . The Commit.tee
also recognizes the practical fact that the enthusiasm for prese~tmg
a suitable program seems to be directly related to the enthusiasm
of the District Inspector for the Constitution Observance concept.
Where an Inspector is energetic and actively encourages the Lodges
of his District to present programs, fine programs are usually the
·result.
The enthusiastic leadership as evidenced by our Grand Master, Sr.
Grand Warden and Jr. Grand Warden, and the cooperation of the
Grand Secretary's office has been particularly encouraging to your
Committee, and we roost certainly express our appreciation for this
fine support.
Finally, credit for the progress to date and for the fine programs
which have been presented must go to the Masters, to their Constitution Observance Committees, and to those Masons themselves whose
interest and support were so clearly illustrated by participation in the
planning and presentation of the various programs throughout the
jurisdiction. Your Committee extends its heartiest congratulations to
every Lodge where a successful program was held, and assures those

159

incoming Masters that your Committee stands ready to do everything
possible to encourage even more successful programs for 1968.
Respectfully submitted,
RICHARD L. RIEMER, Chairman

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M . of California:
Two Lodges have been instituted since the 1966 Communication
of Grand Lodge: Camarillo Lodge U.D. on January 27, 1967, and
Gemini Lodge U.D. on March 17, 1967. Both have petitioned for
charters.
Each Lodge submitted its records for examination and representatives of the Lodges were interviewed by the Committee. In each case
the records were complete and, while minor changes were suggested
by the Committee, the records and proceedings were satisfactory and
met the standards required for the granting of a charter.
Camarillo Lodge U.D. is located in the city of Camarillo. For several years the formation of a new Lodge in this community was delayed
because of a lack of a suitable meeting place. This enthusiastic group
of Masons has surmounted this problem by acquiring their O\\Tn land
and temple. This property is presently held in trust by officers of the
Lodge with ownership to be transferred when it is constituted.
Gemini Lodge U.D. is located in the city of Fremont. Because of
its close proximity to the Masonic Home at Union City, this Lodge
has had a close affinity with our brethren there. The Institution Ceremony was held in Siminoff Temple so that many guests of the Home
were able to enjoy the occasion. The interest and enthusiam of Gemini
Lodge was also demonstrated in the Homes Endowment contributions.
They placed fifth in the Lodges of the Jurisdiction with 100% of the
members contributing an average of $9.51 each.

COMMEMORATIVE STAMP PROJECT

Worshipful Buck R. Nelson, Master of Tuolumne Lodge No. 8,
submitted a proposal that efforts be made to secure the issuance of a
commemorative stamp depicting the old red brick, two story school
house atop Cemetery Hill in Columbia Historical State Park, as a
symbol to education in California.
The school house was originally built by volunteer labor of the
citizens of Columbia, and dedicated by the Grand Lodge of California
on November 5, 1860. The school children of California contributed
their nickels and dimes, and teachers their 50c pieces toward the restoration of the building, 1955-56. After restoration to its original design
and furnishings. it was rededicated by Grand Lodge on November 5.
1960.
The objective would be to have the date of first issue of the stamp
occur during a future Public Schools Week.
The Committee has approved this project, and correspondence has
been initiated with the proper officials. Certain formalities must first
be complied with. In due time it will be appropriate for groups and
individuals to communicate with Postmaster General Lawrence F .
O'Brien, Washington, D.C. 20260, for referral to the Citizens' Stamp
Advisory Committee which is authorized to make decisions on behalf
of the Government.
Correspondence at this time would be premature. When appropriate,
full information will be disseminated to the fraternity.
The Committee is of the opinion that Grand Lodge action is not
required, that the Committee has authority to pursue this subject
as it does other media of promotional efforts in behalf of the Public
Schools; also that when appropriate, the matter of Grand Lodge endorsement is discretionary with the Grand Master.
We are informed that the Postmaster General has a backlog of about
3000 requests for a Memorial Stamp. that about 200 to 300 proposals
per year are received; and that about 15 of the selected and approved
stamps are issued each year. Moreover, there are rather rigid sta nda rds
set forth as to subject matter, which mus t be of national interest. Obviously, a detailed study is called for. Friends in high and low places
may need to be solicited for support. This is not a routine achievement
Further report will be made in due course.

165

The Committee having considered the subject of expenditure of
Lodge funds for purchase and presentation to public school facilities
of a Bag of the United States, and staff. assigned to a sub-committee
the task of preparing a proposal dealing with the subject. The subcommittee reported at the meeting on July 28, 1967.
It is noted that at the 1958 Communication of the Grand Lodge.
then Grand Master Leo E. Anderson announced a decision as follows :
"Question: May a Lodge purchase from its general funds and present a United States Bag and its staff to a public school within the
jurisdiction of the Lodge?"
"Answer: Support of our public schools is a program required by
Grand Lodge. and under Sec. 410. C.M.C .. such a purchase and presentation could be made, but the expenditure should be limited to an
appropriate amount." 1958 Proceedings, p. 25.
The Committee on Jurisprudence approved the Decision. 1958 Proc.
p. 293.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes opposed the Decision. at least in part on the ground that "we fail to connect it with
the support of any particular Grand Lodge program." Grand Lodge
supported the negative recommendation of that Committee, and voted
not to approve the Decision. 1958 Proc. p. 294.
Such action was drafted into a syllabus appearing as 409z C.M.C.
It may be significant that the question ruled on was general as to
time, place, and occasion, and that no reference was made to a public
school cornerston·e or dedication ceremony performed under the auspices
of the Grand Lodge.
It should be noted that the cost of a cornerstone is a proper Lodge
expense as a part of a Grand Lodge Program (Sec. 410c C.M.C.) .
The Committee has reviewed the situation, and believing that a
properly restricted authoriza tion for purchase and presentation of a
United States Bag, and its staff, would be in order, makes the following
recommendation :
That Section 409.z of the California Masonic Code
be cons trued as a general ruling only, subject to specific
exceptions. and that the cost of a United States Bag and
its staff to be presented to a public school or school facility
at the laying of a cornerstone or a dedication, under Grand
Lodge auspices and Masonic ceremonies, is a proper
Lodge expense as a part of a Grand Lodge program.
ALL YEAR ATfENTION

The subject of year around attention to the problems of public
schools offers a problem in itself. When it became known that we were

166

167

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

interested in an all year effort, we were besieged with suggestions and
ideas. We invited suggestions from the school administrative executives,
we received proposals from the local chapters of the Parent and Teachers Association. We were told that we should be concerned whether the
State of California should go back to the old policy of contributing 50%
to the costs of local education, whether the local bond elections in various
school districts should be sponsored, and many other things.
The chairman of this Committee, at his request, has been on the
mailing list of certain associations. The reading time on the publications of these groups. has been inordinately long. It is startling how
many subjects and how many issues involve the public school system
today.
A subcommittee has been appointed, and is working on the topic
of what we can do, and should undertake, in support of the public
education in California and Hawaii on a year around basis.
It is understood that a depth study of our educational system, with
problems presented. is in course by an organization of which the Senior
Grand Warden is a member, and that the results of this study may
be made available to this Committee. Possibly our own programming
may be advanced if and when this occurs.
Meanwhile, we have three broad avenues of approach. The first,
and obvious, is for us to be alert to any issue of major importance to
the whole school system (statewide in California or Hawaii). When
such an issue is detected. careful analysis and thorough dissemination
of information to our membership should be made.
The second is the same type of action by local Lodge groups, with
the aid of this Committee. on local issues concerning the welfare of
the public schools.
The third, and by no means the least important, has to do with
personnel in the school system, ranging from the teaching staff up to
the highest boards in the two states. Some o f the board members are
elected. For the State of California they are appointed by the Governor. Replacements on the State Board of Education, and a newly
created Board for Junior Colleges will be composed of new appointees.
Steps should be taken promptly to inform the Masons of this jurisdiction of such impending appointments, and alert them to steps which
can be taken in selection and support of suitable nominees.
There is a further long range step open to us which will be discussed next.

questionnaire, suggested that an all around benefit could be realized
by handin§" to each newly t'aised brother along with other printed
material supplied him, a brief treatise on Masonry's interest and efforts
in behalf of the Public Schools.

QUESTIONNAIR E

A letter with a questionnaire was sent to the Masters of all Lodges
in California and Hawaii. It was dated July 10, 1967, and requested
return by July 25th. The mechanics of preparing .the ~ore th~n 700
copies and mailing resulted in most of the questionnaires bemg .received a day or more later than the requested return date. In view
of this. some Masters probably thought that a reply would be too late
to be of value, and of course. some undoubtedly were on vacation. As
a consequence, t}le return of nearly four hundred answers is an excellent
response. and the gratitude of the Committee is expressed to those who
furnished answers. As of this writing, 375 answers have been received, and no doubt more will be at hand when this report is Sled.
The information provided is of great value in analyzing, and planning future programs.
For example, the official posters, while not ordered, and apparently
not considered important or useful in their own special circumstances, by
a few Lodges reporting, were ordered by more tha~ 300 of the. Lodges
answering the questionna ire. (The Grand Secretary s office advises that
there were 282 orders, but the discrepancy could be accounced for by
the fact that some of the orders placed with the Grand Secretary were
by Districts, or other unofficial groups of Lodges . As for the remaining
3-400 Lodges. we may only assume that they either had no use for the
posters or followed a local custom of purchasing and using displays
originating with local committees or organizations.
The conclusion is to be drawn that there is enough interest and
response to continue the posters. From information gathered, it appears
that the bumper or windshield stickers do not have enough support to
justify their continuance. True, there are some areas where they are
preferred to posters. but the overall use of them has been too isolated

168

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

and their use too minimal. The Committee, therefore, has decided not
to print or distribute any stickers for the 1968 observance.
. One question asked related to the Lodges holding or participating
m the 1967 Public Schools Week Observance. The Lodges responding
reported that 355 of them did so. Only 20 did not. Moreover, two
of the latter were Research Lodges, and in lieu of actual participation,
these Lodges furnished speakers, and should be considered in the
affirmative group.
On the question as to the type of program which the Masters of the
Lodges considered more effective, the replies were quite enlightening.
Due regard must be given to local conditions, where one program or
the other is peculiarly well suited to conditions. However, taking the
over all situation, we find the following :
Those designating School Open House Visitations as first choice
numbered 233.
First choice of Lodge programs were 35.
For public programs the vote for first place was 90.
No choice, 17.
If you take the vote on a point basis, as first, second and third choice,
you find an overwhelming selection in favor of the open house school
visitations, the second choice is public programs, and well down the
line in third place is Lodge programs.
None can deny that the open house offers a great appeal for parents,
friends, and children. We note that many Lodges combine with that
certain designated committees, or teams, members of the Lodge, who are
assigned to specified schools, as a welcoming or host committee; also
that special programs in the auditoriums or gymnasiums are often staged.
We have a vast amount of material being analyzed and a future
report will be made thereon.

GRAND ORATION
"A TALK ABOUT CANDLEPOWER "
• WARREN HARRISON, Grand Orator
(Delivered by Warren} . Blom~th)

Most Worshipful Grand Master. Distinguished Guests
and Very Dear Brethren:
It is the Grand Orator's duty to deliver an address at each annual
communication, to the Grand Lodge, upon matters appertaining to the
craft, and to deliver such other addresses as may be required. Unless
this is, as I suspect. a dream, I have the privilege and pleasure to address
you as the Grand Orator of the State of California. To me, on this day,
no other order exists than THE MOST WORSHIPFUL GRAND
LODGE, FREE AND ACCEPTED MASONS OF THE STATE
OF CALIFORNIA.
When Brother Dayton assumed office as our Most Worshipful Grand
Master he expressed the desire "to increase the candlepower of Masonry." This is a most commendable theme and should continue to inspire
us in the future, as it has in the past, to take Masonry at its altar and
let it accompany us in our daily lives, that we may reflect the principles
and tenets of our Ancient and Honorable institution and induce others.
also, to hold them in due veneration. Masonry teaches men so to live,
that they may be flt to die, I can pay it no higher compliment.

170

171

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

An experiment in a great amphitheatre in Southern California, demanded that each individual present hold aloft a lighted candle. when
the electric power was cut off the degree of illumination was practically
unchanged. I am sure the impact would be just as effective, if each of
you return to your respective Lodges at the conclusion of this communication with the firm resolve to present to your present members, as well
as to your novitiates, the working tools of Masonry.
I do ~o~ h~sitate to admit that the answer evoked from me on my
first adm1ss1on mto the Lodge made a deep and lasting impression on my
mind. Today I realize that "when we put our trust in GOD" we need
not fear what man can do unto us. The volume of the Sacred Law comes
to us from the hands of Jewish Scribes from time immemorial. and may
w~ll be call~d the cornerstone of Judeo-Christian faith . Perhaps you
will agree with me that in five days the Israelites recent miraculous deliverance from the hands of their oppressors, was wrought by more than
hu~an h~nds._ I am just as confident that with HIS blessing, our own
nation will umte to lead the world as the Champion of Freedom.
Masonry performs its work in the hearts of men and among nations.
To dignify the human race, we must begin with one man at a time, one
initiate at a time. The same working tools that are indispensable to the
jurist must be available to the gardener, the carpenter, the farmer and
the blacksmith. Perhaps the finest example to illustrate this point would
be the invitation extended by Teddy Roosevelt to a friend of his in
Washington, D.C ., during the time he was serving as President of The
United States, to accompany him to Lodge that evening to witness the
conferral of the Third Degree by the gardner down the street. It was
reported this Brother did a very fine job with the ritual. No man reaches
such a pinnacle of success in this world, that he cannot profit from a
refresher course in the principles and tenets of our Ancient and Honorable Institution.
When people are governed with the consent of the governed, it is
essential they be an enlightened and a vigilant electorate. Spiritual and
Moral enlightenment. vigilance and militance are just as important to
our people today as they were in the founding of our country. James
C. Penney-a Mason of the 33rd degree says "Our Country is great, not
by accident, but because our forefathers hewed out an existence on the
eastern shore of this continent, with the Bible in one hand and an axe
in the other."
When citizens the length and breadth of our land. admit to them·
selves, and more importantly to GOD Himself, that they are putting their
trust in HIM, woe unto those who represent us in the halls of congress
or as ambassadors to foreign shores, should they be less dedicated to
their duty to GOD, Their Country, Their Neighbors and Themselves.
The.re is no more practical way to divide our time than we find suggested m Masonry, a part for GOD and a distressed worthy brother.

a part for our usual vocations and a part for refreshment and repose,
nothing more conducive to a well ordered life than to divest yourself
of all its vices and superfluities.
Were one to travel no further than the first degree, he would be in
pcssession of the tenets of brotherly love, relief and truth. Were I to
embark on this subject time would run out on me, and I would not have
begun on temperance, fortitude. prudence and justice. Surely if there is
something wrong with us as individuals, the fault is not to be found in
Masonry, only in our ability to assimilate its teachings and incorporate
them in our daily lives.
When the volume of the Sacred Law becomes the great light in your
profession, when your reverence for GOD is tha t which is due from the
creature to his creator, when you act upon the square with your neighbor
and discipline yourself. you shall begin to expect others to show concern
for that which you hold so dear. Your life takes on new meaning, your
country has a better citizen, and you suddenly realize that you are responsible for the preservation of our Ancient and Honorable Fraternity,
in order that future generations might have access to this unencumbered
source of enlightenment, and the serenity that only the heart can define,
when a task has been well done.
The history of man has witnessed one religion after another spring
up, grow for a time, decay and die, and give place to another. The
frame.rs and the select few, will understand these great principal truths
that are the foundation of all religions, but the people will ever worship
idols and images, either carved of wood or stone, or found on earth or
in the heavens, or the gross material ideas and images which, in their
own minds, they will form and enthrone as representations of the Deity.
The applicant for the degrees of Masonry, may be a member of most
any religiows faith, so long as he believes in GOD and a future existence.
Collectively perhaps it might be said that Masons understand what is
commonly referred to as religion, better than religion understands
Masonry. Among the various religious denominations in America are
those who suspect Masonry to be a threat to their domain. It would be
a great source of satisfaction to me to be able to convince all dedicated
religious leaders that Masonry offers the most fertile soil for them to
cultivate. Just as we choose from many makes of automobiles as a means
of conveyance to our earthly destination, we are most serious in the faith
that will enable us to finally arrive at that House not made with hands,
eternal in the Heavens.
Having an appreciation for the sophistication of today as compared
with yesterday is not at all difficult . As a boy the wall telephone was a
luxury in our home, the telegraph amazed us all and the worlds com~
merce plied the oceans powered by the sail. While I don't consider
myself as an old man, it seems we have traveled quite a way, with the
Tellstar conveying the word and the scene to my living room just as they

172

173

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

are. A debate between statesmen in Washing ton, London and Paris,
as if on stage in your home town, while the atomic powered vessel sails
round the world numerous times without the need to refuel.
Small wonder that man has been impressed with his technological
skill, and most of us have been quite content to help to pay the bill, until,
our ego carried us a bit too far and we asked "Is there a GOD." Herein
lies the danger to us all, and it had to come to this. Lest we put our
trust in mas we have the council of Solomon, the wisest of all; "There is
nothing new under the Sun"-and he said this over 900 years before
Christ. So I appeal to you not to let sophistication interfere with indoctrination.
Shall I humble you further? I'll quote from St. John: "The wind may
blow where it listeth and we hear the sound thereof, but we know not
whence it cometh nor whither it goeth, and so is everyone born of the
spirit." Or if you prefer: "Man born of a woman is of few days and
full of trouble, he cometh forth like a flower and is cut down. He Heeth
also as a shadow and continueth not, seeing that his days are determined,
the number of his months is with thee. Thou hast appointed his bounds
that he cannot pass."
The greatest safeguards for the prevention of letting our pride destroy us are found in our Ancient Landmarks. and most important in
this world of flux, THEY CAN NEVER BE CHANGED.
The immortality of the soul cannot be proven by science, nor demonstrated by the powers of logic, but only by faith , and its own instinctive
consciousness that it is not material nor dissoluble like the body. Science
can no more preform the functions of faith, than faith can decide in
matters of science. To believe and to know are two terms that can never
be confounded, nor can they rightfully oppose each other in any antaganism whatever. Science is absolutely impotent in deciding if we
are right or wrong in believing a dogma. Faith, in itself, considered as
a physiological fact, is evidently a necessity and a force. GOD can
only be defined by Faith. Science can neither deny nor affirm that HE
exists. The true certainty is the reciprocal acquiescence of the reason,
which knows, in the sentiment, which believes. and of the sentiment.
which believes, in the reason, which knows. The definitive alliance of
reason and faith will result from their absolute distinction and separateness. but with their mutual control and fraternal concurrence.
Masonry is defined as a system of moral advancement, veiled in
allegory and taught by the use of symbols. Abraham Lincoln thinks of
the Tree as the symbol of character and the shadow as our reputation.
Only in the light of day is the shadow to be found, just another reason
to take our Masonry out into our daily lives. Some young man may be
observing you and measure the Lodge by the impression you make upon
him.
I must assume that questions that disturb me are of some concern

to you. Do we think that our lives should be devoted to submission to
the leadership of others, or should we strive to become leaders ourselves?
Do our fellow men convince us that we are qualified? Or do we decide
for ourselves? Having decided our role, that of leader or subject, we
must then determine the direction to travel and possibly envision a goal.
This transitory life provides little time for each of us to make these decisions, become qualified, then meet the complexities and changes each era
of man's progress on earth presents.
Today's decisions might be simpler when viewed in the light of tomorrow, but we must make them here and now. First we must realize
our grandchildren's lives will mirror the effectiveness of our stewardship
today. History affords satisfactory assurance that mortal man is capable
of tyranny or love, oppression or compassion, freedom or slavery, with
far reaching consequences.
These are indeed critical times. We have every right to consider
them as such for the pages of history record no period in which worldwide confusion, intrigue, hysteria, falsehood, etc., have been so effectively employed against the masses of peoples throughout the world.
Nations lie against nations, striving to force their way of life into common acceptance. After lies and propaganda have been promoted repeatedly, even the perpetrators begin to confuse their dribble with facts .
Modern communication devices have made of what was formerly considered shocking propaganda, commonplace in our time. We may
conclude that people have been talked out of their liberty with far too
much regularity.
The best defense against mass hysteria and mass hypnosis does not
begin with a treatment of nations or states, it begins with the desire of
each individual to preserve his own dignity, as a duty to GOD, His
Country, His Neighbor and Himself. When a man is sovereign over
himself he is not vulnerable to the glamorous Hauntings of attractive
dogma, he brings his sentiment and his £eason, his GOD given talents
to bear in his judgment of pertinent matters that are vital to the welfare
of himself and mankind. Sincerity and plain dealing are necessary to
convince such a man regarding justice and equity, he is not to be categoried into some division of gullibility, nor is he to be dominated by
mortal man, only by GOD who spake him into existence.
A nation of such men. armed with vigilance, will prove that "Rational
Liberty is the Mother of Freedom." The cry today should not be.
What is the matter with our Nation, rather, what is the matter with
ourselves? An improvement in the spiritual and moral fibre of ourselves
as individuals, will pay a dividend to our Nation not approached since
1776. Perhaps we shall not be greater than our neighbors, but we will
be better than ourselves.
It has always seemed natural for man to seek to dethrone the champion. Our nation, so richly endowed, was given its birth by the founding

174

PROCEEDING S OP THE

fathers. it was welded into a union by their successors, toda,y it remains
to be seen if our nation so conceived, and so dedicated, can long endure.
This is our challenge. as we stand before the world as the "Champion
of Freedom," perhaps its last bastion. the TRUTH is our armour. it has
made us free and it shall keep us free. The TRUTH as tried in the
crucible of time, that indispensab le ingredient to the dignity of man.
the foundation of every virtue.
Masonry is the subjuga tion of the human that is in man, by the divine.
It is the conquest of the appetites and passions by the moral sense and
reason, the continual effort struggle and warfare of the spiritual against
the materia l and sensual.
As the Mason advances from one degree to another, he develops a
desire for further light in Masonry. Often the light may shineth in the
darkness and the darkness comprehend eth it not.
I am sure all of us are aware of the constant struggle in every man's
nature between light and darkness, good and evil. success and failure.
etc .. and though none of us may be licensed to account for the importance
GOD places in our ability to cope with these opposing forces. their constant recurrence in our daily lives compels us to deal with them in a
manner that we hope meets HIS approval. Simply put. it is the struggle
between the divine will. implanted in man by GOD. and the natural
will. prone to vice and error. and caused by the frailty of the flesh.
Nothing great has ever been built, without an opposing force against
it. Consider the birth of our nation; against tremendous opposition. our
founding fathers pledged their lives. their property and their sacred
honor. won the struggle. then met in solemn engagement to debate and
compromise. and ultimately perfect a constitution that has been proclaimed by legal authorities to be "the greatest governing document ever
written by the pen of man." All that remains is the test, eternally. for
each generation to preserve. through our militance and eternal vigilance,
this great heritage of ours.
Do you measure light from the absence of darkness or darkness from
the negation of light? Are you a success because man can point to no
instance in which you have failed, or have you neglected to participate
through fear that you might? Have you enjoyed the serenity of those
who exert the talents wherewith GOD has blessed them? Do you think
of a thing as just because GOD has willed it, or that GOD wills it
because it is just? Would another mortal man's answers satisfy you or
are you sovereign over yourself?
My Mother was fond of reminding me that GOD works in mysterious
ways. HIS miracles to perform; yet most of us have been guilty. on
occasion, of permitting our finite minds to question HIS infinite wisdom
in permitting so much evil to exist here on earth. I suggest we consider
for a moment the lowest form of animal life. the amoeba, that lies on
the bank of the pool, consumes nourishment . waxes fat, grows strong

and multiplies. Here let us pause for a moment and reflect, could this
description apply to man? Perhaps ourselves? Surely the manifold
blessings and comforts which surround us. and the talents HE endowed
to man, combine to make an investment on which HE should enjoy a
rich return. Clearly visible on today's horizon is our need to unite all
of the world's GOD fearing men into one sacred band. or society of
friends and brothers to dispel the godless tyranny of communism .
We realize that in the eyes of The Great Creator. our lives are but
"a speck on the horizon of eternity." But each of us is important to Him ,
so important as to be brought into the world by His Hand. nourished
each day by His Divine Providence. and ultimately harvested for His
Kingdom. We feel that man cannot live by bread alone, and that He
was concerned about our spiritual and moral edification , when He stated
throug h The Son of Man, those prophetic and dogmatic words, " You
will know the Truth and the Truth will make you free."
As your name is dropped into that vast crucible. that melting pot
that we know as America, may we hope it contains enough spice of
independenc e to counter the dregs of apathy. placed there by regimented
thinking and mass indoctrinatio n so popular in the world today.
So you are an individual. Difficult isn't it? So many forces of so
many different natures, vie with each other to make o f you a conformist.
This organization would lead you. and hold you, in a particular religious
tait h; while that one enlists your political support. and still another may
pull at you to perpetuate a racial image. All these and others dictated
by your fraternal associations , business and vocational interests et_c .•
place the burden 'upon you to conform to their requirement s and. still.
if you so desire, try and remain an individual.
Many of us carry the vision of the strong, independent spirit that
carried the 49ers across mountains. plains. rivers and deserts to establish
their homes and their futures, on the remotest frontier of our blessed
land. Their concern, during this trek, for associations and organization s,
was limi ted to the simple requirement of common defense against the
elements and the pirates confronting them on their journey. Only the
indispensable, fundamenta l and humble principles and tenets. gained
passage for them. Faith in GOD. Hope for success of their venture and
sufficient love for each other to form a band to penetrate this vast wilderness.
Once established in a fertile land, only time was needed for the
organization s to appear, demanding their loya lty to this and tha t, until
an organization of ones own self was required, lest his convictions go
out with the tide. The organization s were here to stay. they had followed
man in all his crusades. He must choose those that he identified with,
"for to himself he must be true."
As we view the world scene today, we are grateful that our nation
rates first among the forces of freedom. Men of every land seem eager

to obtain United States citizenship and participate in our many privileges.
For a nation to reach this position of leadership in less than two hundred
years, there must be a reason. I believe this reason to be the separation
of church and state; that each may proceed in its duties without interference from the other, where the religious faith you support, is your
choice as an individual. and where the legislative representative to your
government, has to have your vote to be empowered to act.
We find ourselves confronted with strife in many fields, Communism
-how to judge who among our allies are sincere and dedicated to freedom, and who would appease it for material gain; Civil Rights-how to
implement it in to all our lives, for freedom must be earned, not bequeathed; Technological Change-how to make it serve men, all men;
Social Adjustment-care for the old, the very young and those to whom
life has not been kind; Tolerance and Understanding-a searching for
issues upon which men of all creeds can agree, ·r ather than contend; and
Education-for true enlightenment is a great ally of Freedom.
The success of our country's future depends, not on mass regimentation and indoctrination through modern communication media, but upon
a nation of individuals who can think for themselves. Having been
indoctrinated in the principles and tenets of Masonry, it is up to the
individual Mason to combat the sophisticated, unwarranted departu·r es
from time tested conventions, to guard against any allurement to vicious
practices. This, in one sense, I believe our Grand Master felt, when he
asked us to increase our "Candlepower."

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDENCE
To the. Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The within report is submitted covering the stewardship of the Com~
mittee for the fiscal year 1966-1967.
The members of this Committee have devoted many hours in 'r eviewing proceedings of other Masonic Jurisdictions and to whom Cali~
fornia has extended Masonic recognition.
1 regret to announce the passing of Maurice Ross of San Diego, a
member of the Committee for many years, and his passing has been
a loss to all of us.
The Grand Master replaced Brother Ross with William Mason,
formerly President of the Los Angeles Board of Relief, and his selection has proven to be an excellent one.
We wish to extend our appreciation to the Grand Master, Laurence
E. Dayton, Edward H. Siems, Past Grand Master and Grand Secretary,
and Newcomb Condee, Editor-in-Chief of the California Freemason, for
t.heir counsel and advice.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

177

There are 129 Masonic Jurisdictions which are recognized by the
California Grand Lodge. consisting of 48 Masonic Jurisdictions in the
United States, which include the District of Columbia. The State of
Alaska include their proceedings as a part of the State of Washington
and the State of Hawaii is a part of the California Grand Lodge, the
balance being in Jurisdiction of 48 different foreign countries and who
are fraternally recognized by the Grand Lodge of California.
We endeavor to review all Masonic Jurisdictions, except those
which publish their proceedings in their native language.
The reviews of Masonic Jurisdictions are promptly submitted to
the Editor-in-Chief for publication in the California Freemason.
Available space has not always permitted publication of all reviews
submitted.
We have endeavored to submit our reviews in an interesting and
informative manner, but we are always seeking constructive suggestions
as to how these reports can be improved.
The principal matter of concern to all jurisdictions is the problem of
suspension of members; the loss of members in some jurisdictions, most
of which were primarily due to deaths of the many candidates raised
in the period of and immediately after World War II.
It is heartening to read that Masonic Jurisdictions are intelligently
seeking to handle all of these problems by encouraging lodges to take
greater care in selecting their officers and particularly their Masters. to
the: end that a strong leadership creates greater interest among the
members in their individual lodges, and others who are interested in
becoming Masons:
It is repeatedly pointed out in proceedings of other jurisdictions that
we should not regard 250 or more years of successful Masonic operations with complacency. or as an occasion for reflection upon past
achievements, but rather as a challenge for greater accomplishment
through a continuing dedication to those time-honored principles that
have brought honor and prestige to our venerable Fraternity.
A budget of $150.00 is requested, which represents an increase over
the $I 00.00 existing budget; yet in view of the fact that the greater part
of the $100.00 represents charges by Grand Lodge for its expenses in
connection with the Committee, this has left only a nominal sum, which
is not adequate to finance the Committee's annual breakfast at the Mark
Hopkins Hotel in San Francisco. These meetings have been constructive
and informative and this year the Editor- in-Chief will be present.
Respectfully submitted,
GEORGE W. BURCH. JR., Chairman

REPORT OF BOARD OF LIBRARY COMMISSIO NERS
To the. Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F . 6 A. M. of California:
The summer issue ( 1966) of the California Freemason had this to
say about the Library of the Grand Lodge: "The Library and Museum
were established by legislation enacted by Grand Lodge in 1957. There
has never been a suitable library since the fire of 1906. The functions
of the committee are: To make available to Masons seeking light, books
suitable for (A) the newly made Mason, ( B) the studious Mason,
( C) the Brother seeking to make a more exhaustive study using reference books, ( D) the collection. preservation and display of items of
Masonic interest. especially those dealing with California Masonry.
In this short time, and with the attendant pains which always plague
the organization of a new facility, we have had the gratification this
past year of being complimented on the facility thus far established by
visitors from both England and New South Wales. Our record of
visitors is up by 267 this year, an increase of 12 %. This is a total of
1944 in the twelve months from July 1, 1966. to July 1, 1967.
Other statistics of vital significance to our total Masonic membership
in California. as well as to the governing members of Grand Lodge,
have to do with usage of the Library. From July 1, 1965, to 1966 (twelve
months) 146 books were loaned. And in the like period ending July 1.
1967, there were 235 books loaned. This represents an increase in
usage during the past year of 89 units or 60%.
During this same twelve month period we accessed 267 additional
books, of which 212 were donated to the Grand Lodge Library. Our
total of books now on the shelves is 3250 volumes.
Note should be made of certain items accessed this past year. In
particular, there were 38 items for the Museum:
Certificate of Membership in Meridian Sun Lodge, Georgia, of William W. Traylor, P.G.M., who was the sixteenth Grand Master
of California. Presented to the Museum by Doctor Eugene S.
Hopp. S.G.W.
Items taken from the cornerstone of the Federal Building at Stoc~
ton, California, at the time of demolition in 1965. Building was constructed June, 1901, and the cornerstone laid with ceremonies by the
Grand Lodge of California on June 24, 1901; Past Grand Master
Orrin S. Henderson. Presented to Museum by Stockton Record.
Crocheted antimacassar centering a six inch square and compass
and a two inch letter "G". Presented to Museum by L. Harold
Anderson, P.G.M.
Apron and regalia worn by Cyrus H. Ober at the first inauguration
of George Washington as President of the United States. Presented
to the Museum by his son. Jackson S. Ober. Note: This was pre-

sented to Grand Lodge in 1920 but received in the Museum this year.

It is the consensus that the increase in usage of the Library during
this past year, the increase in accessions, and the increase in interest
evidenced by the record of visitors, is substantially the result of the
publicity so carefully prepared and set forth by the California Freemason. Much of the current interest became immediately apparent upon
publication. And it appears that once our members become aware of
the availability of this service, they continue to use it. We shall. as a
consequence, endeavor to make better known to California Masons the
a~ailability of book lists, both to visitors and by mail, so that this great
Library may be truly a statewide institution and serve all Masons of this
jurisdiction.
With the continued support of Grand Lodge, and the fine foundation now established by some of our really dedicated members, we are
sure that we can add further lustre to a Library of which every California
Mason can be truly proud and make this Library and Museum of great
use and interest to all of our members, regardless of where they find it
convenient to have their homes within the bounds of the United S tates.
Particular credit should be noted for the four regular members of our
staff: Brothers Scott, McMaster, Simpson and Young. These men
have manned the Library and Museum on regular days throughout the
year for our convenience and they have handled all of the detail encumbent on the operation of a lending library as well. The cataloguing,
together with the accessions, are an important detail of the management
of an accessible library. And this is an appropriate place to note that
we will welcome other brethren who will have the time to devote a day
or two to this service during the week.
We call attention to the new Manual in possession of each Lodge.
Un~er the heading of "Masonic Education" there will be found a page
on, Your California Masonic Library." This page explains the use of
the Library; how books may be borrowed; how it may be used for reference work; and gives classified lists of available references to give easy
access to these resources of your Grand Lodge.
If additional copies of this page are desired by any member of any
California Lodge. they are obtainable on request from the Grand
Secretary.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON DeMOLAY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
Your Committee on DeMolay has enjoyed a productive year with
the full cooperation of all members. We find the Order of DeMolay in
California to be in a healthy condition with a modest increase in total
membership. Most chapters are quite active in their pursuit of " Building
Better Citizens." DeMolay inspires boys to become better sons , better
men and better leaders. as well as serving as a dynamic force in combating juvenile delinquency. Your Committee has several recommendations
which it feels will ultimately make DeMolay available to more boys.
The committee members feel an obligation to assist in the expansion of
DeMolay of California.
We have submitted a proposed budget to the Finance Committee in
the amount of $1.500. Itemized, the budget consists of $375 tra vel
expense for 15 members, $350 each for 3 brochures. and $75 for postage
and stationery. We trust that this proposed budget meets with your
approval.
In the past, DeMolay has met its own financial needs and it will
undoubtedly do so in the future. This year your Committee has noted,
with approval, the formation of the DeMolay Foundation of California.
This is a non-profit corporation set up to accept contributions (tax deductible) which will be used for the promotion of DeMolay at the Jurisdictional level. A fifteen member board of trustees representing mos t of
the appendant bodies, serve as incorporators with Merritt Rowland as

182

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

President and Leroy Williams as Secretary. The by-laws of the Foundation have been filed with the Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge.
Interim guide lines were discussed and established at the first meeting of the year for the guidance of the Committee. These guide lines are:
1. To serve as a liaison between the California Grand Lodge F. & A. M.
and the California DeMolay Administration.
2. To develop and propose recommendations to the Grand Lodge concerning the relationship between the Grand Lodge and DeMolay.
3. To develop ways and means of providing assistance to the DeMolay
administration and subordinate chapters.
4. To develop materials to be used to increase understanding and communications between the Grand Lodge and DeMolay.
Several sub-committees were formed to implement the projects selected by the Committee for development:
a. Brothers Lester G. Bruno, Leo J. Green and Garfield G. Laiblin
worked and reported on a sub-committee to create a speakers'
bureau, to make available effective speakers for special youth
organization functions. These speakers would be drawn from over
the entire state and would be able to communicate with their
youthful audiences. Subjects would be varied but it is felt that
the speakers should be Master Masons, if possible.
The sub-committee also indicated that the California Research
Lodges should be informed of the speakers' bureau and should
consider the possibility of developing papers on topics of general
interest to youth.
b. Your chairman headed a sub-committee to draft a questionnaire
to be made available to the DeMolay administration for use by
them. Each DeMolay advisor would be required to complete the
questionnaire before his appointment would be confirmed. The
questionnaire will cover elements of the requirements and regulations of the Grand Lodge of California. The objective is to provide
a better understanding of our rules and regulations for the new
advisors serving DeMolay in California.
c. Brothers Homer Rathbun, Wendell Anderson, Darrall Dickson
and Grover White comprise a sub-committee on brochures. It was
felt two brochures should be developed, "Facts About Freemasonry and DeMolays" and "Information About the Order of DeMolay for the Master Mason." With the appointment of a
committee on Youth Orders, brochures should also be developed
for the Order of Rainbow for Girls, and Job's Daughters. Funds
have been requested for this purpose.
d. The DeMolay Committee as a whole, strongly recommends that
a Masonic Youth Committee be appointed by the Master of every
lodge. It is suggested that the Junior Warden be appointed chair-

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

183

man. The newly raised Master Mason would automatically become a member of this committee. He would be provided with
brochures and information on the youth organizations and urged
to attend and participate in the functions. He would be called
upon at stated meetings for a report, thus involving him in the
affairs of the lodge. He should have a card of introduction from
the Master and act as a representative of the lodge. A committee
of this kind was utilized by Brother Voudouris when he was
Master of Sacramento Lodge, No. 40, with excellent results. The
benefits of a committee of this kind could be considerable, both to
the lodges and to the youth groups.
Your Committee has received every consideration and courtesy
from other Grand Lodge committees and from the Grand Lodge
officers. However, we detect a feeling of complacency in many
of the subordinate lodges. These lodges are the source of the
power and influence of Masonry. To combat this complacency
we strongly urge the formation of Masonic youth committees.
The DeMolay Committee wishes to express its appreciation to the
Grand Master, Most Worshipful Laurence Dayton, for his active interest and support and to the Grand Secretary for his counsel and
guidance. The Committee also expresses its appreciation to the advisors
and adult leaders of DeMolay. Without the dedicated service of a
relatively few men, the Order would wither and our young men would
develop their ideals from others sources.
Respectfully submitted,
JoHN L. WIXON, Chairman
