REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON
MASONIC EDUCATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Four years ago, in I 963, the Chairman of this Committee, Dr. Eugene
S. Hopp, presently our Senior Grand Warden, outlined a brief history
of Masonic education in this jurisdiction. It was noted that in 1854 Grand
Master Charles M. Radcliff spoke to this Grand Lodge concerning the
need for attention to the area of education. Adoption of Article VI of the
Revised Constitution provided for a standing committee on education ,
and the pattern for future years was thus established.

184

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Since 1915, with few exceptions, a Masonic education report is to
be found among the annual reports made to this Grand Lodge. And over
the intervening years, it would be quite impossible to estimate the time
and energy expended by this Grand Lodge in the area of Masonic education. Even a cursory examination of its reports reveals a constant and
consistent effort to stimulate, encourage and foster an even better
program of Masonic education in the Constituent Lodges. Each sue,.
ceeding report contains some evidence of progress, valuable suggestions
and predictions relative to new opportunities for further service, expanded programs and activities.
This annual report is no exception. It follows the well established
path of careful inquiry or investigation in the continued search for means
and methods of carrying forward the concept of Masonic education at
the Lodge level. This is our purpose and constant goal. And as long
as Freemasonry remains, Freemasonry, educational programs such as
we now have will continue, because the individual member needs them.
We would be less than honest if we didn't admit to occasional difficulties
and seemingly slow progress in the cause of Masonic education. But
should we become temporarily discouraged, we need only recall the
wisdom of George John Whyte-Melville: "Education should be as
gradual as the moonrise, perceptible not in progress, but in result".
During the past year, this Committee continued a new assignment
which had been given them in 1966. In a Directive dated March 29,
1966, the Grand Master assigned to this Committee the duty and responsibility to "promote and correlate the work of the Research Lodges".
The Directive was adopted and approved by this Grand Lodge at the
last Annual Communication and included authority to "review all Research Lodge materials intended for publication ... to review all correspondence contemplated by Research Lodges with Grand Lodges of
other jurisdictions ..• and to regulate the display and sale of approved
publications of the Research Lodges". In this latter connection, it was
felt that since the Directive required that all published materials be
approved by this Committee prior to publication, that there could be no
objection to the Research Lodges continuing the display and sale of Research Papers and Research materials at the Annual Communication,
provided that all charges be established to recover only actual cost of
publication and handling. and further that sales be confined to the display area on the ground floor of the Temple. Certain instructions regarding specific steps in the handling and processing of published material also required clarification. Accordingly, the Grand Master issued
an "Instructional Procedure" under date of February 10, 1967 which is
attached to this report as a matter of record.
The officers of the Rearch Lodges have been most cooperative and
helpful in following prescribed steps for screening and submittal. and
most gracious in acceptance of alteration or rejection when such was

To the M ost Worsh ipful Grand Lodge F . & A. M. of California:

The past year has seen many change s in the activities of the Mason
ic
Club at the U niversity, Berkeley. Most o f the change reflects
directl y
the change in schedu le at Berkel ey from a semester to a quarte r
system ,
and has been reflected in progra m. Less time has been availab le
for the
large well-pl anned affairs and more "spur o f the momen t" activiti
es
have replace d these.
The campu s commu nity continu es to have problem areas and again
it must be pointed out that our studen t group have not been
active
partici pants in any of the widely publicized inciden ts. We hope
they
continu e to show the intense interes t in curren t affairs which they
now
have and that the leaders hip which is so necess ary will continu
e to
reflect the practic al approa ch to these problem s.
The two hostess es, Mrs. Janaice Kohl and Mrs. Stuart Keirulff. have
been able to change the functio ns to fit needs as they have develo
ped.
The studen t group rel y heavily on the sound judgme nt and guidan
ce of
these two women and they are to be comme nded for their efforts.
The Club House at Berkel ey has been a member of the commu
nity
since its erection over 40 years ago. The original reason s for its
formation may have been forgott en by many. but its presen ce in today's
academic world proxid es one more visible eviden ce of the Mason ic
suppor t
of free public educati on. No matter what change s may take place
in
years to come, those studen ts who have enjoye d the hospita lity and
congenial atmosp here of the Mason ic Club will never forget the
special
purpos e it serves. If any major change is to be made, it is our hope
that
it will greatly increas e the numbe r of studen ts who have been so
much
benefited by the Grand Lodge suppor t of the Club Houses.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. o A. M. of California:
In our report submitted last year, we reported some of the difficulties
facing the members of our club - the high grade-point average that
must be maintained by the officers, and the constant increase in oncampus activities for all students. The situation is further complicated
by the use of the quarter-system by the University which virtually means
that the college is conducting classes all year round.
We also reported that our membership was down but that the members of the club and the members of the Board of Directors, realizing
that there must be some stimulus to reawaken the interest of other students , embarked on a publicity campaign to bring the club message
before more people.
New enrollees have been sent brochures of the club's activities, the
Board has been successful in getting publicity in various publications of
Masonic and other affiliated bodies. We are indeed happy to report that
we have a complete functioning student council and our membership
shows an increase.
Reference to last year's report will show the various activities in
which our members engage each year. and some additional activities
have been added. this year.
However, we again urge you, the members of Grand Lodge, to go
back to your lodges and tell your members of the facilities available at
both Berkeley and UCLA . This is one of the important activities of
Grand Lodge and we want everyone to know what is being offered.
Those of you who have sons and daughters of college age, urge them
to join these clubs. They will be more than amply rewarded.
The budget for the 1967-1968 fiscal year is attached herewith.
Respectfully submitted,

We have three principal accounts. the Masonic Homes Endowment
Fund, the Masonic Homes General Fund, Grand Lodge F . & A. M. of
California, plus the several smaller funds of the Masonic Homes. The
record is kept by Moody's as one total fund. thereby reducing our cost
very materially. However. Grand Lodge records are kept separate as
to each fund. as are the records of the Investment Committee. As a
matter of interest. we list here the market values of the portfolios of the
individual funds. together with the income and yield at market prices:

- Santa Rosa Savings and Loan Association , Corona Foothill Lemon
Company, Ramona Savings and Loan Association (Fillmore) - to name
a few.
The entire portfolio is listed in the Grand Treasurer's and Auditor's
Reports, and therefore is not included herein. The securities are held in
safekeeping for account of Grand Lodge by the Trust Department of
the Crocker Citizens National Bank, at its One Montgomery Street Office. San Francisco.
We had excellent attendance at our Investment Committee meetings
during this year, as has been the case since this Committee was organized.
It was a pleasure to have M . W. Grand Master Laurence E. Dayton at
several of our meetings. Senior Grand Warden Eugene S. Hopp has attended all of the meetings this past year, and Junior Grand Warden
Robert A. Crigler attended the February and May meetings.
Again we come to that portion of the Investment Committee report
when we try to summarize in few words the financial and investment outlook as we see it.
Our sights always tend very strongly toward conserving assets. We
are sailing very close to shore, yet we recognize the inflationary elements
in our economy. In the judgment of the Investment Committee we should
not venture away from trustee responsibilities. The Prudent Man Rule
continues to be our yardstick. We have what we consider an excellent
diversified investment list of bonds and stocks, which are always under
scrutiny.
This is the f e~ling of your Investment Committee as to its course of
action in these difficult times. Some of its members have been through
many depression periods, and they can always produce plenty of reasons for a cautious and conservative approach.
Our Investment Counsel attends every meeting, and has always given
us sound and profitable advice.
We again repeat that our course of action can be quite different from
that of an individual for a variety of reasons. This statement is made so
as not to unduly influence individuals in their personal investment programs.
Our thanks to the Grand Secretary and his staff. and my thanks to
the members of the Investment Committee for their wholehearted and
generous cooperation at all times.
Respectfully submitted on behalf of the Investment Committee:

REPORT OF THE CODE COMMISSION
To the. Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F . 6 A. M. of California:
As this Commission has done after each Annual Communication of
Grand Lodge, a Cumulative Pocket Supplement to the California
Masonic Code Annotated was prepared, printed and distributed after
the 1966 Communication. In view of the changes, repeals and additions
to our Masonic Code over the last ten years, your Committee each year
makes a conscientious effort to succinctly state the changes and in keeping with this policy the 1966 Pocket Supplement contains only four
more pages than the 1965 Supplement.
The work of the Special Committee on Definition of Committee
Responsibilities and Code Review, of which your Code Commission
Chairman is a member, has made fine progress toward a complete Code
revision as has been suggested and needed. The continuing work by
subsequent Committees on Code Revision will produce a Code that
may be easily read and understood. The members of the Code Commission are ready and willing to assist this Special Committee in any
manner necessary to achieve the desired result.
This year your Commission has requested appropriation of $200.00
for its normal activities and a contingency fund in the event its services
are necessary to assist the Special Committee on annotations to our
Code.
Respectfully submitted .
HARLAN P. HUEBNER, Chairman

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC INFORMATION
To the. Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
The Public Information Committee held three meetings this year one in the northern part of the State, one in the south, and the third in
San Francisco; and a joint session at the opening of this Grand Lodge
Communication. To this last meeting, the presidents of the two Masonic
Press Clubs were invited.
The question that found greatest interest at all three meetings was
that of our Public Information policy. Should it be, as most now agree,
"If Freemasonry is good, let's talk about it," or should it be, as some
still feel. strictly a matter of behind-the-door secrecy.
The Public Information Committee re-affirms its position that indeed
Masonry IS good and we can very well do some talking about it.
This does not mean, of course, that everything pertaining to Masonry
be laid out to public vision. There are some things which are ours alone,
and rightfully should be. But there are, at the same time. many projects
of our Fraternity which are better for not being hidden. Our Public
Schools Week observance, for one. and our Constitution Month are
both projects of which we are justly proud, and about which we can
talk without hesitancy at any time.
To assist in this talking about Freemasonry, the Public Information
Committee has prepared. and now has on hand in the Grand Secretary's
office, a mailing list of selected statewide newspapers. These are on
addressograph plates and are so set up that a press release can be made.
statewide. in a matter of a very few minutes. It is the committee's recommendation that this Grand Lodge's press mailing list be expanded to
include radio stations. weekly papers. and certain periodicals making
an all inclusive Grand Lodge press mailing list for our general use.
It is also the Committee's recommendation that regular mailings to
these various media be made possibly. if not every month at least every
other month, cove.ring not only our Public Schools Week activities and
Constitution Month. but particularly our cornerstone ceremonies and
such. We should also give attention to such ceremonies as are attendant

202

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

upon the presentation of 75 year veterans' pins, as was the case this
year of the Brother, a member of Charter Rock Lodge in Berkeley.
There are good and ample reasons for such regular mailings. in the
opinion of the committee, not the least of which is the fact that the press
may thus become aware of us and will recognize our releases when they
arrive on the editor's desk.
The Public Information Committee recommends the setting up of
a definite annual Public Information program at the beginning of the
Grand Lodge year to include such activities as were started this past
year and which it is hoped can be carried on in the years to come. At
the suggestion of one of our members, the Committee set out to obtain
in-depth coverage on our Public Schools Week Observance in two, and
perhaps more, metropolitan papers in California. We met with and
discussed with among others, the western representative of the Sunday
magazine "Parade," a feature on Public Schools. We had not s tarted
soon enough, however, and so it was necessary to hold it over for the
coming year. We hope the new Committee taking over this year will
follow through and that proper emphasis will be given to the fact that
indeed Public Schools Week did start here in our own California Grand
Lodge.
As a final recommendation, the Public Information Committee asks
that careful consideration be given at an early date to the employment
of a full time professional Public Relations consultant to implement the
annually adopted program and to carry on any other public information
duties as may be assigned to him. This recommendation came originally
from the Northern California Masonic Press Club, and the Public
Information Committee further suggests that he be under the direct
supervision of the Grand Master, with such advice and assistance as
may be given him by the Press Clubs of Northern and Southern California.
This report is respectfully submitted for reference to the proper
committees.
WILLIAM H. ADAMS, Chairman

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PAY OF MEMBERS
To the. Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Pay of Members submits the following report
covering the I 18th Annual Communication of Grand Lodge.
Those entitled to mileage compensation are the Master, or in his
absence the ranking Warden or, in the absence of the Master and
Wardens, the duly Elected Representative; each Inspector, provided
he is reported present on the certificate filed with the Committee on
Pay of Members by the Grand Lecturer; Past Grand Masters; Officers
of the Grand Lodge; Chairmen of Committees enumerated in Section
192 of the California Masonic Code; members of the following Committees:
Jurisprudence, Policy and General Purposes, Grievances, Finance,
Credentials, Pay of Members, Charters, By-Laws, Correspondence,
Lodge Financing, and Code Commission who are actually in attendance
at Grand Lodge and who comply with all provisions as noted in Section
176 of the California Masonic Code.
Mileage from the various points within the State of California to
San Francisco has been taken from the published records of the California State Automobile Association. Mileage from points in the State
of Hawaii to San Francisco has been taken from the published records
of air lines, in accordance with Sections 171 and 176 California Masonic
Code. No compensation is allowed to members from San Francisco or
the immediate vicinity. Compensation of members from the State of
California has been computed on the basis of seven ( 7) cents per mile,
the rate fixed by the Committee on Finance. Compensation of members
from the State of Hawaii has been figured on the basis of the published
first class round trip air rate of regularly scheduled major air lines from
Honolulu to San Fra ncisco, plus inter-island air fare to Honolulu when
necessary.
The payroll has been checked with the registration records as submitted to us by the Committee on Credentials and the amounts required
to meet the transportation costs for the 1967 Annual Communication are
as follows:

REPORT OF COMMI TTEE ON CEMETE RIES
To the Most Worshipfu l Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committe e on Cemeterie s submits the following report of their
activities for the Masonic year of 1966-1967.
Our report for this year will be a very short one as the Committe e
encounter ed no new problems and was unable to progress any further
in the one problem left over from last year's report. This continuing
problem is the acquisition of the Red Dog Cemetery site as an Historical
Cemetery Area.
First in our general report we will cover those cemeteries now under
Grand Lodge care.
Columbia and Jamestow n being in the same area, Sonora, California ,
and under supervision of Committee member Marcel Baer, required
this year the usual spraying for weeds as well as general upkeep. Jamestown suffered greatly from the severe storms of the past winter. This
cemetery is surrounde d by very large and beautiful trees and the winds
damaged these to some extent. The severest damage, however, was to
the cemetery from falling hmbs. Some headstone s were damaged and
some castiron grill work was broken. As a result of this, more money
was needed for this cemetery than was planned for in the budget submitted last year. To cover the expense of repairing this cemetery and
trimming the trees, Brother Baer found it necessary to use some funds
allotted the Sonora area for Columbia . As a result of this we were not
able to paint the fence at Columbia. Our new budget for Jamestow n and
Sonora will reflect this in that a request is again being made for money
to paint the fence in our 1967-68 Budget.

206

207

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Both Jamestown and Sonora are being kept in a manner that presents
a picturesque setting to the visitor and reflects well on our Fraternity.
Brother Adrian Taylor, Committee member in charge of the Fiddletown Cemetery, reports that cemetery to be improving each year. The
usual spraying for weeds was carried out but in addition, large amounts
of brush overgrowth were removed. It was necessary to delay the installation of the projected gate to the lower area of the cemetery as requested
in last year's report as such an installation concerned other interests
besides Grand Lodge. These negotiations are being brought to an harmonious close and we are again asking Grand Lodge in this year's
budget to provide funds for this gate. This will allow the lower area
of the cemetery to become useful to the craft.
Brother Berkline at Quincy, a new member of the Committee, has
worked this year on the cemetery at Beckwourth. The Committee Report of 1957 called attention to the condition of this cemetery and to
the fact that the local Lodge was trying to solve the problem. This
cemetery was, three years ago, deeded over to the Portola Cemetery
District and is now called .. Whispering Pines Cemetery." A well bas
been dug, new trees and shrubs have been planted, a new fence has
been erected and grave markers replaced. The 1966-67 budget for the
cemetery district was $9,335.00 and Brother Berkline feels this cemetery
is well on its way to proper care.
In Southern California, Committee member Basil Gordon, Jr. reports
that the only activity there has been the projected dedication of a section
in a private cemetery in Bloomington for Masons and their families.
Marble for an altar is being sent from Italy and construction and composition will be supervised by Brother Gordon. The dedication is expected to be after the first of the year.
It is the suggestion of Brother Gordon that the Committee re-survey
all cemeteries and dedicated plots in private cemeteries. This would duplicate, after ten years, the survey of 1957. It would be our suggestion, if
such a survey is approved by Grand Lodge, that the survey of 1957 be
re-read by the Committee and plans made after such a study.
In the Valley area, our committee has the help of Brother Leslie
Woodworth and, though not a Committee member, it is due to his efforts
that we now have saved the remaining headstones and relics of Michigan Bluff and Omega. He also has worked to keep Red Dog Cemetery,
a very historic and heavily visited one, in presentable condition. As past
reports will show, Grand Lodge has voted each year that the Committee
try to have this cemetery and the land it is on given to Grand Lodge.
Our budget again this year requests the amount of $1,000.00 to rehabilitate Red Dog, should we be able to prevail on the land owner
to make a gift of the site to Grand Lodge. We feel this may be accom.P lished by continued work of the Committee and Brother Woodworth.
We also feel this cemetery has very great historic value to Masonry

and California , and that every means should be made to preserve it:
therefore. we ask that you of Grand Lodge again approve our request
for permission to continue these efforts.
In our budget for this year we are including an estimated amount
to cover a survey as suggested by Basil Gordon. This will cover travel
charges, etc. It is suggested that this report and budget request be considered by Grand Lodge in two parts - first, the formal report and
budget and, second, the supplementary suggestion of a re-survey of
cemeteries and the budget request for this survey.
Each year, as the cemeteries now under Grand Lodge care have
been brought up to better standards, it has been possible to reduce the
Committee's budget requests. Our budget request for the ensuing Masonic year of 1967-68 is as follows:

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON TAXATION
To the. Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A . M . of California: ·
Since filing our report for 1966. there have been changes in the payroll tax laws which apply to our various Masonic organizations.
As has been our custom in past years, we present, for reference
purposes, the usual schedule of tax rates and wage bases for the various
payroll taxes which will be in effect during the calendar year 1968 and
thereafter.
FEDERAL WITHHOLDING (INCOME} TAX

All wages paid to employees of a Masonic Lodge are subject to
Federal income tax withholding. In order to determine the amount of
income tax which is to be withheld from wages paid to its employees,
the lodge should ask each employee to complete and file with the Secretary of the lodge a Federal Form W-4. "Employee's Withholding
Exemption Certificate. " Reference to withholding tax tables furnished
by the Treasury Department will enable the Secretary to determine
the amount to be withheld. As you know from the coverage accorded
it in the press, there is a definite possibility of a tax increase in 1968
(and possibly by October 1st of this year) . In this event you would,
of course, have to secure new withholding tables.

209

As the law now stands an employee of a Masonic Lodge is subject
to tax for each calendar quarter during which he earns $50, or more.
The tax rates shown below are applicable to the first $6.600.00 of wages
paid to each employee during the calendar year. These rates are to be
paid by both the emplbyer and the employee.

more individuals who are paid $50 or more per calendar quarter, providing they have first qualified as an "employer" by employing four or more
employees on at least one day in each of twenty or more weeks during

Masonic Lodges will be subject to this tax if the total wages paid
during a calendar quarter to taxable employees are in excess of $100.
For this purpose a taxable employee is one who is paid $50 or more per
calendar quarter. However , whether or not elected or appointe d officials
of a Lodge are to be counted as taxable employees will depend upon
whether or not the Lodge is subject to the Federal Unemplo yment Tax
Act.
If the Lodge is not subject to the Federal Unemplo yment Tax Act,
then the wages paid to an elected or appointe d official will be exempt
from Californ ia Unemplo yment Insuranc e Tax unless the wages paid
to these officials exceed $100 per month.
If the Lodge is subject to the Federal Unemplo yment Tax Act, then
the wages paid to an elected or appointe d official will be subject to California Unemplo yment Insuranc e Tax if the wages paid to these officials
amount to $50, or more, per calendar quarter.
For purposes of this tax, the term "elected or appointe d official" will
include any official of the Lodge who is compens ated for his services.
Those usually compens ated for their services a.re the Secretary , Tiler,
Organist , and Soloist.

The Committee on Jurisprudence made the following explanatory statements:
Three years ago, G. M. Theodore Meriam appointed a Special Committee to study the use of liquor as it relates to Masonry. The report was
rendered at the I 965 Communication and the recommendations of the
Committee were adopted by the Grand Master in his Annual Message
at his own recommendation. The Grand Master referred the report to
the Jurisprudence Committee to draw the implementing legislation for
the 1966 Communication. This we did with the assurance of P.G.M.
Phil Myers, Chairman of the Special Committee, that the proposed
resolutions which the Jurisprudence Committee prepared carried out the
recommendations of his Committee.
Briefly stated; the Special Committee clarified and liberalized the
provisions of the Masonic Code relating to the use and sale of liquor
in the following material respects: (I will indicate the action taken by
the Grand Lodge on each item.)
( 1) Masonic Temples or temples of concordant bodies could be located and meet in buildings where bottled liquors were sold as incidental
to other businesses as in a grocery store, unless the advertisement of the
liquor was offensive or dominated the exterior advertisement of the building. Also, if a lodge inherited property having a prohibited use or, in good
faith, was burdened with an offending lease, the lodge was given the
reasonable time required to rectify the situation. This was passed by a
516 vote and is now Masonic law.
( 2) The membership of Masonic lodges and that of concordant
bodies (i.e., organizations requiring that their members be Masons)
were to be allowed to serve and consume intoxicating liquors at social
affairs or meetings in hotels, restaurants or other establishments serving
liquor but liquor was not to be served or dispensed in Masonic Temples
or in the temples or meeting places of concordant bodies. Also, open
installations could be held in public establishments but no liquor was to
be consumed or served during ti).e installation ceremony itself. Further-

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The Grand Master at the l 965 Annual Communication of Grand
Lodge requested your Committee on Jurisprudence to prepare legislation
for the purpose of effectuating the re·c ommendations of his Special Committee appointed to consider possible modifications of present Masonic
law respecting liquor. Your Committee has carried out this assignment
and hereby suggests the following legislation:
BE IT RESOLVED: That a new section be added to the California
Masonic Code, to be numbered section 324.2, to read as follows:
"Sec. 324.2. A Masonic Lodge, or an organization the prerequisite
of i:nembership wherein is that a person be a Master Mason, may hold
social gatherings, dinners, dinner dances, or other social events at which
intoxi~ating li.quors may be used, served and consumed, or may hold an
open mstallat1on of officers in a hotel, restaurant or other establishment
~erving ~iquor or operating a bar; provided, however, in case of an open
mstallat1~n of a ~asonic Lodge, the Grand ·Master must first approve
the locati_on as smtahle to the solemnity of the installation ceremony;
and provided further that no liquor shall be served to or consumed by
members or guests during such installation ceremony; and provided

215

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

more, the Grand Master had to approve .a s suitable the location of any
Blue Lodge installation. This extension was not passed last year but did
receive well over a majority vote and thus was carried over to this Communication and is embodied in Section 324.2 which the Grand Secretary
has just read to you.
( 3) A bartender or one in the bar business could apply for the degrees of Masonry and be judged by the same standards as any other
applicant, i.e., on his merits and not by his means of making a living so
long as his business was lawful. This section was passed last year by a
516 vote and is Masonic law.
( 4) The membership of all Masonic related organizations in this
jurisdiction, i.e., those requiring that members be Masons, were to be
governed by the same rules of conduct and propriety as is required of
Blue Lodge members in this jurisdiction. There were to be no classes of
Masons in this regard. This was passed last year by a 5/6 vote and is
Masonic law.
( 5) California Masons, while in other jurisdictions, were to abide
by the practices, policies or laws of those jurisdictions and also the practices, policies or laws of the California Grand Lodge which were not
inconsistent therewith. Masons of this jurisdiction, whether they lived
in the jurisdiction or outside, were to do nothing within this jurisdiction
contrary to the Masonic law thereof. This section was passed last year
by a 5/6 vote and is Masonic law.
In summary, as I have stated, the only material part of the Grand
Master's and the Special Committee's program not adopted last year
was proposed Section 324.2 which the Grand Secretary has just read
to you. It received about a 2/ 3 majority.
The Committee's proposed Section 324.2 and that proposed by
Brother Leo Anderson as number 5 of this year's resolutions, which you
have all received, are in irreconcilable conflict. The essence of the matter
boils down to this: The Special Committee's Section 324.2, carried over
from last year, liberalizes the Masonic law on the use of liquor at social
affairs, but it treats Blue Lodge and concordant bodies precisely alike
on the liquor question and would not permit liquor to be served or dispensed in the buildings and temples of either the Blue Lodges or the
Shrine, Scottish Rite and other concordant bodies. Brother Leo's proposed Resolution No. 5 would prohibit the use of liquor in Blue Lodge
temples but not in the meeting places of the Shrine, Scottish Rite or
other concordant bodies.
The real issue which you must decide, then, is whether all Masonic
organizations shall be treated alike on the liquor question or whether
there is a sound basis for distinction between the Blue Lodges and the
concordant bodies.
I might say that legislation is necessarily general in its application

and cannot define every precise factual situation. There may be individual cases which are unclear or difficult to determine. In these cases. the
Grand Master must give his interpretation of the sections, but I have
stated to you the basic issue and this is the one that you, the Grand
Lodge, should determine.
We move the adoption of Section 324.2 as recommended by the
Special Committee.
Failing a 2/3rds vote, the resolution was not adopted.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON DEFINITION
OF COMMITTEE RESPONSIBILITIES AND
CODE REVIEW
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Sixty days prior to this communication, copies of a report by this
special committee together with copies of thirty-six proposed amendments to the California Masonic Code were circulated with the copies
of the resolutions filed in accordance with Section 104 of the Code. As
the Grand Master stated in his message, most of these proposed amendments had been drawn prior to the 1966 Communication but the committee voted to defer presentation at that session. In preparing those
sections, it had become apparent to the committee that the mandate to
the committee could not be met merely by defining, in most instances for
the first time, tqe duties of the many committees which have been
functioning for varying spans of time.
Accordingly since last October the committee has prepared, debated
and approved additional proposed sections, to a total of eighty, covering
the matters presently found in Sections 2 to 265 of our Code, with the
exception of financial matters which had been referred to the Committee
on Finance. In July, looking back over what it had completed, the committee felt that some parts of its product might be said to be beyond the
limited boundaries of the direction given by the Grand Lodge. It accordingly withheld forty-four sections and filed for circulation only the thirtysix proposed amendments which were mailed out.
After the mailing, a majority of the committee became dissatisfied
with a piecemeal presentation of proposed sections and voted to recommend that action as to adoption or rejection be def erred to the 1968
Communication in the hope that next year's committee be authorized
beyond question to suggest changes in the Code w hich its deliberations
have caused it to believe should be made.
This special committee believes a committee should be appointed in
this area to serve during the ensuing year and that you should authorize
it, as the Grand Master suggested in the first paragrnph of his recom-

VETERAN BUTTONS-TWENTY-FIVE YEARS

(2)
To the. Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F . & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the Most Worshipful Grand Master has repeatedly
called our attention to the loss of members and the desirability of good
public relations; and
WHEREAS, we have been asked to build an image of Dignity, Quality and Substance, and be willing to show a personal pride in being
Masons; and
WHEREAS. many Masons are deprived of exhibiting their long
association with our Craft by wearing a Masonic emblem indicating their
years of membership;
THEREFORE. BE IT RESOLVED : that C.M.C. Ordinance 150
( b) which reads as follows:
"Veteran Master Mason buttons are to be provided by the Grand
Secretary, made from pure gold of California's hills, for presentation to
members of our Lodges who have been Master Masons in good standing

The Committee on Finance:
Resolution No. 2 proposes that Grand Lodge provide Veteran Master
Mason buttons, made of pure silver. to members of our Lodges who have
been Master Masons in good standing for twenty-five years.
The thought back of this resolution would appear to be a fine and
worthy gesture. However, no consideration has been given to the cost of
material or level of staff and effort to carry out the proposed presentation.
In order to give the Brethren some facts upon which to judge this pro~
posal, we offer the following:
A systematic count made of our membership 61es indicates that 16%

224

225

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

or 38,700 of our memb~rship would be eligible for the twenty-five Year
buttons.
What is the cost of an appropriate button, made of pure silver and
design we would be proud to wear? The supplier of our present fifty
button we feel should be well qualified to estimate such a cost. He estimates that the cost per button would be slightly more than $5.00 each.
Using $5.00 each as the initial cost of the button only would total approximately $193,500.00. The cost of mailing is estimated to exceed 20¢ each
and would add about $8,000.00 to our total cost. In addition to the cost
of the button is the cost of additional staff required to research the rec.
ords, package and mail the buttons.
Just to get the twenty-five year button program started, we estimate
that it would take an immediate increase of at least $1.00 per capita tax
per member. This is only the first step. A further study of the membership files shows that approximately 40% of the remaining membership
will be entitled to this button within the next four years or about 24,000
buttons per year. This would require that a substantial per capita tax
must remain in effect for a period of at least five years.
After a five year period it is anticipated that the program would continue at about 10,000 to 15,000 buttons per year or a yearly cost in the
area of $50,000.00 to $75,000.00.
The proposed program compared to ou,r fifty year buttons is monumentnl. We average about 700 of the fifty year buttons presented each
year, mostly through our Inspectors. The proposed twenty-flve year button program would be thirty-five times this number.
It is doubtful that we would be satisfied with an inexpensive or inferior button in material or design. We are also aware that certain Lodges
have been giving a button for some time and a Grand Lodge program
would result in duplications to many members.
In light of these facts, your Committee on Finance must conclude
that such a program would be an extreme financial burden on our membership, which cannot be sustained. Therefore, we strongly urge a no
vote on this resolution.

HISTORICAL LECTURER-LODGE OFFICER
(4)
To the. Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A . M. of California:
WHEREAS the Masonic Order is an ancient and venerable institution with its origins in time immemorial, and
WHEREAS its very antiquity is the basis and pattern for most
other lodges. conclaves, fraternities, even labor organizations, and
WHEREAS the genius of Freemasonry cannot have existed and
survived through the perilous centuries, often under hostile and tyrannical rulers, outlived the fires of anti- Masonic furore and hatred in our
own country in the nineteenth century, without creating for itself a
monumental. awe-inspiring. enviable history, and
WHEREAS. thousands of volumes containing this history repose
in libraries both public and Masonic, and
WHEREAS little has been and is being done to disseminate their
profound store of knowledge among our brethren in the constituent
lodges from the youngest Entered Apprentice to the eldest Master
Mason, and
WHEREAS many o f our brethren are thirsting for more light in
Masonry beyond that emanating from degree work and have demonstrated their interest and desire in one constituent lodge where the dissemination of such knowledge has been going on for the past four years.
now therefore be it

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

227

RESOLVED that this Communication of the Grand Lodge F&AM
of California herein assembled, establish officially the post of HISTORICAL LECTURER in the "line"of all constituent lodges under its jurisdiction, such station to be filled by said constituent lodges at their option,
this resolution merely constituting an authoriy for said office, nothing
contained herein to be construed to mandate the appointment of said
officer, but be it
FURTHER RESOLVED that said constituent lodges be strenuously urged and encouraged to exert every effort to seek out and appoint as HISTORICAL LECTURERS qualified and dedicated brethren
whose task it shall be to research and discuss Masonic history and related events at least monthly or oftener as decreed by the lodges themselves.
Respectfully submitted,
ED KE1Gw1N, M .. No. 315
Referred to Committees on Policy and General Purposes, on Masonic
History, and on Masonic Education.

The. Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 4 proposes that the Grand Lodge of California "establish officially the post of HISTORICAL LECTURER in the line
of all constituent Lodges under its jurisdiction" and that the filling of
such station be at the option of each Lodge. While your Committee on
Policy and General Purposes agrees wholeheartedly with the author of
the proposed re~olution that there is need for greater attention being
paid to our history and herita ge, we believe that this can be obtained
without the addition of another Lodge officer. The " line" of Lodge
officer service is amply long at present. The addition of another post
implies one more step (presumably a year in duration) in the time process of progression through the various officer stations. The dissemination of historical knowledge concerning Masonry should be the concern
of each Master of a Lodge. but it should be his decision as to how best
to do this. He can appoint a committee of any size, from one person
up, for this worthwhile purpose; he can designate a Brother as historian
for the Lodge; or he can even provide the information himself. In some
Lodges there may be one or more Brothers who are pa rticularly interested
and knowledgeable concerning Masonic History, and their talents should
be used. The establishment of a line office for such brethren should not
be necessary for the procurement of their specialized service. In order
to place the proposal before the Grand Lodge I move the adoption of
Resolution No. 4 and your Committee on Policy and General Purposes
recommends a no vote.
The Committees on Masonic History and on Masonic Education indi~
cated their concurrence in the recommendation.
A majority voted against the resolution.

PLACE OF SOCIAL MEETING OTHER THAN A
LODGE HALL-WHERE LIQUORS MAY BE SERVED
(5)

to whether or not Lodges and other Masonic organizations can hold
dinners, dinner dances and other social gatherings in hotels, restaurants.
clubs and similar locations, where intoxicants may and will be consumed.
This Resolution proposes to add to our Masonic Code, a section
to be numbered Section 324.2, which would permit any Masonic Lodge,
or any dependent organization, such as the Scottish Rite, York Rite
or the Shrine Temples to hold gatherings of a social nature in places
of public accommodation in or at which liquor, wine or beer is sold or at
which a bar is operated.
A second clause of this Resolution provides for the amendment of
Section 408 of the California Masonic Code by striking therefrom the
following language:
"nor shall any such liquors be used or served at any Masonic banquet or gathering".
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes is opposed to the
adoption of both or either part of Resolution No. 5.
We invite your attention to the report s ubmitted at the last session
of this Grand Lodge by the Committee on Jurisprudence. and concurred
in by the Committee on Policy and General Purposes. (See p.p. 224. 225
and 226 of the 1966 Proceedings)
This report did recommend that Grand Lodge relax to some extent
our existing law relative to control of the use of liquor at Masonic meetings. The vote on this proposal last year was less than the 5/ 6ths required to adopt it, and it was therefore carried over to this communication for action, and defeated. Resolution No. 5, which is now under
consideration, would relax our liquor controls even further.
We are deeply concerned about the effect on public opinion, and
the effect on many Master Masons, if this Grand Lodge should now
further relax the controls upon the use of intoxicants at Masonic gather~
ings. It is our unanimous opinion that the adoption of this Resolution
would dangerously relax those controls.
In ·o rder to bring this matter to the floor for your vote, I move the
adoption of Resolution No. 5. The Committee on Policy and General
Purposes recommendi a no vote.

To the. Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. o A. M . of California:
WHEREAS, there is a great de.al of confusion as to whether or not
Lodges and other Masonic organizations can hold dinners , dinner dances
and other meetings and gatherings of a social nature in hotels, restaurants, clubs, picnic grounds and similar locations, and as to whether or
not Masonic groups may follow the usual and generally accepted social
customs at such affairs; and
WHEREAS, prior to 1964 there were no restrictions on the holding
of such gatherings in the normal American way and there will be presented to this Grand Lodge at its 1967 Communication a proposed Section 324.2 of the California Masonic Code which is somewhat similar
to the Prohibition Amendment of the l 920's which proved to be unworkable and unenforceable and therefore was repealed by the American
people, and a substitute resolution should be adopted;
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED: That the following
section be added to the California Masonic Code:
Section 324.2. Social and other gatherings and meetings. A Masonic
Lodge, or an organization the prerequisite of membership wherein is
that a person be a Master Mason, may hold social gatherings, dinners,
dinner dances, picnics and other meetings of a social nature or other
social events in a hotel. restaurant, dining room, club, convention hall.
picnic area or other establishment or place in or at which liquor, wine
or beer is served or a bar is operated regardless of the ownership of
such premises; provided, however, that in the case of an open installation
of a Masonic Lodge, the Grand Master must first approve the location
as suitable to the solemnity of the installation ceremony, and provided
further that no liquor, wine or beer shall be served to members or guests
during such Lodge installation ceremony or in a Masonic Temple.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED: That Section 408 of the California Masonic Code be amended by deleting therefrom the following:
"nor shall any such liquors be used or served at any Masonic banquet
or gathering".
Respectfully submitted,
LEo E. ANDERSON, P .M .• No. 355

General Purposes.

SUSPENSION N.P.D. -PLURAL MEMBER
PRIOR NOTICE
(7)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M . of California:
Experience having proven that opportunity for membership retention would prevail were notice of intent to suspend for NPD received
by Lodge ( s) in which Plural Member is in good standing, following
revision is submitted;
Section 432-; (6) C.M.C. Insert after first sentence: "When nonpayment of dues is cause, such action however is to become effective
only after a sixty day prior Notice Of Intent To Suspend is issued to
other Lodge( s) in which member is enrolled, during which period, or
less, said Lodge( s ) is to contact member in effort to avoid automatic
suspension. In absence of said advance notice of intent, Lodge ( s) in
which member is in good standing is granted period not to exceed sixty
days after receipt of Grand Lodge office "Memo" for aforementioned
action. In either instance, automatic suspension is to be immediately com-

231

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 7 is concerned with plural members. If a plural member is suspended in one Lodge, he is thereby suspended in all other
Lodges to which he belongs.
Resolution No. 7 would require a Lodge that proposed to suspend
a member for non-payment of dues, shall first iss ue a sixty day prior
"Notice of Intent to Suspend" to all other Lodges in which the member
is enrolled.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes that this
resolution would be beneficial in that it would provide an additional
avenue for member retention.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a yes
vote.
The Committee on furispruden ce:
The purpose of the proposed resolution is to delay the suspension of
a multiple member for non-payment of dues for a period of sixty days, to
enable other Lodges of which he is also a member to contact him in an
effort to avoid suspension.
Your Commi~tee on Jurisprudence think that the purposes of the
proponent of the resolution will be served by the following amendment :
RESOLVED: That there be added to subdivision 6 of Section 432
of the California Masonic Code the following language:
"When non-payment of dues is the cause of suspension, such action
shall become effective only after a sixty-day prior Notice of Intent to
Suspend has been sent to every other Lodge in which the member holds
membership, during which period such other Lodge may contact the
member in an effort to avoid such suspension. If within said sixty-day
period such member has failed to obtain good standing in all Lodges
involved, he shall be suspended, and such suspension shall immediately
terminate his membership in all Lodges in this Jurisdiction".
We move the adoption of the resolution, without recommendation.
Adopted 5/6 vote.

The Committe e on Ritual:
The ritual for the Installatio n Service, adopted by this Grand Lodge
in 1946 and most recently revised in 1957 states in the instruction al
notes:
"A sufficient number of seats in the first row in the northeast corner
of the Lodge may be reserved for Past Masters of the Lodge."
This addendum to the instruction s governing the Installatio n Service
was adopted by this Grand Lodge at that time for the following reasons:
1. To provide, on a permissive basis, a seating arrangeme nt for the
P ast Masters (if group seating is desired) in an area where they could
best view the Ceremonie s of the Installatio n.
2. To accommod ate all of the Past Masters in a man ner consistent
with the physical limitations of the majority of Lodge rooms - many
Lodge rooms not having sufficient sea ts (or the capacity for seats) in the
East which could accommod ate all of the Past Masters present for the
Installatio n of Officers.
The invitation to seats in the E ast, referred to in the resolution, is a
part of the ritual of the opening ceremonies of every California Masonic
Lodge, and is intended as a proper courtesy to be accorded the Past
Masters. It should be noted, however, that in most instances that invitation is not accepted by the Past Masters present at the opening cere~
monies. Also. it should be noted that in a majority of instances Lodges
being opened for the purpose of installing its officers are opened at a
time earlier than the usual hour for opening and at a time when few. if
any. Past Masters are present. hence the Past Masters would not hear
any invitation to seats in the East.
Further, this invitation to Past Masters is made only at the opening
ceremonie s of a Tiled Lodge and during an open Installatio n the Lodge
is at refreshme nt.
Your committee, therefore. fully subscribin g to the desire to retain
uniformity in all phases of our ritual. according to the duties ascribed
to them by our Masonic Law, respectful ly submits the following points
for considerat ion:
1. During the open Installatio n the Lodge is at refreshme nt. therefore the invita tion to seats in the East no longer is apropos.
2. The Past Masters of the Constitue nt Lodges, having served well
and faithfully and having attained a position of respect and honor. should
have their presence a t the open Insta llation acknowled ged, a nd the ritual
now permits said acknowled gment by:
a. A provision for group seating in an area where all Past Masters
present can be accommod ated, regardless of the physical limitations for
seating in the East, as might well occur in the ma jority of lodge rooms.
This provision a lso allows for proper introducti on of the Past Masters.
b. Seating the Past Masters in the Northeast also provides sufficient
space for their ladies to be seated with them, rather than separating them.

3. The fundamen tal purpose of the Installatio n is to install the
Officers of the Lodge. duly elected and/ or appointed - the focal point
of the Installatio n to be upon the newly installed Master and his corps
of officers.

The Committe e on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 9 proposes that it shall be optional for the Past
Masters of a Lodge to be seated in the East during an open installatio n.
At present, the installatio n service for constituen t Lodges states that
Past Masters may be seated in the first row in the northeast corner of
the Lodge. Although the preamble of the proposed resolution acknowledges that the word "may" connotes permissive ness rather than compulsion, there has apparentl y been some applicatio n of the instruction
making it a requireme nt that the Past Masters be seated in the first row
in the northeast corner. While your Committe e on Policy and General
Purposes feels that any requireme nts or restriction s having to do with
a ceremony are properly the concern of the Grand Lodge Committee on
Ritual. we neverthele ss believe there is a point of general policy involved
in the proposal - namely that of constituen t lodge discretion in matters
of form that may necessaril y be dependent upon purely local or individual
Lodge situations or circumstan ces. If indeed there is at present a requir~­
ment that Past Masters must sit in one certain row in the Lodge, and m
that row alone, then we believe that the Grand Lodge instruction should
be. "Past Masters may be seated in the Lodge as the Master directs".
Such an instruction would provide the degree of local discretion which
we believe is the proper policy in such matters.
I. therefore, m'ove that proposed Resolution No. 9 be amended to
read as follows:
"Be it resolved that during the ceremony of installatio n the Past
Masters of a Lodge may be seated in the Lodge as the Master directs."
I now move that Resolution No. 9, as amended, be adopted and your
Committe e on Policy and General Purposes recommen ds a yes vote.
The amendmen t to the resolution was adopted.
A majority voted against the amended resolution .

MORAL QUALIFICATIO NS-APPLICAN TS FOR
DEGREES
(11)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. c A. M. of California:
WHEREAS. a felony is the offense and not the sentence for an
offense, and
WHEREAS. a person on a felony probation must have been convicted of a felony, and
WHEREAS. such terms as "youthful", "depravity", "viciousness",
and "lack of fundamental morals" are not defined in the California
Masonic Code. and
WHEREAS. Section 511-g was written in 1875 when a prison was
a place to punish an offender. and
WHEREAS. under present law, the function of a prison is not

238

239

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

only a place in which to punish but also a place where an attempt to
rehabilitate an offender is made, and
WHEREAS, a person who has been convicted of a felony, has
served his sentence, and has lived an upright life for a given number of
years may receive a pardon and have his record cleared and can legally
say he has never been convicted of a crime, and
WHEREAS, the sentence received for a particular crime is determined by the presiding judge and thus for the same crime one person
may be charged with a misdemeanor and his crime partner with a felony,
and
WHEREAS. Sections 511-h and 511-q of the California Masonic
Code are in direct contradiction with Section 511-o of said Code, and
WHEREAS. these sections of the California Masonic Code render it
almost impossible for the Master of a Lodge to determine if some applications for the Degrees of Masonry can be properly received, and
NOW. THEREFORE. BE IT RESOLVED . that Sections 511-g,
511-h. 511-o, 511-p and 511-q of the California Masonic Code be deleted, and a new section be added to be numbered 511.1 and entitled:
Moral Qualifications. This new section is to read as follows:
511.1 Moral Qualifications. A Lodge ma'Y properly receive an application for the Degrees of Masonry from an applicant who has been convicted of a crime which is morally wrong in itself. and it shall be the
du~y of the investigating Committee to determine the moral qualifications
of the applicant.
Respectfully submitted,
WILLIAM M. HEAD, P.M .. No. 777
WILLIAM K. HEAD, P.M .. No. 777
ERNEST R. BINSACCA, f. W., No. 777
LAWRANCE A. REED, S. W ., No. 777
PERCY H. DUNLAP, P.M .• No. 777
ROBERT W . DUNLAP, P.M., No. 777
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, and on Policy and General
Purposes.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution number eleven proposes a drastic change in our policy
as to the eligibility of men who have pleaded guilty or have been convicted of committing crimes. It would establish, if adopted, an "opendoor" policy making possible, to illustrate the extent the door of eligibility
would probably be opened, the receiving of a petition for the degrees
from one who at the time was a prison inmate.
Normally, this committee would comment on a proposal to so change
our policy; however you have adopted Recommendation No. 5 made
by the Grand Master that the Committee on Policy and General Purposes and the Committee on Jurisprudence study the entire subject of
eligibility of men who have been involved in criminal activity and to

propose legislation at the next communication which will more clearly
define our policy and establish guidelines.
Our committee feels it would be most unwise to anticipate that study
by adopting the drastic change proposed by this resolution.
To present the resolution to the Grand Lodge, I move the adoption
of resolution number 11.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends you
vote no.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
This resolution, which would make any convicted criminal eligible
to apply for the degrees of Masonry, goes beyond a mere change in the
Ordinances, and in our opinion encroaches on Dr. Mackey's Eighteenth
Landmark, viz. "the qualification of candidates for initiation".
It has always been a rule of Masonic law that a candidate must be
" under the tongue of good report", and this rule has been imbedded in
our ritual from time immemorial. Certain jurisdictions have expressly
declared it to be a landmark; and if so, it cannot be changed.
Many years ago, Grand Lodge approved a decision that applications
from persons under indictment should not be received until the charges
were cleared in court; and likewise that one who has served a term in
state prison is not under the tongue of good report.
It is true that distinctions have been made in the case of minors who
pleaded guilty to felony, but were granted probation, and distinctions
have also been made on the basis of misdemeanor versus felony. However, the latter distin~tion is confusing. A felony is defined by the California penal code as a crime punishable by death or imprisonment in
state prison; but if the crime is also punishable by fine or imprisonment
in a county jail, and the latter sentence is imposed, it is only a misdemeanor.
In 1957, in order to clarify the law, on recommendation of the Jurisprudence Committee, this Grand Lodge adopted the following rule:
"A person who has pleaded guilty or been convicted in the courts
of a crime which is morally wrong in itself is not eligible to apply for
the degrees of Masonry". ( 1957: 369-370)
This is the rule stated in section 511-o of the Code. It was not a
decision of the Grand Master; it was legislation adopted by five-sixths
vote of Grand Lodge. and should have been set forth in a new section
of the Code, not merely an annotation.
Subsequent decisions, involving crimes by minors. may be explained
on the basis that the accused either was not guilty of the crime charged.
or the act did not show lack of fundamental morals, or was within the
Juvenile Court ]aw, where there is no conviction of crime. These decisions are not, as proponents state, in direct conflict with section 511-o.
But in any event, the 1957 legislation is now the law of this Grand
Lodge.

240

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The proposed Resolution No. 11 would completely reverse this rule
and permit a Lodge to receive an application from a person "who has
been convicted of a crime which is morally wrong in itself". It would
open the doors of our Lodges to applications of persons who cannot be
"under the tongue of good report". It would, in our opinion, be in violation of the Landmarks.
Perhaps a different rule might apply to one who, under the procedures
of the state law for probation, rehabilitation and pardon, has been purged
of guilt, but that is not the question presented by this resolution.
Accordingly, we recommend that the resolution be not adopted.
A majority voted against the resolution.

qualified to receive the degrees, if such person shall reside, or have his

or have his business location, in territory within the concurrent jurisdic~

shall be that prescribed in cases of concurrent jurisdiction. (Former R.D.

The Committee on furisprudence:
The purpose of this resolution is to make a "business location" within
the jurisdiction of a Lodge equivalent to residence there, for purposes of
applications for the degrees. It proposes a departure from the timehonored rule which requires an applicant to reside in the vicinity of the
Lodge to which he applies, unless he secures a waiver of jurisdiction
from the Lodge in whose jurisdiction he does so reside.
In order to effectuate the purpose of the proponent of this resolution,
it will be necessary to amend sections 517, 518 and 522 of the California
Masonic Code. We do not think that section 524 should be amended.
since an applicant's business location within the jurisdiction of a Lodge
should not entitle that Lodge to grant a waiver.
We offer the following legislation to implement the resolution, using
the term "sole business location" in lieu of the term "business location."
RESOLVED: That sections 517, 518 and 522 of the California
Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:
Sec. 517. An applicant for the degrees must have been a
resident within the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge during twelve
months, and must have been a resident or have had his sole business location within the jurisdiction of the Lodge during six
months, next preceding the date of his application, except as
hereinafter provided.
Sec. 518. If two or more Lodges are located within the
corporate limits of any city. town or place, they shall have concurrent jurisdiction therein. Any of them can receive and act on
the application for degrees of a person who is a resident thereof
or has his sole business location therein, or of a person residing or
having his sole business location nearer thereto than to any other
place where a Masonic Lodge exists. Each of such Lodges has
separate jurisdiction over its own members, and concurrent jurisdiction over all Masons not members of one of them, who reside in
or have their business locations in such city. town or place, or
nearer thereto than to any other place where a Lodge exists, and
each shall within ten days after receipt of an application by the
Lodge notify such other Lodge or Lodges of any application it
may receive for degrees or affiliation or waiver of jurisdiction.
Sec. 522. Anything in these Ordinances to the contrary notwithstanding, without any waiver of any sort being sought or ob-

The Committee ort Finance:
There has been referred to the Committee on Finance, Resolution
No. 14 which would create life memberships for all Past Masters who
have attained twenty-five-year membership in this jurisdiction.
Although the purpose of this resolution appears to be meritorious,
we believe it would seriously reduce needed financial support to the
Grand Lodge and also to the constituent Lodges. In some cases it could
result in a complete financial crisis to certain Lodges.
A review of our membership records indicates that approximately
10,000 Past Masters would be eligible for life memberships the first
year. A resulting loss of financial support in the form of dues to the
constituent Lodges would occur, as well as a loss in per capita tax to
the Grand Lodge. We are aware of our financial loss in the continuing
drop in membership which, coupled with the reductions due to creatinglife memberships, would result in a serious loss of needed support fur
our Fraternity in general.
Lodges with large memberships may not be materially affected by
this proposal. However, ma ny smaller old Lodges will be in dire fi nancial
trouble because of the large proportion of living Past Masters to their
total membership.

Referred to Committee on Policy and General Purposes.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 17 proposes that an early announcement be sent to
Masters of Proclamations by the Grand Master concerning observances
to be held by the constituent Lodges.
The resolution offers no guidepost for the determination .of .what
would be deemed an early announcement. The prea.mble mere~y indicates
that some Masters are not sufficiently dose to their Secretaries to learn
of Proclamations before they are read at Stated Meetings. To ove~come
such lack of communication between the two officers of a particular
Lodge. the resolution would require separate notices to all Masters.
Customarily, annually. four Proclamations are issued by the Gran.d
Master : The DeMolay Week. the Public Schools Week. the Ma~on1c
Homes Endowment Month and the Constitution Month Proclamations.
Usually. these have been issued sixty or more days i~ advance. for reading at the Stated Meetings leading up to the proclaimed obser:ance: A
copy of each Proclamation. attested by the Grand Secretary, is mailed
by his office to each Secretary of the constituent Lodges.
.
The proponents of the resolution are to be congratulated on high-

250

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

lighting how important it is that Masters plan their trestleboards well
in advance. Your Committee on Policy, however, believes that there
are alternative solutions, more desirable than directive legislation, such
as this resolution. for apprising Masters of observances to be included
in their trestleboards.
Indeed, the determination of the time of each observance is now
governed by rules which make it possible for every Master to know long
before his election and installation when observances are to occur during
his term of office.
DeMolay Week. By long tradition. the Imperial Council of DeMolay
at Kansas City, Missouri, has established that DeMolay Week shall
start each year on Monday of the week in which March 18th falls.
DeMolay selects the week of March 18th because this was the day on
which Frank S. Land, founder of DeMolay, held his first meeting with
a group of boys to establish that great order. In support of DeMolay,
annually our Grand Lodge follows the same rule for determination of
DeMolay Week. Thus, next year DeMolay Week will be the week containing March 18th, which is the week beginning Monday, March 18,
1968.
Public Schools Week. During recent years our Committee on Public
Schools has recommended that Public Schools Week shall be the last
week in April, Monday through Friday, and this recommendation is
now being followed by our Grand Masters. Thus, next year Public
Schools Week will be the week of April 22, 1968.
Masonic Homes Endowment Month. Ever since May. 1939, it has
been the custom of this Grand Lodge to observe the month of May for
Masonic Homes Endowment Month. There is every reason to believe
that this custom will continue. Thus, next year the month of May. 1968,
will be Masonic Homes Endowment Month.
Constitution Month. Beginning in September, 1941. our Grand
Lodge has observed the month of September as Constitution Month,
September 17, 1787, having been the date of adoption of our Nation's
Constitution. Thus, the month of September will, in all likelihood, continue to be Constitution Month.
There are being distributed to all Lodges during this Communication newly designed Lodge Manuals containing many guideposts for
Lodge officers. The Table of Contents includes sections on Public
Schools, Constitution Observance, Masonic Education and Endowment,
and several other subjects. In the section on Public Schools there appears
the following instruction for the month of November:
"Chairman of the Grand Lodge Committee on Public Schools notifies
Lodges of the dates and theme of Public Schools Week. Lodges should
make sure that local public school officials are correctly informed. The
date will be the last week in April which includes Monday through
Friday."

Your Committee on Policy understands that forthcoming pages for
the Lodge Manual will contain similar guideposts for other observanc~s
and is firmly of the opinion that through the Lodge Manual Masters will
have available far better notice and knowledge of observances to be
scheduled than possible by means of the early announcement proposed
by Resolution No. 17.
To place the resolution before you, I therefore move adoption of
Resolution No. 17 and, on behalf of the Committee on Policy. recommend a no vote.

Referred to Committees on Polioy and General Purposes, and on
Public Schools.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes to which was referred Resolution No. 18, reports as follows:
This resolution would command the Grand Master to issue an order,
edict, "or whatever it takes" to cause all organizations meeting in Ma-sonic Temples "to be dark during the five-day Public Schools Week."
The proponents recite as the reason for adopting the resolution that
presently attendance at Public Schools Week observances is being decreased because Masonic affiliated organizations such as "the three youth
groups and Eastern Star" occasionally hold meetings during that week.
While this Committee finds it regrettable if all Masonic affiliated
groups are not giving their support and hearty cooperation to the appropriate observance of Public Schools Week, we believe such instances
can better be corrected by conferences between the Masters of the Lodges
involved or the Inspectors of the particular Masonic Districts and the
officers of the affiliated groups than by closing the doors of our Temples
to them throughout the five days of the week, whether or not their meetings happen to fall on the day or night of the observance. Furthermore,
there are Masonic Temples in which groups such as churches and fraternal orders, having no connection whatever with Masonry, meet regularly and it seems questionable whether our Grand Master should issue
such an order or edict as to those organizations. In effect, the resolution
attempts to compel all other organizations-whether Masonic affiliated
or not-to join with us in observances of Public Schools Week. In our
opinion this resolution is unnecessary and unwise. We are authorized to
state that the Committee on Public Schools concurs in our conclusion ..
In order to place the resolution before Grand Lodge, I move the
adoption of Resolution No. 18. The Committee recommends a no vote.
A majority voted against the resolution.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes :
This resolution proposes that a filing fee of $35.00 be required for
each resolution submitted to this Grand Lodge to help defray the cost
of producing and distributing the resolutions.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, while recognizing
the purpose of the proponent of this resolution to discourage the filing
of frivolous and poorly conceived resolutions, is perfectly convinced
that the free submission of ideas and proposals for the betterment of
Masonry lies at the very heart of our democratic process and that the
protection of this right in the representatives of the Craft must be continued.
Under Section 104 of the Code, it is provided that "The transaction
of business in Grand Lodge shall be upon written resolutions and reports." Consequently, any burden or limitation upon the right of a member of Grand Lodge to file such a resolution or resolutions as he desires
to present would be a serious limitation of the process of transacting
the business of this Body-and this, to your Committee, would be
wholly undesirable as a matter of policy.
In order to get the resolution before Grand Lodge, I move the adoption of the resolution, but the Committee on Policy and General Purposes
recommends a no vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Be it now resolved that Section 104 of the California Masonic Code
be amended to provide as follows:
The transaction of business in Grand Lodge shall be upon
written resolutions and reports. All such resolutions must be
presented to the Grand Secretary at least ninety days prior to
the commencement date of the next Annual Communication and
shall be accompanied by a fee of thirty-five dollars; provided,
however, that this time restriction and fee charge shall not apply
to emergent matters which may be presented and considered at
any time upon consent of five-sixths vote of the members present.
and provided further that this time restriction and fee charge shall
not apply to resolutions which form a part of the report of a com-

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

255

mittee and do not purport to amend the law of this Grand Lodge.
Be it further resolved tha t section 781 be amended as follows:
Any proposed amendment to these ordinances shall be presented by written resolution or recommendation to the Grand
Secretary at least ninety days prior to the commencement date
of the next Annual Communication and shall be accompanied by
a fee of thirty-five dollars; provided, however, that this time restriction and fee charge shall not apply to emergent matters which
may be presented and considered at any time upon consent of
five-sixths vote of the members present. All such resolutions and
recommendations shall be referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence which shall report theron before a vote is taken. When
the report of said Committee is presented, the vote shall be taken
on the amendment.
We move the adoption of this resolution and recommend a no vote.
A majority voted against the resolution.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This resolution proposes an amendment to the C.M.C. to permit
constituent Lodges to appropriate not to exceed 5 % of their gross annual
revenue for the purpose of providing scholarships to worthy high school
graduates.
The purpose and intent of this proposal is both obvious and commendable. Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes is of the
opinion. however, that the adoption of Recommend ation No. 8 of the
Grand Mas ter on the proposed creation of a multi-purpo se foundation to
"administer a flexible program of student aid" - the present consideration of Resolution No. 21 - would be premature and unnecessary .
To bring the matter before this Body, the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes moves the adoption of Resolution No. 21 and recommends a no vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Be it now resolved that the California Masonic Code be amended by
the creation of a new section numbered Section 411.1 which shall provide
as follows:
Each Lodge may appropriate funds from its treasury to worthy
high school graduates within its jurisdiction for scholarship purposes.
The recipients shall be selected by a committee appointed by the
Master for this purpose. Said recipients shall be selected without
regard to race. creed or color. The amount of money so appropriate d
s hall not exceed five per cent ( 5 % ) of the gross annual revenue of
the Lodge.
Be it further resolved that Section 412y shall be deleted.
We move the adoption of this resolution but make no recommenda tion.
A majority voted against the resolution .

CREATE RESERV E FUND BY GRAND LODGE FOR BOARD S OF RELIEF
(23)
To the Most Worshipf ul Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREA S, to relieve the distressed , is a duty incumbent upon all
Masons. Far too many Lodges have said "We take care of our own"
and feel secure in the belief that their obligation ends there;
WHEREA S, Masonry today is a universal organizati on and has no
boundarie s. Every Lodge in California, without exception, should contribute in some degree to the support of our Boards of Relief;
WHEREA S. every Lodge which is a member of one of our Boards
of Relief pays an annual per capita tax to maintain these boards;
WHEREA S. these Boards of Relie f are primarily to assist the Sojourners who not only come from Lodges outside our state. but from
Lodges in California which are not members of a Board of Relief. and
which do not assist these Boards in any way;
WHEREA S, the Lodges which are members of a Board of Relief
are subsidizin g non-partic ipating Lodges. In order to meet increased
costs, it now becomes necessary for some Boards of Relief to increase
the per capita tax;
WHERE AS, some of these costs should be borne by all of the
Lodges in our jurisdictio n.
THEREF ORE. BE IT RESOLV ED, that the Grand Lodge set up
a Reserve Account of $I 0,000.00 for Boards of Relief. with the proviso
that;

l. All Boards of Relief operate as they have in the past and maintain
their present per capita tax, with no major increase in present
operationa l costs.
2. Any deficit in operationa l costs (expenses over per capita income)
be drawn from the Board of Relief Reserve.
WHEREA S. BE IT FURTHE R RESOLV ED. that any saving be
placed in this reserve account and that all the above be subject to annual
audit, as provided for in the rules and Regulatio ns relating to Boards
of Relief.
Respectfu lly submitted ,
GEORGE C. ComrnEGE s. P.M .. No. 349
Referred to Committe e on Finance and to the Board of Control.
The above resolution was withdrawn by its proponent .

completed a Will leaving entire Esta te to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund, at his demise.
Fraternally yours,
HARO LD G. EARLY, M., No. 380
R. D . WoLF, P.M., No. 380
DENE C. CooK, P.M., No. 380
Referred to the Committees on Jurisprudence. on Finance, and to
the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Resolution No. 25 was referred to your Committee on Jurisprudence,
It proposes that entrants into the Masonic Homes should not be required
~o divest themselves of all their properties, but rather merely will their
estates to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund. This is a matter entirely wtihin the province of the Board of Trustees of the Masonic
Homes. We do point out, however, that a will is subject to change by
the testator at any time before his death. A person can make as many
wills as he desires and the last will is the only one effective. Thus there
is no assurance that the Masonic Homes will receive anything from a
recipient of the Homes' services regardless of his earthly wealth. We
recommend a no vote.
The Committee on Finance and the Board of Trustees of the Masonic
Homes concurred in the recommendatio n.
A majority voted against the resolution.
